There being a constitutional representation, the Grand
Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with music by the
Grand Organist, assisted by a quartette and prayer by the
Grand Chaplain.
The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address
to the Grand Lodge "as follows :
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
As is not unusual in human affairs, events wholly unanticipated
have, during the year now drawing to a close, in large measure
rendered impracticable the pursuit of plans for the administration of
the stewardship entrusted to my keeping, the fruition of which, it was
thought, would bring results of bcmefit to the Craft; and, this account
is submitted with a keen appreciation of your charitable indulgence and
sincerest thanks to my associate officers and the members of the several
committees, to whose conscientious and unselfish labors we are indebted
for the avoidance of those sins of omission or commission, which, but
for their efforts would have been the natural and inevitable result of
my own shortco:nings and necessarily extensive absence from the State.
The Fraternity has progressed in a manner which affords the
utmost satisfaction: 3,971 Masons have been added to the rolls by
initiation, restoration and affiliation, while 1,633 have been lost by death
and otherwise, leaving a net gain of 2,338, and a total membership at
the present time of 41,007.
Dispensations for the formation of Lodges have been granted as
follows:
October 22, 1908, Bay View Lodge, Oakland, Cal.
February 8, 1909, Brawley Lodge, Brawley, Cal.
February 11, 1909, Yerba Buena Lodge, Oakland, Cal.
March 26, 1909, Glendora Lodge, Glendora, Cal.
May 25, J9(9, Meneta Ledge, Meneta, Cal.
June 28, 19C9, Burbank Ledge, Burbank, Cal.
All of the eleven Lodges chartered at our last Communication were,
in due time, regularly constituted and started on their respective careers

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

•

under auspices auguring well for their continued usefulness in the
great cause of human advancemen't.
The substantial progress in our development, source of pride and
gratification though it is, must also serve as an admonition of increased
responsibility. The world at large demands, and rightly so, a course
of personal conduct upon the part of members of our venerable organization in ke.eping with its high ideals and exalted station as a moral
institution. Each individual is responsible for the maintenance of the
honor and reputation of the Craft, and he who falters or fails in the
iiue performance of this duty, brings discredit, not only upon himself,
but upon each of the more than 40,000 Masons in the State, and
humiliation into the body of each of our Lodges.
• By the ·process of elimination, the careful performance of duty
on the part of investigating committees, and the judicious use of the
black ball the increase in our ranks has been in keeping with its
traditions.' It is not improper, however; to call attention to the regrettable fact that there has been brought to our knowledge instances
of retrogression on the part of Lodges, occasioned by internecine difficulties and factional qivision, reaching such a degree of bitterness as
that any proposal for membership advanced by one side is invariably
forestalled by senseless and apparently vicious opposition upon the other.
The black ball is purely a defensive weapon, to be used only in
the fulfillment of a solemn duty to prevent invasion by those unworthy
of Masonic association; and th~ Mason who, through motives of selfishness or cowardice, or for any other reason, fails to perform that duty
upon proper occasion, is guilty of the grossest violation of his obligation. Equally reprehensible, however, is the conduct of any brother
who, for the purpose of venting personal spleen or rendering effective
a factional difference, will, protected by the secrecy which Masonic
association affords, strWce from the dark an unsuspecting and innocent
v1ct1m. There is as little room in our Fraternal household for the
coward as there is for the knave; each is equally an object for the
contempt of "right-thinking men, and it is to be hoped that the conduct
complained of will be so frowned upon by the fraternity at large as to
render its continued existence impossible.
NECROLOGY.
Enjoying, as we have, with due appreciation, the bounteous blessings
of an All Wise and beneficent Providence, we have also been made ·to
realize that "in the midst of life we are in death." The Grim Destroyer
has stricken some of the noblest and most illustrious of those great
and stu·r dy characters, whose accomplishments form the corner stone
of Masonic history in California, and whose lives have been a guide
and inspiration to us all.

9

At the last Communication we received from our distinguished
brother and beloved friend, Reuben Hedley Lloyd, the sad intelligence
that his affliction prevented advancement from Deputy Grand Master
to the highest office within our gift; on March 10, 1909, Death beckoned,
and a great soul was called unto its own.
On March 26, 1909, the Silent Messenger laid his chilling hand
upon that sublime exemplar of Masonic virtue, Past Junior Grand
Warden Jacob Hart Neff. It will indeed be difficult for us to realize
that that devoted worker will no more be found in his accustomed
place, giving to the Fraternity the benefit of his advice and counsel.
Great Mason, sincere and true friend, patriotic, upright and honored .
citizen; constant exemplar of those homely and simple virtues which
demonstrate that the creature is indeed made in the image of his Great
Creator, the world is better for his having lived; with the pangs of
parting there comes to us a feeling of gratitude for the value and
inspiration of his noble example...
He was:
"One who never turned his back, but marched breast forward,
Never doubted clouds would break,
Never dreamed, though right were worsted, wrong would
triumph,
Held we fall to rise, are baffled to fight better, sleep to wake."

affairs, but the impress of his influence during the time of his service
remained for a long period after his retirement from active Masonic life.

which in many instances have been felt far beyond the boundaries of

MASONIC HOME.
Oi)t: ·Of the first and most irnpQrtant matters requiring att~rition was
the Masonic Home at Decato. The board of trustees app_ointe.d. pur,
suant to your authorization, . consl'stliig ~f Past Grand Master' Wells,
P~st Master Wm. H. Waste, Past Grand Master Thomas Flint and
Past Masters Elmer E. Stone and Ralph :Low, promptly convened and

10

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

formally organized. The special and extensive judicial and public
experience of the two first named peculiarly qualified them to examine
into and aid in the determination of the many and important questions
presented for consideration. The technical knowledge of Brother Stone,
known as he is throughout the entire country as one of the most
capable institutional men within its borders, has been of ·the greatest
assistance, and the wide and extensive business experience and sound
judgment of Brothers Flint and Low rounded out a committee which
for ability and fitness, could not well have been excelled. Its labcirs, a~
may be readily imagined, have been most arduous and engrossing, and
attended with peculiar difficulty. Petty complaints from residents have
been investigated with patient consideration, and the great and farreaching questions of general administration and management have
been given the most careful, deliberate and painstaking attention. In
their deliberations they have naturally not always been of one mind and
upon important questions their opinions have widely differed. Good
and able men and Masons that they are, however, these differences
have never in the slightest particular been attended by feeling or friction,
and when a majority once voiced its judgment the entire board, with
one accord and a 111ost hearty unity of effort, has proceeded to carry
that judgment into effect.
· We shall never realize the extent of their individual and collective
sacrifice in behalf of the Fraternity in a most perplexing and difficult
situation, and it is appropriate at this time and by this means, to convey
to them expressions of personal obligation as well as to testify to the
inestimable .value of their services. They will make a detailed presentation of the situa tion, and their recommendations will I am sure be
given respectful attention and weighty consideration, as' the deliber;tely
formed conclusions of brethren of t'Pie highest character and attainments, who have given to the matters involved the.i r best efforts.
The . water supply of the Home had become practically depleted,
there bemg absolutely none for fire protection, and an entire insufficiency for even bathing purposes ; the septic tank was found to be
seriously defective and a menace to the health of the residents; all of
the buil~ings were in need of repairs, especially plumbing and painting ;
the heatmg apparatus was deficient and wasteful in fuel consumption ;
hospital facilities were entirely inadequat~ and without opportunity for
isolation. Notwithstanding heavy expenditures necessitated by these
conditions, the Home has been administered upon considerably less
!han the amount appropriated for its uses and its efficiency greatly
improved.
Brother Edwards· relinquished his post as superintendent and the
Board was required to employ a new matron and superintendent.
The Special Committee, consisting of Brothers Valentine Plum
Owen, MacLafferty, and Billings, duly organized and proceeded vigor~

11

ously with the problem of determining, in co-operation with the board
of trustees, a plan for future administration. It has been most painstaking and conscientious in its labors, the i:esult of which will be presented in due course. To that committee, individually and collectively,
it is also proper to express sincerest appreciation and gratitude. The
difficulties were great and problems delicate, and its efforts will, I have
no doubt, throw valuable light upon the matters requiring your consideration.
Extensive inquiry and investigation satisfied the committee, the
board, and such of the Gran·d Officers as could be consulted in reference
thereto, that it was essential to the well being of all of the residents
of the Home that some system of segregating the aged and infirm from
the children, and ultimately the boys from the girls, be devised. Various
methods of accomplishing that result were considered, including the
construction of a new and independent building on the Decoto property.
Inadequate water supply, however, independent of the expense involved,
seemed to render such course impossible.
Additional hospital facilities were also deemed essential, including
a provision for necessary medical and surgical conveniences and appropriate means for the isolation of those whose illness might render such
course appropriate.
In this state of affairs, in February last, matters were brought to
my attention which convinced me that separation of the children from
the male adults was not only desirable, but imperatively necessary, whatever the difficulties or expen.se involved in accomplishing that end.
The Board was advised of my views in the premises and directed
to proceed with such segregation, which, of course, could only be
accomplished by the construction of a new building upon some part of
the premises at Decoto remote from the present quarters, or by securing
quarters elsewhere.
Additional buildings could not be considered without augmentation
of the water supply. Experts reported that the Home property was
without the area of water bearing gravel, and that the expense of boring
for water would be from ten thousand to thirty thousand dollars, with
no .assurance of success. The only alternative was to build a pipe line,
·about five miles long, from the main of the Spring Valley Water
Company, at an expense of approximately twenty-five thousand dollars.
Assuming adequate water supply, buildings and equipment sufficient for
the purpose of segregation would have involved an outlay of from
twenty to thirty' thousand dollars, making necessary a total expenditure
of anywhere from thirty to sixty thousand dollars.
While these matters were being canvassed Brother John F . Hughes,
president of the· Southern California Masonic Home, inquired of me
as to the extent to which the Grand Lodge would go in extending
financial aid to that institution. While not presuming to speak for the

l

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Fraternity at larg~, he was advised that it was contrary to my conception of Masonic policy for the Grand Lodge to make further contribu!ion to the maintenance of an institution in whose management it was
not the controlling, if not the only factor. Shortly thereafter the board
of trustees of that institution, because of their inability to accomplish
the establishment of an endowment adequate to maintain their Home
proposed turning th~ property owned by it over to this body. Certai;
restrictions and conditions having been attached to the offer, it wa,,
declined; but, later, an unconditional proposition was made with the
suggestion that the contractual obligations of that institution, consisting
of its agreement, for a consideration, to maintain and provide for
certain of the persons (two in number) resident in its Home at San
Gabriel, be assumed.
In view of the imperative necessity of segregation, as hereinabove
indicated, and in consideration of the insurmountable difficulties ln tne
way of accomplishing that result, through any utilin.tion of the property at Decato, the proposition was, on March 19, 1909, accepted and
segregation ordered by me, with the full belief that within a comparatively short space of time arrangeµ:ients would be made for transporting either the children or the old people from Decato to San
Gabriel. A transfer of title could not be accomplished without judicial
p"roceedings. After some c-0nsiderable delay, and during my absence
from the S.tate, the Southern California Masonic Home Association
commenced such proceedings. On my return it developed that by
order of court it was directed that the property be transferred to me,
.and, being advised that the acceptance of a· conveyance in the manner
directed would complicate the title, the deed was not delivered.
The Southern California Home Association, with the c~nsent of
practically its entire membership, and without opposition, authorized
the transfer, and it was suggested that the proceedings which had been
taken in the Superior Court of Los Angejes County should be vacated
and set aside, possession of the property assumed by our Board of
Trustees, deferring the formal steps necessary to transfer title until
this Crand Lodge should specify the mam!er in which it desires the title
transferred. All of thes.e matters .will be submitted in detail b; the
Board, together with a recommendation as to the proper method of procedure. They will require careful and studious consideration by men
learned in the law, and upon their satisfactory solution depend matters
of the utmost moment to the Fraternity. I have requested Past Grand·
Master Charles L. Patton, Brother Charles Albert Adams and Grand
Orator Benj. F. Bledsoe to investigate and recommend the proper course
to be pursue.d.
When instructions were given that segregation should be promptly
brought about, the Board wa~ requested to make careful investigation
as to which class o_f re~idents should be removed from Decoto. After

full inquiry, a determination was reached that the Home in Southern
California was better adapted to the care and maintenance of the
children.
In the latter part of August I was advised that the Southern Home
Association, relying upon the assumption that my direction would be
carried into effect by the first of May, had become seriously embarrassed
ip its efforts to carry on its home after that date, and the Deputy Grand
Master was advised of my views in the premises, and I requested prompt
adjur.tment of the difficulties, w~th the result that the children were
removed' to the Home at San Gabriel.
The Board of Trustees has been criticised for the action taken. I
desire to state in the most emphatic manner that such criticism is misplaced, in that everything done has been pursuant to my direction, after
conference and the most serious and deliberate consideration, ·aod if
anyone is to be criticised therefor it is myself and not the Board. For
myself, I,. must state with equal emphasis that no considerations of
policy, convenience, fear, favor, finance or apprehension of criticism
were permitted to interfere with the performance of what was deemed
to be a solemn. duty; I acted in accordance with a conscientious conviction, which would prompt similar action under the same circumstances
were the matter before me at this moment. I was profoundly con. vinced that the morals of those whose characters we have undertakerl
to mould were involved; and my conception of my obligations as a man
and Mason, not only to those children, but to you, required that the
segregation be accomplished at the earliest possible moment.
In order to assure myself that my own determination was correct
and in accordance with our duty to the children involved, all the Past
Grand .Masters available and numerous brethren throughout the State
were conferred with, and the consensus of opinion was in favor of
prompt segregation. Viewing the matter in retrospect, I repeat with
emphasis my conviction as to the propriety of the action taken, and
assume entire responsibility therefor.
As heretofore indicated, the Board has labored hard and consistently, under adverse conditions and most trying circumstances, having in view but one purpose, and that the performance of fraternal
duty and the fulfillment of Masonic obligations. Personal considerations have been absolutely ignored and disregarded, and any suggestion
that any member. thereof was prompted by selfish interest or individual
preferment is most cruel and unwarranted. Masons like those who
comprise the Boar<i d-0 not .pursue personal ends over the heads of
innocent and helpless. charges o( the Fraternity.
With refer-ence to the so-called farm and the operation thereof at
the Decoto Home, a misconception has existed which, in justice to those
brethren who have heretofore labored so assiduously on the Board of
·T rustees, should be· corrected. It has been generally understood that

the farm has been a source of constant and consistent loss, but it

portion devoted to the Home itself and to the stables, vegetable gardens,
etc., and the more or less dry hills, too high for cultivation. This has
not interfered with producing the articles above mentioned, but has
avoided the hazards arid disadvantages of long distance farming.

&PECIAL COMMUNICATIONS, CORNER STONES, ETC.
The Grand Lodge has been specially convened on numerous occa·
sions during the year to officiate at the laying of corner stones and
dedication of Masonic and public buildings, a list of which has been
prepared and will appear in the published proceedings. These frequent
invitations from municipal, school and other public authorities to
officiate at ceremonies of this character, are most assuredly a source of
pride and gratification to us all, for they demonstrate that our insti- ·
tution is regarded as an important factor in the community at large,
whose influence is recognized as a force in the great moral uplift of the
human family.
In accordance with what was considered the appropriate course to
be pursued under such circumstances, there has been deposited with the
local lodge most directly concerned in the several corner stone ceremonies the instrument presented as a souvenir of the occasion, there
to remain as a memento of an ausI>icious event, emblematic of the
spread of that cement which unites us into one sacred band or society.
ITALIAN RELIEF.
On the 30th day of December, 1908, the Island of Sicily was visited
by a terrible earthquake. Realizing the debt of gratitude due by our
own State to all of the jurisdictions of the world f~r the prompt response to the cry which went up when California was stricken, the
Grand Master of Italy was instructed to draw to the extent of $1,500
for relief, and the lodges throughout the State were authorized to
raise an additional relief fund. The total contributions aggregated the
sum of $4,868.50; $2,500 has been remitted and a balance of $2,368.50
remains in the hands of the Grand Secretary. Some direction should
be given by this body as to the disposition to be made· thereof. To
return the same to the several lodges from which the contributions were
rrceived would be difficult and probably not desired, and it is suggested

· OLD REPORTS.
Attention has, on previous 'occasions, been directed to the fact that
our entire library, including a large supply of reports of proceedings
from the .foundation of this Grand Lodge, was destroyed in the conflagration of 1906, with the result that few, if any, complete sets of
such reports are available for the use of the Grand Master. In order,
in a measure at least, to supply the deficiency, and to avoid the almost
prohibitive expense of reprinting, a circular letter was sent to the various
lodges of the jurisdiction, requesting that any ~xtra volumes of the
reports in their possession be sent to the Grand Secretary. This has
resulted, as will be reported to you in detail by the latter, in the reception of"a considerable number of odd volumes and a few full sets of reports; some means should be evolved whereby these may be rebound
and made available for future use. In such rebinding much matter
may be eliminated and the volumes consolidated.
MANUAL.
It is proper to draw attention to the state of Masonic Law in this
jurisdiction. 'i'here are numerous conflicting decisioos upon various subjects, and the form of the Manual is such that Masters may be pardoned
for failing to discover the conflicts. In my opinion the decisions should
be topically digested so that all of the law upon a given subject may
. be found at one place and under one head.
This suggestion is made with the fullest appreciation of the extremely able and careful manner in which Brother Anderson has performed the labor involved in preparing the volume bearing his name.
As the edition of that work has become practically exhausted, however,
further publication in the form above recommended would, I think, add
to the value of his work.
DECISIONS.
Numerous requests have been made for opinions upon mooted
questions of Masonic law. Many of these have been answered by a
simple reference to the provision of the Constitution or to decisions
digested in the Manual, which could have been located by the inquirer
with less effort than was involved in correspondence. To decisions of
that character no special reference has been made; all of those involving
matters of interest and consequence have been digested and submitted
for the scrutiny and consideration of the Committee on Jurisprudence,

16

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

and time, space and possible confusion will be saved by leaving those
matters until the report of that committee is presented.
Some of the questions propounded have suggested the necessity for
legislation, which are here referred to.
1.

CONCURRENT JURISDICTION OF LODGES.

As the State becomes more thickly populated, and particularly in
and about what are popularly known as the Bay Counties, and the
centers of population in southern California, numerous small communities are springfog up and growing with great rapidity, in most of
which one of the first steps in town development has been the· formation
of a Masonic lodge. In some ihstances the boundaries of these separate
incorporated municipalities are contiguous; in others the space between
them ver:ir limited and settled to a degree almost equal to that of the
incorporated tei:ritory itself. Under the latter circumstances much confusion and no little friction could be avoided if a discretion were vested
in the Grand Master to declare concurrent jurisdiction similar to that
which exists in cities having more than one Mas;nic lodge.

2.

RESTORATION OF NON-RESIDENT SUSPENDED FOR NON-PAYMENT OF DUES.

Suggestion has also been made for an amendment to our laws in
reference to the matter of restoration of one who has been suspended
for oon-payment o• dues, the !farticular question having arisen with
reference to a brother who for seventeen years had been under suspension, and during most of that time a non-resident of the State. The
proposition ;was advanced that the lodge from which he had been
suspended could not entertain an application for restoration without
infringing upon the jurisdictiQn of the Grand Lodge of the State in
which he now resides. With this suggestion I found myself unable to
agree, holding that the petition should be presented to the lodge from
which suspension took place, accompanied by payment of dues·, as
required by the Constitution. Should this decision be sustained, no
legislation, it seems to me, will be necessary, unless it be your desire to
specifically authorize the lodge in which. the restoration is sought in its
discretion to remit all or p~rt of the dues accruing between the time of
suspension and the ·application for Testoration, regardless of the financial
ability of the brother to pay the same. Should, however, this decision
be not concurred in, it will Jie necessary to adopt some legislation in
otder that a brother suspended (probably under adverse circumstances),
because of inability to pay his dues, wlio removes from the State, may
"llDi; be forever debarred from again entering the Fraternity ; because,
manifestly, a petition to a foreign lodge by a brother under suspension
would receive scant consideration.

17

CONFERRING DEGREES UPON CANDIDATES FOR LODGES IN OTHER
JURISDICTIONS.

It is imperatively necessary that some regulation be adopted governing the matter of conferring degrees by lodges within this jurisdiction
on behalf of lodges of other jurisdictions in which a candidate has been
elected to receive them, and vice versu.. Under the present practice,
such degrees are usually conferred pursuant to a formal request direct
to or from the lodge in this jurisdiction to or from a lodge in another
jurisdiction. This affords no insurance whatever against correspondence
with clandestine bodies. It is suggested th~t all such requests should be
made through the Grand Masters and Grand Secretaries of the respective jurisdictions. · This would insure the sanctity of our correspondence
and protection against imposition and invasion.

4.

PROCEEDINGS AGAINST MASONS CONVICTED OF CRIME.

Upon examination of the rolls appended to the. report of the last
annual proceedings I was most chagrined to observe the name of a man
convicted of a felony under the laws o f the United States and who has
but recently completed service of sentence in the penitentiary. Were it
not for the fact that as attorn~y for the Government I prosecuted the
case, I would have directed proceedings loo1dng to the preferring of
charges and a Masonie trial.
The attitude of Free Masonry as an institution, irrevocably committed to enforcement of and obedience to the law, is so well known,
and has been so frequently and emphatically declared by this Grand
Lodge that there is no possible excuse for any. lodge or o~er thereof
in failing to give proper attention to one who has so far debased himself
as to steal moneys entrusted to his care, or do any other a11t violative of
a solemn trust which, in all probability was the more readily imposed
because of membership in a Masonic Lodge.
To guard against such lapses, however, the law. should be so
amended as to make it the imperative duty of the appropriate officer
of a lodge whenever a member has been convicted of a crime involving
moral turpitude to prefer charges against the person so convicted and
press to conclusion a tr'.al thereof, and prescribe sev~re penalty for
failure so to do. If the conviction has been erroneous the error will be
readily. discovered-if correct, the criminal should find no abiding place
in Free Masonry.

Immediately after adjournment, feeling that a serious responsibility

It further comes to our notice that there are in those Islands

CLANDESTINE "MASONRY."
Some attention has been attracted by the so-called clandestine
lodges, a few of which have sprung into existence in or ahout the city
of San Francisco, and abortive attempts at the organization of which
occurred in Los Angeles and in the city of Oakland. Like most things
of base conception; they have, upon being brought to the light, languished, and languishing will soon die. The promoters are frauds and
adventurers, compared to whom Benedict Arnold might be reckoned a
patriot and Judas Iscariot a Christian martyr. They and their efforts
have been treated with that silent contempt which was their due, and,
while we have been advised that, in a few instances innocent and unsuspecting men have been imposed upon, paying money for so-called
initiation under what must have been false pretenses, in the main it is
not believed that their efforts have entitled them to serious consideration.
In this connection it is highly appropriate that specific mention be
made of the service rendered the community at large by Officers Brown,
Greene and Peterson of the Oakland police, who, hearing of a meeting
to be held for the purpose of drumming up material for one of those
bogus organizations, appeared thereat, advised those assembled of the
character of the institution and gave to the promoters a limited time
within which to seek a different climate. The invitation was promptly
accepted and several unsuspecting victims probably saved from imposition.
After conference with the Deputy Grand Master, the Grand Secretary, and others in authority, it was deemed proper to send to the
lodges of the State, with instructions that the same should be carefully
read at three successive meetings, a notice, warning against imposters,
and setting forth in detail the plain and specific mandates of our law
in the matter of Masonic recognition. If Masters and Master Masons
would exercise even ordinary precaution they could never be imposed
upon; but, unfortunately, because of our security~ we are all at times
inclined to be more or less careless. This became painfully evident
through the conduct of certain members of one of the lodges who had
been advised that a resident of their town had received the degrees of
Masonry at San Francisco. Notwithstanding this should have apprised
them that a violation of one of the fundamental Masonic laws had taken
place, the brothers mentioned, out of the goodness of their hearts, discovering that the imposter was not proficient in the arts of the Craft, proceeded to enlighten him therein, discovering to their own and our chagrin,

20

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

that he was not a Mason at all, but had been the victim of some sort of
spurious ceremony at the city of San Francisco. It was seriously suggested that for this infraction punishment should be meted out to those
responsible therefor. But it occurred and still occurs to me that the
humiliation suffered by the brethren participating therein was greater
punishment than anything which could be imposed by law.

It could also arrange some uniform style of receipt and diploma with
such possible legal establishment as to make forgery or false .use thereof
a crime.

GENERAL CONFERENCE.
Clandestine Masonry has from time to time received the attention
of Grand Masters in almost every jurisdiction of the United States·
this has suggested the great desirability of formulating some plan of
general and c_oncerted action by all of the Grand Bodies of the country,
whereby a umform system of receipts and identification could be adopted
which would insure against the carelessnes's or neglect of Masters and
members. While this matter was under discussion, there was received
from Past Grand Master Mikels of Indiana and Grand Secretary Williams of Rhode Island, suggestions that this Grand Lodge delegate
some one or more of its members to attend a general American conference, looking to that end, and withirt the past few days invitation has
been received from Grand Master Shryock, of Maryland, to attend the
dedication of the new Masonic Temple in Baltimore on November 17th
next, on which occasion it is anticipated that Grand Masters from
numerous jurisdictions will be present and this and other subjeets
considered. (The correspondence is ·submitted herewith.)
Sue!) a conference would be a most decided step, and it is hoped
this Grand Lodge may see its way clear to authorize participation
therein.
There are numerous matters to which serious and careful consideration by such a gathering would be of great benefit to the Craft.
In the first place, there is, a wide divergence of view upon the
matter of jurisdiction; some Grand Lodges claiming a perpetual and
exclusive juri~iction over a rejected applicant for the degrees·1 others
limit 'the period to five or ten years, while in our own State it is limited
to one year.
It would also be a source of decided advantage if some system for
the. collaboration of the law as announced from time to time by the
various Grand Lodges and the bringing of the same into some concise
form for ready use and reference, could 'be adopted. This would have
. a strong tendency to bring about a greater uniformity.
. Such an organization could; by its sanction, provide for the publication of an authentic and reliable directory of regular Masonic organizations, not only thr~ughout the United States, but throughout the world:
For this purpose we are now obliged to rely upon a private publication
as to the authenticity of which we have no means of satisfying ourselves.

VISITATIONS.
On the 26th day of May the Grand Lecturer and mys.elf started on
an extensive tour of visitation, commencing at San Frandsco, extending
along the coast northward to Crescent City in the extreme northwest
corner of the State, thence across the mountains by way of Grant's
Pass, Oregon, down through the Shasta and Sacramento valleys, and
back to the metropolis. Arduous as the journey was in many respects,
involving travel by almost every means of conveyance, and in one
instance twenty-four hours of continuous staging, the pleasure and profit
derived from our experiences more than compensated our efforts. For
.the uniform courtesy, kindness and consideration of our brethren we•
desiTe to express our sincere and deep appreciation, our one r~gret
being that the limited time at our disposal required us to hurry on
without opportunity to do more than participate in formal Masonic
gatherings.
To travel continuously for thirty days, covering a total distance of
over two thousand miles, and be able to visit only a third of the lodges
in the jurisdiction, gives some impression not only of the extent of our
.State, but of the magnitude of the fabors devolving upon the Grand
Master, and particularly upon the Grand Lecturer, if any serious attempt
is made at general visitation.
Strong as is the temptation to do so, to detail our experience would
und 11ly prolong this document. To enjoy, however, for four weeks continuously, the beauties of our Great State and at the same time the open
hearted hospitality of the· Masons within her borders is an experience
which will always be recalled with pleasure and gratification. To a
Californian, no ocean is so beautiful as the great Pacific, whether it be
rclling with regular and rhythmic precision its lines of foam upon the
sands of San Diego, or dashing with resistless force against the cliffs of
Mendccino; no flowers so beautiful as those which carpet our valleys
and crown our hilltops; no mountains so magnificent as our rugged
Coast Range and towering Sierra Nevadas, upon whose heads there
;ests the crown of ever present snow and down whose sides there dance
the myriad streams of crystal fluid which is the life blood of our State.
These are the gifts of Nature and or' Nature's God, and as one who
has broken bread with those who live along and sail that ocean; who
ccntqnplate and enjoy association with those flowers or delve into
and take the precious metals from those mountains and harness and
distribute the energy producing and life giving products of those
streams; and with others yet who throng the busy thoroughfares of our
great municipal centers, where throb and pulsate the arteries of com- ·

mercial enterprises, can testify that they are Nature's Noblemen and
the noblest of God's creatures,
Instances were frequent where brothers walked from ten to twentyfive miles over difficult mountain trails to a meeting in honor of the
Grand Master, and the gratifying intelligence was realized that they
would go an equal or greater distance on foot and out of their way to
serve a worthy brother.
Crescent Lodge, of Crescent City, in the extreme northwestern
corner of the State, although in continuous existence since the year
1854, had never been visited by a Grand Officer. We found it, however,
in most healthy condition, with a membership the peer of any throughout
the jurisdiction. Although no degrees had been conferred for some
time, we were agreeably impressed with the proficiency displayed and
were gratified to learn that that proficiency was due in large measure
to the earnest and unselfish efforts of the late Brother William A.
Ke!ler, Past Master of Starr King Lodge of San Francisco. In the
pursuit of his employment Brother Keller had been called to Crescent
City, and, althollgh his duties were arduous and occupied his undivided
attention from sunrise until dark, he gave his evenings, at the sacrifice
of devoted and delightful family associations, to the improvement of the
Masonic education of the brethren of Crescent Lodge.
To those privileged to know him, no encomiums are necessary.
He was one of those plain and simple, yet sturdy and stalwart characters, wholly devoid of that outward show and ostentation which is so
frequently the cloak of shallowness and insincerity. His constant care
was to guard those over whom he had supervision against accident and
injury in the hazardous occupation of the logging camp. That he himself should have fa!len a victim to those very hazards, was indeed a sad
and afflicting dispensation. In his taking off: the Fraternity and the
community of which he was part, have suffered a great and irreparable
loss. To Starr King Lodge, of which he was so justly proud, and to
Crescent Lodge, the last beneficiary of his Masonic labor, we extend our
heartfelt sympathy, and to his bereaved family, esp.ecially, we i;nay be
permitted to offer that solace which comes from a realization that the
helpmate so lately taken from them possessed qualities of heart and
mind which were a source of pride, profit and inspiration to all with
whom he came in contact.

RELATIVE TO RESUSPENSION OF BROTHER J. N. PASCOE.
There was turned over to me by my predecessor, certain correspondence concerning the suspension of Brother J. N. Pascoe by Rising
Star Lodge, No. 83, ·of Forest Hill, Placer County, California, Brother
Pascoe claiming that his suspension, which was for non-payment of
dues, was improper and under circumstances entitling him to reinstatement. He is, as I am advised, in enfeebled health, but the
information which I have been able to obtain and which is set
forth in the correspondence hereto attached, is meager and uncertain;
that he is blind and was practically so at the time of his suspension,
and thus incapaciated from earning a livelihood, seems to be admitted
a·nd was, it is claimed, at the time of his suspension, known by Rising
Star Lodge.
I respectfully recommend that Rising Star Lodge be directed
to report the facts fully to the incoming Grand Master, or to the
Inspector of the proper District, not only as to the standing of
Brother Pascoe on the books, but also as to his physical condition
and the knowledge of the Lodge . in reference thereto at the time
of his suspension.
Correspondence in reference to the matter is herewith submitted.

.
Of necessity, in civil affairs, geography forms an important element in political considerations, but in Free Masonry no such neces~ity
exists or should be considered. Manhood and merit of a Mason
can not ile subordinated to the place from whence he comes. Cha~acter
and ability alone are the open sesame to Masonic preferment, and
there is no b ody of men better able to judge of those qualifications
than the membership of the Grand Lodge of California. To that
Body, inust be left the selection of its officers uninfluenced by combinations of any character or description. I hope that the incident referred
to died at its birth. I know from ·personal acquaintance with the

brethren prirtcipally sought to be involved therein, that the movement
was without their knowledge or consent, and that they are absolutely
free from any connection, remote or approximate, therewith.

hoped that my own conduct has not occasioned any unnecessary
augmentation of his official cares or your responsibilities. The task
has been a great one ;---at times assuming proportions which we~e

the character of our institti'tiori; that upon those occasions I have

members of said Southern <:;alifornia Masonic Home, and after proceedings duly had therefor, the Superior Court of said County of L9S
'Angeles duly gave and made its order and decree, authorizing said
Southern California Masonic Home to deed, transfer and convey to said
Oscar Lawler said property, and authorized the President and Secretary
of said corporation to make, execute and deliver to Oscar Lawler such
deed, conveyance or other instruments of transfer as might be proper
etc., in order to convey to said Oscar Lawler the said property, togethe;
with the furniture, carpets, furnishings, fixtures, appurtenances and
other appliances used in connection with said Southern California
Masonic Home; and
WHEREAS, Such ~eed has been made, executed and delivered to said
Oscar Lawler, which deed is now in the hands of the President of this
Board of Trustees of the Masonic Home of California; and
WHEREAS, Said Grand Master has authorized this Board to assume
control of said Southern California Masonic Home; now, therefore, be it
Resolved, That under and by virtue of said authority so confirmed, and pursuant to said offer of March 20, 1909, and its acceptance
by said M.". w:. Grand Master, and on no other terms, this Board of
Trustees does hereby assume control of said Southern California
Masonic Home, and subject to said offer, acceptance and· authority,
does hereby accept control and management of the same;
Resolved, That this Board, through its President, .request of the
Grand Master the use of ,the funds of the Grand Lodge for the purpose
of maintaining the Southam California Home at San Gabriel.
A telegram was sent you requesting you to instruct the Grand
Secretary to allow the use of the Grand Lodge funds to pay expenses
of conducting the Southern Home, to which you replied by authorizing
the Grand Secretary .to furnisl;t us the necessary funds.
Brother Wells, the President, and Bro. Elmer E. Stone, the Secretary, were authorized to proceed to San Gabriel and to assume full
charge of the Southern California Home and to arrange for its future
management. On August 14th, Brother Wells and Brother Stone left for
the Soqth, and on· the evening of the 15th of August, Brothers Wells
and Stone met with the Trustees of the Sou.them Home, and the final
transfer of the management of the San Gabriel Home was completed.
On August 24th, the Board met in special session for the purpose of
hearing the report of the committee sent South, and after hearing· said
report, the 1ollowing resckticn w2s offered and tmanimously adoptoo:
Resolved, That the children now housed at the Decoto Home be
transferred to the Southern California Home a.t San Gabriel, and. that
the old people now residing at the Southern California Home at San
Gabriel be transferred to the Decato Home.

The report of Brothers Wells and Stone recommended necessary
improvements and repairs, which the Board approved and authorized
made.
The following improvements and repairs were made: Cutting pai:titions between rooms to make dormitories ; partitions to divide one floor
or building so as to accommodate the girls on one side and the boys
on the other. Some new plumbing and the overhauling of the old
plumbing; painting, cleaning carpets and furniture, making over mattresses and pillows; the purchase of iron beds.
·
The work of preparing te> receive the children was no easy task
and took some little time. In the early part . of September, five old
people were sent to Decoto from San Gabriel, leaving two female resi<lents at the Southern Home and two male residents. The female
residents being entitled to remain under a contract existing and which
you are familiar with. The two male residents were kept at the
Southern Home as they were willing to do the garden work, thereby ·
relieving us of the necessity of employing a gardener.
On September 17th, Brother Wells and Brother Stone left with
·twenty-six children for the Southern California Home at San Gabriel,
where these children are now comfortably domiciled.
W,e attach to this report a 'statement of the money furnished by
the Grand Secretary and the manner i~ which it has been disbursed.
Fraternally submitted,

Tuesday, October 12, A. L. 5909.
The Grand Lodge was called on at two o'clock, the
Grand Master presiding.
The Grand Secretary presented the Annual Report of
his office, as follows :

•

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Immepiately following the last Annual Communication, and pursuant to the resolution of this Grand Lodge, I prepared a form of
uniform receipt for dues for use in the jurisdiction, and Lodges now
very generally use that form. It has worked well, and has preved
a source of protection to the members and to Lodges. A similar form
is now in general use throughout the jurisdictions of the United States.
On December 22d last fifteen hundred copies of the Journal of
the Proceedings were distributed, or · reserved for future binding in
the customary manner, and on March 23d a copy of the Roster of
Lodges was forwarded to each Lodge, Grand Officer and Inspector in
the jurisdiction.
I also forwarded to each Lodge and to each Inspector a <;opy of
Anderson's Manual, revised to include the decisions of 1908.
The proceedings of the various Grand Lodges with whom we
are in correspondence have been received and delivered to the chairman
of the Committee on Correspondence.
On the first of July, 1909, by direction of the Grand Master, a
commission was issued to M: · W . .' · Royal J. Allen of Duncan, Oklahoma, ·as Representative of the Grand Ledge of California near the
Grand Lodge of Oklahoma.

At the close of the last Annual Communication there were three
·hundred and twenty-four Lodges borne on the roll of the Grand Lodge,
with a membership of thirty-eight thousand, six hundred and sixtynine. Since that time six new Lodges have been farmed, making
the total number of Lodges in this jurisdiction at this time three
• hundred and thirty, with a membership of 41,007, a gain of 2338.

On the first day of January, 1909, I received a telegram from the
Grand Master, then at Baltimore, Maryland, directing me to cable
the sum of one thousand dollars to the relief of the sufferers by the
earthquake in Italy. Before I could certainly ascertain who actually

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

35

represented the Masonic Bodies in Italy, members of the Italian Lodge
in San ·Francisco, Speranza Italiana, No. 219, generously came forward
with offers of money for the same cause, and immediately following
came other offers from Masons of California; and at the suggestion
of the Deputy Grand Master I issued a general circular letter asking
for contributions from the Lodges ()f this jurisdiction. On the 4th
of January, by direction of the Acting Grand Master, I cabled to
Ettore Ferrari, Grand Master of the Grand Orient of Italy, to draw
on our Grand Lodge for money needed, not to exceed fifteen hundred
dollars. A cablegram expressing thanks was received in reply, and
on the 21st of January, by courtesy of the Bahk of Italy, I wired to
Grand Master Ferrari the sum of twenty-five hundred dollars for the
benefit of our brethren in the stricken sections of Italy. The total
sums received by me from the several Lodges and members aggrt:
gated $4,868.50, and I have now in my charge the sum of $2,368.50,
not needed in Italy, so far as I am advised, and I desire instructions
as to the disposition of this money.

Many brethren who secure Grand Lodge diplomas object to the
large size of the parchment, and I suggest that in addition to the usual
form in vogue for so many years; a small one be prepared and offered
to the craft at a small advance over cost. They can be lithographed
on parchment, in size of receipts for dues, in lots of 500, for ten cents
each.
I suggest, also, that Lodges should, in their annual reports, include
all sums paid for account of charity.
I recommend, too, that by proper resolution, you provide for admission to Grand Lodge without the tedious and to my notion fruitless
purging of the Grand Body an.d useless calling of the roll.
At the last communication of the Grand Lodge the matter of reprinting the Proceedings was considered, for reasons sta~ed in the
address of Grand l\faster Perine, and because of the practically pro-.
hibitive cost of reprinting, it was decided to abandon the plan. Later
a circular letter was sent to the several lodges of the jurisdiction,
requesting donations of extra copies, with encouraging response. Pursuant t'o the request, I have rereived the following copies:

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Special Committee, appointed in 1906, to whom was referred

whose preliminary report was printed in the Proceedings of the Fiftyninth Annual Communication,. held in October, 1908, have continued
their investigations at the request of the M." . w:. Grand Master and
have sought to obtain accurate and reliable information on the s~bject
from various sources, and beg leave to report as follows:
The request, inviting correspondence from all Masons throughout
the world, printed in the Proceedings of the last Grand Lodge, has
been entirely barren of results.
Your Committee have received the following communications, and
have sent the following letters in reply thereto on this subject, all of
which are attached hereto and made a part hereof.
In response to a letter from Grand Master Oscar Lawler requesting
information as to whether or not the Grand Orient of Spain had been
infringing on the juriSdiction of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania,
Bro. George B. Orlady, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, ·replied as follows:
January 5, 19G9.
Oscar Lawler,
Room 901, Call Building,
Los Angeles, Calif.
Most Worshipful Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of F. &
A. M. of California.
My Dear Sir and Brother:
Answering yours of the 14th ultimo, I have to say it has
been the policy -of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania since 1831
to decline all applications for the establishment of subordinate
Lodges beyond our territorial lines; and when the question of
granting a warrant to a subordinate Lodge in the Philippine
Islands, subordinate to the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, was
first broached, it was then decided, and which has been consistently adhered to, to decline such application, though a
number of them have been presented by our affiliated members
resident there. The reason for this decision was two-fold:
First-The one above suggested.
· Second-That as these American possessions were more
directly in touch with California, it was right and proper for
the purpose of investigaticn and ordinary proceedings that the
Grand Lodge of California should have control of the Masonic
life in those islands.
The Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania is not in affiliation with
the Grand Orient of Spain in any manner, for the reason that
we have in Pennsylvania a number of clandestine bodies working
under warrants issued by the Grand Orient of Spain.

While we have made no records in relation to the Philippine
Islands, it has been the policy of my predecessors in office since
1899 to ignore and condemn the Grand Orient of Spain, and to
regard the Philippine Islands as the Masonic property of the
Grand Lodge of California.
With Fraternal Greetings for the New Year, I am,
Yours very cordially,

67

GEORGE B. 0RLADY,

Grand Master.

Henry M. Owens, Esq.,

My Dear Brother Owens:
I thank you sincerely for your kind letter of the 23d ultimo.
Since writing you on January 23d I have · received an inquiry
from Pennsylvania as to whether or not we are in Masonic
intercourse with the Grand Orient of Spain, which indicates the
~egree of interest being taken in our possible relations with
the latter institution. I enclose you copy of communication
this day forwarded to the Grand Secretary, which has also
been submitted to the Deputy Grand Master. I think that most
serious complications would most likely ensue were a Grand
Lodge to be organized in the Islands, which can in a measure
be avoided by retaining our present relations with the Craft
in that dependency.

impelled me to the conclusion that, had the same been known
to the Committee and the Grand Lodge, said resolution would
not have been presented or adopted.
Therefore, after conferring with many of the brethren,
including several members of the Committee, and with a full
sense of my responsibility in the premises, it is hereby ordered
that the resolution referred to be suspended and the recommendation theteby made be withheld until the next Annual
Communication of our Grand Lodge.

San Francisco, Cal., March 4!6th, 1909.
Amos G. Bellis, Esq.,
P. 0. Box 199,
Manila, P. I.
Dear Sir and Brother:
Your favor of February 18th, 1909, reached me yesterday and I
am eJreeedingly glad to hear from you. The tone of your letter certainly
shows that the report has awakened new interest in regard to Masonry
in the Philippine Islands. If you will read the report carefully you
will see that the committee did come to the conclusion that it was
impossible for it to arrive at any conclusion, therefore the Grand
Orient of Spain nor any other Masonic body in Spain was recognized
as the proper Masonic power in Spain, and it was the intention to
leave this matter entirely in the hands of the Grand Lodge of the
Philippine Islands, (when formed) to deal with the situation as they
found it, because they would be on the ground and could better
determine the matter than we, who are thousands of miles away.
The Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of California has set aside
the resolution, as will more fully appear by his letter to the Masters
of the three Lodges in Manila and adjacent thereto.
Personally, I would like to have the "Report, Synopsis, and this
letter" taken up by the Lodges (i. e. our own Lodges 342, 350 and 386),
thresh out the entire matter at a Special Meeting called for this purpose, keep a record of the Meeting and forward same to me as soon
as done. I would suggest that the questions to be settled are :

,70

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

1. From what source were the Charters. issued to these Lodges?
2. Have the Charters been revoked or s.uspended, and are the
Charters in actual existence at the present time, and in whose possession?
3. What is the membership of each Lodge, as actually shown by
existing records?
4. What is the character, i. e., nativity of the members, and what
is the moral standing of the members as a whole?
5. Where is each Lodge located, and what is the population of
the place where located?
6. Would you consider the members of sufficient moral worth as
to be willing to have them members of your own Lodge?
7. How many meetings have they held since 1900, and to whom
do they report, and have these Lodges a continuous chain of title to
the present date from the first Grand Lodge in Spain?
The above seven questions can be determined by the Masters and
Wardens and Past li.fas~ers of the three Lodges, as a Committee,
appointed for that purpose.
They, (the Spanish and Native Lodges) are the ones seeking
recognition and would have no hesitancy in supplying you with this
information; and when all of this is done, we can decide whether
it would be proper for us to recognize the Spanish and Native Lodges.
It ,is not up to your Lodges or individually for you to say which
are regular p.nd which are not; the Grand Lodge of California alone
can determine this · question.
In re~ard to the two Lodges under the Supreme Council of France,
we have no control over them and could not legislate for them one way
<;ir other, but in ' the event of a Grand Lodge being formed in the
~slands, if they desired, they could surrender their Charters, and ask
for a Charter from the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands, but
these are all matters which are not necessary for the determination
of the regularity of Spanish Masonry, and need not be taken into
consideration until the question arises.
The Grand Lodge of California is not trying to cut the Lodges
in the Islands off, but while we admit that we have had a hard time
in trying to arrive at sqme definite conclusion in the matter, I am
now thoroughly satisfied and for one of the Committee can render
my opinion now, if it is admitted that the Grand Orient "of Spain
is the supreme authority over the Spanish and Native Lodges in the
Islands ; this Grand Orient has chartered Lodges in Pennsylvania
and Iowa thereby placing herself outside of the pale of recognition
by the Grand Lodge of California.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

71

That if any of the so-called Spanish Masons in the Islands desire to visit our Lodges, they must first present their petition for
Degrees, and pay the Initiation Fee required by our Lodges, and
come in as a profane would have to do; this will settle the matter
entirely and will allow the Lodges there to ·be able to select the
wheat from the chaff, and in my opinion this is the stand we should
take from this time forward, unless there are good reasons to the
contrary.
There should be no Grand Lodge formed in the Islands for
at least five years or until the ban is removed from Spanish Masonry,
and it is up to that body to remove the same, not us.
I wish that you would at once take this matter up with the Masters
of all of our Lodges there, subject to the suggestions herein contained,
follow them out, and have a full report for next Session of our Grand
Lodge.
You say, that there are many reasons for not forming a Grand
Lodge in the Islands, I would be glad to know them in full and would
thank you for your views, as well as the Masters of the other Lodges.
I would be also obliged to you if you would send me copies
of the "Boletin Official" and any other publications which will throw
any light 011 the subject.
Trusting that we may be able to clear up these uncerta.inties
by the next Session of the Grand Lodge, I am,
Yours fraternally,
H. M. Owl!Ns.

Manila, P. I., September 4th, 1909.
Mr. Henry M. Owens,
Chairman of Com. on Philippine Masonic Conditions,
San Francisco, Calif.
Dear Sir and Brother:
Your letter of March 20th, addressed to W · ·. Bro. Amos
G. Bellis, was duly received and brought to the attention of
Manila 342. Cavite 350, and Corregidor 386, all of which are
Ledges in the Philippines, holding under the Grand Lodge of
California, F. & A. M. In accordance with your suggestions,
each of said Lodges appointed its Masters, Wardens, and

72

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Past Masters to act as a joint committee in making the ·investigation requested, and as a result of their investigations, the
following report is submitted.:
At the outset, it should be understood that the members
of the native Lodges under the Spanish Grand Orient have
not, for a long time, made any attempt or request to visit
the American Lodges, nor has there been any request by
them for membership in the American Lodges. You state in
your letter that "the Spanish and native Lodges are the ones
seeking recognition and would have no hesitancy in supplying
(us) with this information." In this, you are mistaken, as
on the other hand, they are not seeking recognition and are
somewhat grieved at the action taken by the Grand Lodge
of California in 1906, in suspending Masonic intercourse with
them, and they are not inclined to impart much information
as to their interior workings. Some of the information requested by you could only be obtained by having members
of the Committee visit their Lodges, but, as we understand
it, this visitation is prohibited.
Dr. Barcelona, Grand Master of the Regional Grand Lodge,
stated to members of the committee who had approached him
on the subject, that it was the earnest desire of the members
of the Filipino Lodges that they might be able to exchange
fraternal courtesies with the members of the American bodies.
We find that the following Lodges, regularly chartered
by the "Grande Oriente Espanol" (Spanish Grand Orient),
a re now working in the Philippine Islands :

These Lodges are all under the immediate jurisdiction
of the "Gran Logia Regional de Filipines" (Regional Grand
Lodge of the Philippines), which is itself subject to the
"Grande Oriente Espanol." The headquarters of the "Grande
Oriente Espanol" is in Madrid, Spain.
The active membership of the Spanish-Filipino Lodges,
as a whole, is about 500. The individual Lodges, as a rule,
are weak in membership, and are not composed of the best
element of the Philippine population, although a number of
prominent Filippinos of good reputation, are members. The
great majority of the members of the Lodges under the
"Grande Oriente Espanol" are natives of the Islands. It has
been charged that the Lodges had been used for political
· purposes, but Dr. Barcelona informed the committee that it
was the earnest desire of the Regional Grand Lodge to stamp
out such practices if they existed.
To sum it all up, you may rest assured that all of the
Spanish-Filipino Lodges in the Philippines, under the "Grande
Oriente Espanol," are working under regular and legitimate
charters as far as that Grand Body is concerned. To our
minds, the only question for the Grand Lodge to consider is
"Is the 'Grande Oriente Espanol' a regular Masonic Grand
Body entitled to and worthy of recognition and fraternal
relations, as such, by the Grand Lodge of California, and
consequently, by her three Lodges located in the other Masonic
Bodies in the Philippines, outside of those holding American
charters."
Rizal Lodge, No. 377, in Manila, and Isarog Lodge, No.
378, in Nueva Caceres, Province of Camarines, both of which
work under charters from the Grand Lodge of France (not
the Grand Orient of France) . Both of these Lodges are very
weak in membership. The members of Rizal Lodge are all
natives, and it is understood that there are some Americans
in Isarog Lodge. Membership of both Lodges about 70.
La Perla del Oriente Lodge, No. 1034, in Manila, wor\<ing
under a charter from the Grand Lodge of Scotland. Membership about SO, composed of Americans and natives. This Lodge
was chartered in 1908, and is in fairly good condition. It might
be stated, by the way, that this Lodge recognizes the SpanishFilipino Lodges under the Spanish Grand Orient, and their
members frequently exchange visitations. ·Members of the
American Lodges also visit Li!. Perla c;lel Oriente Lodge.

In Manila, P. I.
Lusong, No. 185

Worshipful Sir:
The Grand Lodge of California, F. & A. M., at its Annual
Communication of 1906, appointed a Committee on the Status of
Masonry in the Philippine Islands. We find that the Lodges
there (other than those chartered by our Grand Lodge and the
Grand Lodge of France) are working under Charters from the
Grand Orient of Spain, or some other Grand Body in Spain.
We want to know which is the legitimate Masonic Grand Lodge
of Spain.
The Grand Orient of Spain has and is now invading the
jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania.
Kindly tell us all you know about Spanish Masonry and
help us out.

It is shown by the Report of the Worshipful Masters, Past
Masters and Wardens of the Philippine Lodges working under the
jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California that the numher of
Masons belonging to the Lodges in the Philippines subject to the
jurisdiction of the Grand Orient of Spain does not exceed 500, and
that the number belonging to the two Lodges under the 'jurisdiction
of the Grand Lodge of France does not exceed 70, arid this is quite a
contrast with the report heretofore received, to wit: 2,000. (See page
104, Proceedings of the Grand Lodge of California, 19Cl!.)
Your Committee desires to thank the Worshipful Masters, Past
Masters and Wardens of Manila Lodge, No. 342; Cavite Lodge, No.
350, and Corregidor Lodge, No. 386, Philippine Islands, for their
interest and action taken in this matter, and also for the interest taken
and assistance rendered by Bro. 0 . M. Goldaracena, Past Master of
La Parfaite Union Lodge, No. 17, and Bro. C. L. P. Marais, Past
Master King Solomon's Lodge, No. 260, in translating Spanish documents into English.
The Grand Orient of Spain cannot justify itself in chartering new
Lodges in a jurisdiction where another Grand Lodge has been in
existence for many years prior thereto, any more than the United
States or any other country would be justified in colonizing any particular county or province in the Kingdom of Spain, and having such
colony to render allegiance to such countries instead of to the la'Yful
authority existing in the Kingdom of Spain. That SQch colonization
cannot be done without the consent of the Kingdom of Spain has
been ~n elementary principle in international law for centuries ; therefore, the Grand Orient of Spain, whether a regularly constituted body

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

86

PROCEEDI1'i"GS OF THE

or a clandestine body, has no right to charter Lodges in another ·
state or country where another Grand Jurisdiction· exists, without
the consent of such jurisdiction; and when the Grand Orient of Spain
charters such Lodges in another jurisdiction, which jurisdiction is
recognized by the Grand Lodge of California, it becomes the duty of
the Grand Lodge of California to uphold and protect the jurisdiction
which has been infringed upon.
The next question arises as to whether or not the Lodges in the
Philippine Islands, working under the jurisdiction of the Grand Orient
of Spain, can in any manner have Masonic intercourse with the members of the Lodges in the Philippine Islands working under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California. ,
In the opinion of your Committee, the only manner in which the
Lodges in the Philippine Islands working under the jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge of California and the members of the Lodges working
under Charters issued by the Grand Orient of Spain or under the
Regional Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands, which is subject and
reports to the Grand Orient of Spain, can hold Masonic communication or have Masonic intercourse is, that the Grand Orient of Spain
must first withdraw all Charters of all Lodges which have been issued
by it or by any Regional Grand Lodge subject to the control of the
Grand Orient of Spain, in all of the jurisdictions of the world where
such jurisdiction existed and was in communication with the ~rand
Lodge of California prior to the date of the issuing of such Charters ·
by the Grand Orient of Spain.
The Grand Orient failing to withdraw such Charters, the only
alternative left for the members of the Lodges working under the
Grand Orient of Spain in the Philippines is to <limit from such Lodge,
and to make application to the Lodges working under the jurisdiction
of the Grand Lodge of California in the same manner as if they had
never received any degrees in Masonry, and if elected they must
conform to all the forms and ceremonies that a profane is now com·
pelled to conform to, and pay the regular fees demanded by such
Lodges from such profane.
And after mature deliberation and the evidence placed before this
Committee, this Committee is satisfied beyond any reasonable doubt
that the Grand Orient of Spain has not only chartered Lodges in the
State of Pennsylvania, but also in the State of Iowa, which is shown
in the Bulletins of the Grand Orient of Spain above referred to.
Having thus unlawfully infringed upon the jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodges of Pennsylvania and Iowa, which Grand Lodges are and ·have
been for many years in fraternal c;:ommunication with . the Gr~nd
Lodge of California, the Grand Orient of Spain has placed itself
ou~side _of the · pale of a regular Masonic
power ' reeog~ized
by. the
·'
.•.
. ·,·.
'

Grand Ledge of California, and is therefore not entitled to any recognition by the Grand Lodge of California.
Therefore, your Committee offers the following resolutions and
recommends their adoption :
R esolved, That the action he~etofore taken by Grand Master Oscar
Lawler in ordering that the resolution passed at the last session of
the Gr~nd Lodge of California be suspended and the recommendation
thereby made be withheld until the next . Annual Communication of
the Grand Lodge of California, be and the same is hereby ratified,
confirmed and approved; and, be it further
Resol; ed, That the Grand Orient of Spain, . or any Lodge owing
its allegiance thereto, is not entitled to recognition by th.e Grand Lodge
of California ; and, be it further
Resolv ed Tha~ all Ma~ons. owing allegiance to the Grand Lodge
of Californi; or to the sub~rdinate Lodges thereof be . and they are
hereby forbidd~n from holding any Masonic intercourse or communication with any member or Lodge, or Regional Grand Lodge, owing
allegiance to the Grand Orient .of. Spain.
H. M. OWENS,

w. FRANK PIERCE,

The Grand Lecturer presented his annual report as.
follows:
To the M: . w:. Grand Lodge of California:
I herewith submit to you my report as Grand Lecturer :
In the ·year just past I have visited every district in the State and'.
have held schools of instruction, both day and night sessions. In
quite a number of the districts I have held schools of instruction in
each Lodge. Most all of these schools have been well attended by
the officers and brethren striving to perfect themselves in the rituaf
and fioor work.
Great interest has been taken by the Lodges and brethren in.
learning the revised candidate's lecture, and most of the Lodges have·
now learned the lectures and are instructing their candidates therein.
The Lodges throughout the State are generally in good financial
condition, and· most of them are doing much work. Quite a number of
them have during the past year completed new temples or have them
now under process of construction. Six new Lodge!\ have been formed

88

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

since our last Comm,unication, and the net gain in membership, while
not so numerous as last year, has shown great prosperity. The Inspectors of the several districts are all qoing excellent work, and they
are entitled to much credit for the splendid condition of the Lodges
under their care. I wish to express to the Inspectors and brethren
throughout the jurisdiction my sincere thanks for the uniform courtesy
and kindness they have extended to me, and for the keen interest the
brethren have shown in attending the schools of instruction.
I have had the great privilege and pleasure of visiting a number
of districts with our M.". w:. Grand Master, and have listened with
admiration to the beautiful lessons of morality and Masonry inculcated
by him at these meetings.
I have received reports from every Inspector in this Grand Jurisdiction, and all report' the Lodges in their district, with few exceptions,
to be doing well. A large majority oi the Inspectors have recommended in their reports that a candidate's lecture be formulated for
the Third Degree, which lecture the Lodges may use if the brethren
desire to learn it. And that such brethren as pass a satisfactory examination therein shall, if the Lodge desires, be presented with a Grand
Lodge diploma.
I am under obligations to the V.". w:. John Whicher, Grand
Secretary, and his assistant, Bro. Harry S. Johnson, for courtesies
extended to me in their office the past year.
I have given private instruction in my office to many of the Inspectors, officers and brethren, and am always ready and willing to
instruct them when in the city.
Fresno Lodge, No. 247, of ,Fresno, exemplified the Second Degree
on Monday evening, October 11th; on this evening, Tuesday, October
12th, the First Degree will be exemplified by Berkeley Lodge, No. 363,
of Berkeley. On Wednesday evening, October 13th, the Third Degree
will be exemplified by Evergreen Lodge, No. 259, of River~ipe. These
Lodges have all been working hard on the several degrees, and will
exemplify the work as near letter perfect as it is possible to be done.
I regret to report that since our last Communication the Great
Architect of the Universe has seen fit to call to the Celestial Lodge
above two whose faces have been familiar in Grand Lodge for many
years: Bro. Max Goldman died November 21, 1908; he was Inspector
in this city for several years and was ever ready and willing to assist
the officers and brethren in the work. Bro. Thomas J. Richards,
Inspector of the Second Masonic District, died September 2, 1909.
Brother Richards devoted much time to perfecting the brethren of his
district in the work. The Grand Lodge and the Fraternity in general
have sustained a severe loss in the death of. these brethren.

I desire to thank the Grand Lodge and brethren for the honor
they have conferred upon me as their Grand Lecturer, which position I
have endeavored to fill to the best of my ability.
Respectfully submitted,
THOS. J. BAKER,
Grand Lecturer.

hither. Not a few have packed their belongings ·and shipped them by

Far too many are too far advanced with disease and come here

those working by the Square, would be among strangers. These we
have buried with full Masonic honors and their graves will be forever
kept green.
Brethren of the Eastern States, keep your invalid members at home
and allo~ them to pass to · the Supreme Grand Lodge among their
friends and relatives.
THE MASONIC EMPLOYMENT BUREAU.
The Masonic Employment Bureau, established under the auspices
of the Masonic Board of Relief, Scottish Rite bodies and Commandery
and Shrine, as an experiment, and which has proven a great success,
opened for business Ncvember 15, 1905, and up to date has been the
means of filling over seventeen hundred positions, either temporarily or
permanently, thus affording many brethren the means of providing for
themselves and their families.

San Francisco, August 10, 1909.
John Whicher, Grand Secretary,
Of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California.
Dear Sir and Brother:
Inasmuch as the portraits of all of the Grand Masters of
our Grand Lodge were destroyed in the conflagration of 1906,
and as I possess the only oil portrait extant of my late brother,
Wm. C. Belcher, who was Grand Master in 1862, 1863 and 1864,
and who, at the time of his death, in 1895, had been Chairman
of the Committee on Jurisprudence of the Grand· Lodge for
nearly Jhirty years, I have thought it my duty-in view of all
the circumstances-as indeed it is my pleasure, to present this
portrait to the Grand Body in which he labored with such
untiring zeal f~r so many years. Masonry, to him, was, as it
were, his wedded love; to it he gave a life-long devotion. His
brethren of the mystic tie are, therefore, in a certain sense,
more entitled to this fine portrait than I am, or at least they
are equally entitled. Accordingly, I hereby present the accompanying portrait of Wm. C. Belaher, Grand Master, as aforesaid, to the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California.
Fraternally and sincerely yours,

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:

As President of the Masonic Temple Association I herewith submit the Annual R eport of that body :
At the last Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge the Directors reported that early steps would be taken toward the erection of a
Masonic Temple on the lot owned by the Association, but owing to the
continued illness and death of our beloved Brother Reuben H. Lloyd,
who was President of the Association, and also owing to conditions
arising whereby the Supervisors of the City of San Francisco decided
to submit to the choice of the people the proposition of issuing bonds
and purchasing a site for a civic center, which proposed site would include our Masonic property., our plans were somewhat frustrated and
no action was taken by the Board of Directors until after the proposition was defeated; though while the civic center proposition was in
abeyance I, with the able assistance of Past Master James H. Humphreys of Golden Gate Lodge, No. 30, drafted floor plans which very
materially assisted the architects in designing the plans which we will
submit.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

On May 13th, 1909, I was elected to succeed Brother Lloyd, both
as a Director and President of the Association, and after the civic ·
center proposition was defeated, appointed the necessary working committees, and the Directors selected the firm of Bliss & Faville as architects (Brother Walter D . Bliss, the senior member of the firm, being
a member of California Lodge, No. 1), feeling that under their guidance
our fondest expectations would be realized in the erection of a Temple
which would stand as a monument to the Masons of this Grand Jurisdiction ; and the Directors now take pleasure in submitting to this
Grand Body the plans and elevation designed by the aforesaid architects, and which they considered most fitted for such a Temple.
The cost of the building and furnishing, as estimated by the architects, will not exceed eight hundred thousand ·dollars, the architects
being instructed to figure liberally so that we can surely erect and furnish the building inside of their figures.
It is proposed by the Directors to raise funds for the purpose of
building in the following manner : To issue bonds in the sum of eight
hundred thousand dollars, one-half of which-four hundred thousand dollars-to be designated as "Class A," to run for the term of
twenty-five years, and four hundred thousand dollars to be designated as "Class B," to run for the term of forty years, both issues t.o
bear five per cent interest. There could be no better or safer investment than these bonds, and as we would wish to place the forty-year
bonds first, we feel satisfied we would have no trouble in placing the
"Class B" issue with the various Masonic Bodies having funds to invest
for the purpose.
The Trust Compa~y who will act as trustee for the bonds will
underwriter all of the remaining bonds which we would be required
to sell.
The Directors are of the opinion that it would be for the best
interest of Masonry and this Grand Body to have the whole of the·
capital stock owned by the Grand Lodge, and to have a Temple which
is purely Masonic in all its appointments. The subscription at the
present time is as follows:
