To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had under consideration the
following decisions of the Grand Master, reported and referred to this
'
Committee, to wit :

8. Jurisdiction to Enterta4n Charges.
A Lodge may entertain charges of un-Masonic conduct against
one residing within its jurisdiction, but who belongs to a Lodge without
the State,

122

DECISIONS.

1. Re•ligious Services-Wearing Lodge Clothing Thereat.
While ther~ is no reason why Masons should not, if they so desire,
attend church m a body, there is no authority for the wearing of
Masonic clothing on such occasion.

2. Jurisdiction.
The Grand Master has no authority to grant concurrent jurisdiction
to two Lodges situate in different incorporated communities over unincorporated territory lying between them.
3. Advancement Denied.
An Entered Apprentice .denied advancement should have refunded
to him the fee in excess of that properly chargeable for the Entered
Apprentice degree, and he must be carried on the Lodge rolls. (Proceedings, 1906, page 204.)
4. Ballot-Black Ball Overlooked.
Where, immediately at the close of a Lodge meeting at which a
ballot had been taken, found clear and the candidate declared elected
the Master observed that, through some defect in the ballot box ~
cube and two white balls remained lodged in the aperture between ~he
two compartments of the box, and a brother advised him that such
~ondition had been observed by him at the time of balloting and before
it closed, the Master should, at the ensuing meeting, order a reballot.

5. Funeral Benefits N ot Allowed.
A by-law providing for the payment of a fixed sum in the matter
of funeral expenses is unauthorized.

6. N on-affiliate-Right to Visit.

A_ Mason holding a <limit twelve years old from a Kansas Lodge
occupies the status of a suspended Mason, is "unworthy of Masonic

*

* *

co~s.ideration," an·d· "is not entitled to
any of the· rights,
pnv~leges or charities of the Order." (Constitution, part V, article II,
s~c:1on 1; part VI, article V, section 8.)
VlSlt a Lodge in this jurisdiction.

Hence he is not entitled to

7. Degree.
Degree m~y be co~fcr:ed at a meeting called for the purpose on
the same evenmg at which mstallation of officers is to take place.

Same-Effect of Suspension for Non-P<;Jyment of Dues.
The fact that a Mason is under suspension for non-payment of dues
does not relieve him from liability or trial on such charges.
9. ltistallation of Officers-Failure to Qualify.
No officer can be installed without certificate of qualification;
failure of the Master elect to qualify and secure certificate within sixty
days after election ( or such further time as may be allowed), will
render a special election of another Master necessary. (General
Regulation, 28.) While no such mandatory rule is prescribed as to
W a rdens, the Grand Lodge has declared itself upon the subject in no
uncertain terms. ( General Regulation, 82; Manual, section 661.)
A failure of such officer willfully or through incapacity to qualify would
justify declaring the office vacant and appli1::ation for dispensation for
a new election.
Where a Warden gives notice that he will not serve, declaration of
vacancy and dispensation for election to fill same is proper.
10. Lodge R oom.
A Lodge may forego holding a meeting at a time when the room
is at its disposal and permit another organization to meet therein without
collecting compensation therefor, and not be chargeable with paying
out its funds for or on account of another organization. Such practice,
however, is not to be encouraged.

11. Dues-W hen P eriod of Neglect to Pay Commences.
For the purpose of calculating the twelve months' period of neglect
to pay dues, which imJ>oses upon the Secretary the duty to notify the
delinquent, a.s provided in Constitution, part 11, article III, section 11 ;
the date when such dues become due shall be taken as a commencement
thereof. See Uniform Code, article IX, secticn 1.
12. Dues-Delinquency.
Constitution, part IV, article I, section 3, declares that none but
members whose dues are paid may vote at an election, and article IX,
section 2, of the Uniform Code, provides that no member in arrears for
dues shall be permitted to vote or be eligible to any office. Article IX,
section 1, of the Code, requires dues to be paid quarterly in advance.
In order to entitle a brother to vote at an election, his dues must
be paid in conformity with these requirements.

.l?ROCEEDINGS OF THE

Same-A,.reo«aig,..,.,..D•t'Y of S.uref.o.lfy at Election.
'l'bere is no rule requiriug the Se<::r11fary to present a written
i;eport of the status of members with reference to the payment of dues,
nor as to how the Master shall secure the ballot against votes of delinquents, these things being left to the good judgment of the latter.

13. Charity Committee-Expenditure of Funds By.
Technically, drafts of the Charity Committee (article X, section 1,
Uniform Code) should be signed by the members jointly. Only in
extreme cases, however, would the Master be subject to legitimate
criticism for granting relief upon his own initiative.
14. Degree of Master Ma.son Conferr.ed Upon a Fellow Craft of
Anothe11 Jurisdiction.
A member who has received the Entered Apprentice and Fellow
Craft degrees in another State may, after removal to and residence in
California for the requisite pericd, petition for the remaining degree,
upon showing permission of the Lodge in which he received the former
degrees and from which he holds a so-called certificate of dismissal;
such petition must take the course prescribed for petitions for degrees.
(Constitution, part HI, artide Ill, secticn 7; Manual, sections 97, 162
and 414.)

15. Trial-Right to be Represented by Counsel.
An accused who. is so situated by reasons of conditions beyond his
control (impri~onment by public authorities) as to render it impossible
for him to be presef\t at a trial, is entitled to be represented by counsel.
Under ~u1:h circi\rnstances, the Masonic trial should be deferred until
the criminal proceedings are concluded.
16. Evidence.
Admissions and confessions made by defendant in the course of a
tri~I may be used as evidence against him at a retrial ordered 'by the
Grand Lodge. (Manual. section 277.)
17. Liquors.
The policy of the Grand Lodge in the matter of the use of liquors
is unequivocal and no narrow interpretation should be given to its
regulation relating thereto. A banquet, which is part of the celebration
of a Lodge anniversary, is a Masonic gathering, and the facts that
ladies are present and the Lodge does not contribute thereto do not
deprive it of its Masonic character. (Proceedings, 1908, page 190.)
18. Chaplain.
A member who is not a member of a Lodge in California is not
qualified for appointment as Chaplain.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

125

Installation and Ceremony-Who May Conduct.
A Past Master of a Lodge in this jurisdictio.n who has removed and
transferred his membership to a Lodge .in Nevada is qualified to conduct the ceremony of installation, the Lodge being in the immediate
charge of its proper cfficers. (Proceedings, 1894, pages 540-707.)

19. Restoration.
Proceedings by motion and resolutiqn reciting restoration of a
member under suspension for twelve years for non-payment of dues
nre void. (Constitution, part III, article III, section 11; Uniform Code,
nrticle IX, section 3.)
20. Dues-When Liability for Ceases.
From the moment of the issuance of certificate of withdrawal or
<limit liability for dues to the Lodge issuing the same ceases.
'

21. Metttbership-Tran.rfer of-Certificale of Standi11g.
The certificate of standing provided for by the Constitution, part V,
article II, section S, need not be directed to any particular Lodge; the
form set forth in Anderson's Manual has never been adopted as a part
of our Constitution or laws. (Proceedings, 1906, page 462.)

22. 'Burial.
A Lodge may accord Masonic burial to one under suspension for
non-payment of dues against whom no other offense has been established. (Constitution, part V, article II, section 5; Manual, section~.)
23. Hall.
Renting of hall to other than Masonic organizations is not restricted.
24. Advarncemtnl--Objection to.
Any Master Maston, whether a member of the Lodge, or not, may
make objection to advancement, the procedure upon which is pre·
scribed in the Constitution, part III, article III, section 6, and Manual,
sections 84, 85, 86, 152 and 533.
The candidate is entitled to be heard before jcdgment.
Evidence received by the committee should. on demand, be read
to the Lodge in order that it may act intelligently.
When it acts it is the duty of all Masons to submit thereto ul1less
unconscionable.
25. Jurisdiction.
\Vhen a Ledge has ccnferred the Entered Apprentice degree under
the mistaken understanding that the candidate resides within its jurisdiction, it should, immediately upon discovery of its mistake, suspend
prcceeding, and both the candidate and the Lodge request the waiver
from the Lodge having jurisdiction, the infringing Lodge tendering

126

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

t~ the latter the full amount of fees. Such request should then follow
the regular course. (Constitution, part III, article III, section 2;
Manual, sections 81, 130, 398, 792, 923 and 984.)
26. Charges.
Where charges of a criminal nature have been preferred and a
commission appointed, trial should be proceeded with, notwithstanding
~eques.t of complainant that they be withdrawn. When proceedings
mvolvmg the same facts are pending in the courts, trial should be
deferred until the conclusion thereof.

2.7. Co11solidatio11 of Lodges.
A Master can not refuse to entertain a motion regularly presented to consolidate his own with another Lodge. He may, however,
and should e:icercise a restraining influence on acrimonious debate.
Written notice of proceedings to consolidate must be sent to all
members three months in advance of the stated meeting at which
they are to be acted upon.
Consolidation can only take place upon the assent of three-fourths
of . the memb~rs of each Lodge involved. (Constitution, part III,
article II, sect10n 11 ; Proceedings of 1883, page 277.)
28. Fees-Forfeiture of.
One who was elected in March, 1898, to receive the degrees failed
to present himself within three months for initiation and the fee was
declared forfeited. In 1908 he wrote from Alaska, asking that a
Lodge in that jurisdiction be delegated to confer the degrees. H eld,
that he had lost his status as a petitioner in California, and that the
Lodge had no jurisdiction over him.

29. Liquors.
Meetings of an organization, eligibility to which requires Danish
birth and good standing as a Master Mason in some Lodge in San
Francisco, an: Masonic gatherings, at which the use of liquors is
forbidden.
'30. Age Qualifimtion.
Petition for degrees can not be received from one under twenty-one
years of age. (Proceedings of 1902, page 704.)
31. Dimit.
A brother holding a dimit issued in Ohio in 1902 may, provided he
has not resided in the State six months, deposit the same with his
application with a Lodge in this State in the same manner as if the
dimit were less than six months old; if he has resided in California
more than six months, he must pay the affiliation fee and a sum equa!
to six months' dues, which must be returned if the petition is rejected.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORl:'."IA

127

32. Petitio11-0bjection to.
Objection to a petition may be made by a member of the Lodge
by written communication. If not withdrawn within sixty days it will
operate as a rejection, which should be reported to the Grand Secretary. (Proceedings of 1905, page 117.)

33. Jurisdiction.
It is not an invasion or a violation of jurisdiction for a Lodge in
('nlifornia to receive and act upon petition for restoration by a
member thereof suspended twelve years before for non-payment of
dues, although he is no longer a resident of the State.
34. Life Membership-Power to Rescind.
Life membership can not be rescinded without the consent of the
Grand Lodge, and a life member desiring to discontinue his status as
such is not entitled to withdraw a proportion of the net life membership fund based upc n the number of members contributing thereto.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE.

The Grand Master has made a most valuable innovation in regard to his decisions, one that, looking to the best interests of the
Grand Ledge, we hope will serve as a precedent for all coming Grand
Masters. Copies of his decisions were submitted to the Chairman of
this Committee several weeks ago. This has enabled us to give them
much more careful consideration than has heretofore been possible.
It is obvious that if this method be followed in the future this Committee will be in much better position to assist the Grand Lodge than
it has occupied heretofore, where it has been compelled, within a few
hours, to review, consider and report on a great number of rulings,
many of which involved doubtfol questions of great importance. The
thanks of the Grand Lodge should be extended to Grand Master
Lawler for inaugurating what we are sure will be an established
custom.
The Grand Master submitted with his 'decisions the original
papers in each case, thus contributing to a better understanding of
the facts. The decisions show much investigation e n his part and an
earnest desire to arrive at conclusions that are in full accord with the
principles of our Order, and the letter of our written law. They a re,
in the main, clear and correct expressions of the law as it exists in
this jurisdiction.
We will take up each decision separately and report thereon.
· 1.-Decision 1 correctly states the law as declared in numerous
d ecisirns. We recommend its approval.

129

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

2.-Decision 2 is obviously correct, the matter of jurisdiction of
Lodges being regulated by provisions of our Constitution, and the
Grand Master being without power to allow action contrary t9' the
terms of such provisions. We recommend its approval.
3.-Decision 3 is correct (Proceedings, 1906, page 204). We
recommend its approval.

16.-Decision 16 is correct and requires no notice. We recommend its approval.
17.-The same is true as to Decision 17. We recommend its
approval.
18.-Decision 18 consists of two parts. The part holding that a
Past Master of another jurisdiction may conduct the ceremony of
Installation, the Lodge being in the immediate charge of its proper
•>fficers, is in accord with a previous decision (Proceedings, 1894, pages
240, 707). The part holding that one who is not a member of the
Lodge is not qualified for appointment as Chaplain thereof is correct.
No one can be an officer of a Lodge unless he be a member thereof,
except the Tyler. (See amendment to By-Laws, Proceedings, 1908,
page 189.) We recommend that the decision be approved.
19.-Decision 19, as applied to the facts of the particular case were
correct. It was attempted to restore a brother who had been under
suspension for non-payment of dues for over twelve years, by a resolution at a stated meeting, without any petition for such restoration
having been presented at the preceding stated meeting (Constitution,

28.- The papers accompanying Decision 28 showed that the applicant had resided in Alaska for over ten years, and so far as appears
had not, prior to his application in 1908, made any attempt to obtain
his first degree. Under the provisions of our Uniform Code of
By-Laws, the fee paid by an applicant for the degrees is forfeited if
he does not "come forward" to be initiated within three months after
his election, "unless the Lodge shall otherwise direct." (Section 2,
article IV.)
This would seem to contemplate that all the rights of one elected
to receive the degrees shall expire at such a time, and that he is
henceforth as one who has not been elected at all, or even petitioned
for the degrees, unless the Lodge shall otherwise direct. Of course,
the Lodge should "otherwise direct" where the delay is not unreasonable and was unavoidable so far as the petitioner was concerned, as,
for instance, where sickness or ~ necessary temporary absence pre-

6-31.-Decision 6, made during the necessary absence of the Grand
Master from the State of California, relating to the status of a Mason
holding a dimit twelve years old, from a Kansas Lodge, to the effect
that such Mason occupies the status of a Mason suspended for nonpayment of dues, and is not entitled to visit a Lodge in this jurisdiction, was erroneous, unless such Mason had resided in California for
six months and had failed to make application for membership to some
Lodge in California. The papers submitted with the decision indicate
that he had just arrived from Nevada, and had not lived in California
six months. If so, the decision was wrong. The law applicable in this
regard is correctly stated in the decision of the Grand Master numbered 31, where it was held that the brother holding a <limit issued
by a Lodge in the State of Iowa in the year 1902 may deposit the same
with a Lodge in this State in the same manner and upon the same
conditions as if the same were less than six months old, if he has not
resided in this State for six months. The latter ruling is apparently
in conflict with Decision 6. It is thoroughly settled that under our
constitutional provisions, a non-affiliate does not lose any of his
Masonic rights and privileges unles·s he has resided in this State for
six months without having made application for membership to some
lodge therein. This matter was fully discussed in the address of the

Grand Master in 1889 (Proceedings, 1899, page 32), and the decision
of the Grand• Master in regard thereto was approved by the Grand
1,odge. We recommend the adoption of this report, the effect of
which will be the overruling of Decision No. 6, and the affirmance of
Decision No. 31.
15-26.-Both Decision 15 and 26 relate to charges of a Masonic
offense constituting also a crime under the law of the State, and as to
which a criminal proceeding is pending in the courts. The Grand
Master ruled that where such charges have been presented and a
commission appointed, the mere ·request of the accuser that the
charges be withdrawn is not a sufficient reason for their withdrawal.
As to the correctness of this ruling there can be no doubt. The good
name and best interests of Masonry are involved in such a matter, and
the desire of the accuser or his willingness to waive the alleged
offense is absolutely immaterial. The Grand Master also held that
if by reason of imprisonment, the accused was unable to _be present, he
is entitled to be represented by counsel. This, of course, is also correct.
The Constitution in terms authorizes the presence of counsel in any
case on the part of both accuser and accused, the only limitation being
that such counsel must be a Master Mason in good standing ( section 6,
article IV, part VI, Constitution) . The Grand Master further held that
under such circumstances the Masonic trial should be deferred until
the criminal proceedings are concluded. Our decisions do not go to
that extent. It has been held that where one has been charged with a
crime in the courts we may ordinarily defer a Masonic trial for the
same offense until the result of a trial therein has been announced.
In this we entirely concur. But we can conceive of cases where no
such delay would be necessary or proper, and where the best interests
of Masonry demand a speedy investigation of the charges and a
prompt disposition of the matter. Each case must depend upon its
own circumstances. It may be well to note that it is settled in this
jurisdiction tha·t an acquittal in the courts is not a bar to a prosecution
of the same charge as a Masonic offense. With this modification we
recommend the approval of both Decision 15 and 26.
24.-We are of the opinion that Decision 24, as to the legal right
of one not a member of a Lodge to make the objection to the advancement of an E . A. or F . C. therein, provided by section 6, article III,
part III, of the Constitution, is not in accord with our law. The constitutional provision in that regard is very explicit, the same section
providing both for objection to initiation and objection to advancement and as to each case it is provided that the objection may be
mad: by "a member." It is very clear that it was not meant that one
not a member of the particular Lodge could interpose art objection to
an initiation that would have the effect of a rejection if not withdrawn
in sixty days. Must not the same meaning be given to the word

133

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"member" in relation to an objection to the advancement that compels
reference to a committee and operates as a basis for a ·vote by which
advancement may be denied.
Grand Master Taylor, in 1882, ruled explicitly that objection to
advancement could be made only by a member of the Lodge for whom
the degree was to be conferred (Proceedings, 1881-2, page 445), and
this ruling was affirmed by the Grand Lodge. (Proceedings, 1881-2,
page 687.) Section 533 of the Manual is apparently not a correct
statement of Grand Master Taylor's decision. In 1899 it was expressly
held that where a Lodge had been requested by another Lodge to confer
the remaining degrees on an E. A. Mason, no one but a member of the
requesting Lodge could make legal objeCtion to his advancement.
This ruling was also affirmed by the Grand Lodge (Proceedings,
1899-1900. pages 22, 274). There is no explicit ruling to the contrary,
and we are satisfied that the constitutional provision will admit of no
other construction. Of course, it is entirely proper and commendable
for a Mason not a member of the Lodge to inform the Lodge as to
any objection. that he considers sufficient to the advancement of a
brother of which he has knowledge. If the information thus given is
deemed of sufficient importance and weight to warrant investigatil'n at
all, doubtless advancement would be deferred, and if a formal inquiry
under the Constitution is then found advisable, some member of the
Lodge should interpose the objection which is the essential basis to
a proceeding having for its purpose the deprival of the right of
advancement. The remainder of the decision is correct and requires
no notice, and that portion should be approved; the first disapproved,
as herein set forth. We recommend the approval hereof.
29.-This ruling was made in view of the regulation adopted at our
last Communication, as follows :

but Blue Lodge Masonry and include nothing else. The word "Masonic" was used in this regulation with the same restricted meaning
that it has in all the other written laws of this Grand Lodge. In one
acnse of the word we might properly term a meeting of a Temple of the
Shriners a Masonic gathering, for all members are Masons as well as
Shriners, but we could not properly do so in the sense in which we
use the word in our laws. And if we did not intend to include such a,
body as this, by what logic can it be held that we intended to include
what the papers in the case before us show to have been simply a
social club, solely because it has seen fit to confine its membership to
Masons? It has not the remotest connection with Masonry, and the
members thereof cannot meet in the character of Masons. Whatever
the test of eligibility to membership may be, the members meet therein
solely as members of their club, just as two or more Masons might
meet socially in the privacy of the home of one of them. Such meetings
are not "Masonic gatherings" within the meaning of our regulation.
A letter accompanying the decision shows that it was proposed to
name the social club the "Danish Freemason Club" or "Danish Masonic
Club." We do not believe that Masons can with propriety use the
name of Freemasonry for such a purpose and so report.
We recommend that Decision 29 be disapproved, and that this
report be adopted as the sense of the Grand Lodge on the questions
discussed therein.

Most Worshipful Grand Master, and B rethren of the Grand Lodge:

I have come forward at this time to speak a few plain, simple
words and not to deliver an elaborate address. The words that I shall
speak' must come from the impulse of the moment, yet I realize that
there are moments in life when the heart swells with emoticn that the
tongue cannot express. With me, I fear that moment is now.
As the years go by, we assemble here in Annual ·communication to
perpetuate the sublime principles of Freema.sonry, and to legislate for
the good of the Grand Lodge and the guidance of the subordinate
Lodges throughout the jurisdiction. These annual meetings we regard
u.s Masonic home-comings. Here assembled, we exchange fraternal
gre-etings-take our brethren by the hand, solicitous for their welfare,
and bid them God-speed over the rough and uneven journey of life. It
seems to me that at the recurrence of these Annual Communications
God sends out a summons to call us to Special Convocation to take
into consideration the brevity of life, to commemorate our honored'
dead and to make due preparation for that great Ch,mge which must
com: to all the living. As I speak these words there comes to my mind
a Grecian legend :
Alexander, after a hard fought battle, summoned his war~i o rs to
meet him in the banquet hall, and ere the feast began, he rcse and
asked: "Are all who fought at Issus here ?" And Clitus, the Macedcnian l!encral, ma<le answer and said : "All, Alexander, all save those
who fell." "Then," said Alexander, "all who fought at Issns are here,
for the dead are here in memory."
Mv brothers, for long', long years, we have fought life's battles together~battles for the weak against the strong, for the rig·ht against
the wrong.
Many of our valiant comrades have fallen from c;ur ranks, and
have been borne to the great Valhalla cloisters of the ever-living years.
Vt/e shall never again meet them in Grand Lodge, around the festal
hcar<l, or nn the broad highway of life. But they shall not be fo rgotten.
In the soil of our bosoms we have prepared their graves, and there
they shall rest beneath the immortelles of brotherly love, an<l me~ory's
perennial acacia shall bloom above their sacred dust. Gone, bu: ":1th us
still; dead, yet still they .live; their silent influences are brmgmg us
r:earer and nearer to the light of our eternal home.
"O, the stars never tread the blue heavens at night,
But we feel where the ransomed have trod,
And the day never smiles from its palace of light,
But we feel the bright smile of our God."
Veterans in the cause of Truth and Justice! I seem to see them
r:ow; and a halo of glory will hang over the Grand Lodge of C~lifornia
so long as their names shall remain emblazoned upon memory s walls.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

I desire at this time to acknowledge the honor conferred upon me
by our Most Worshipful Grand Master, in inviting me to say a few
words commemorative of our lamented brother, Past Junior Grand
\Varden, Jacob Hart Neff. At the mention of that name I know that
many a brother will recall sad, sweet memories of one of the noblest
Masons ever borne upon the roll of this Grand Lodge. Brother Neff
was one of God's noblemen. He was faithful in the performance of
every duty, and loyal to every trust. In his daily walk he exemplified
those characteristics which go to make up the noble man, and the sincere and devoted Mason.
Brother Neff was born in Strausberg, Pennsylvania, in 1830. When
but a young man he came across the plains to California, the El Dorado
of the West, and after casting about for a few diiys, he drove his
stakes in Placer Cqunty, and gave his attention to mining. He was
made a Mason in Wisconsin Hill Lodge, No. 74, in 1856. When that
Lodge surrendered its charter, he was instrumental in fanning Ionic
Lodge, No. 121, and was for several terms its Master. On account of
change of residence, he dimitted, and united with Eureka Lodge, No. 16,
at Auburn, and was a member thereof when he passed away. He came
into Grand Lodge in 1859, and commenced his valued work on important committees, and for long years was thus engaged. At the time of
his death, he was Chairman of the Committee on Finance. In 1875 he
was elected Junior Grand Warden, and at the close of his term made
a most unusual request; he asked his brethren not to advance him, for
he felt that he could be of greater service to the Grand Lodge in other
capacities.
By his intrinsic worth he rose from the miner's humble cabin to
honorable stations in the capital of the State. As State Senator, he was
cautious and far-seeing, devoted not only to the interests of his constituents, but to the welfare, the honor and prosperity, the development
and the upbuilding of this great Commonwealth. As Lieutenant Governor, he earned the respect and lasting esteem of every citizen, irrespettive of party affiliations.
I have known little of Brother N eff's l"arly life. It is enough for
me to know that such a man has lived, that the world has been made
better by his life of truth and probity, that the Grand Lodge has so long
had the benefit of his valued services, and that it has been my privilege
to hold pleasant relations with him for a period of mo;e than thirty
years.
Brothei: Neff was a great lover of nature, and looked through
nature up to nature's God.
In the early days of our acquaintance, it was my pll"a~ure often to
visit him in his mountain home. On one occasiOn we were riding in
the high Sierras, and at a certain point the team was halted ; I was

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

· GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

requested to alight and pass up a short path leading to the edge of a
prec1p1ce. On doing so, there burst upon my vision one of the grandest
and most soul-inspiring views that I ever beheld, and the words of the
psalmist immediately came to my lips: "I will lift up mine eyes to
the hills, whence cometh my help." I involuntarily raised my hat, and
I heard Brother Neff's voice: "That's right, that's right; no man who
has a soul can ever stand upon that point without uncovering."
We returned to his home, and in the evening, seated by his cheerful
fireside, we talked long into the night. We talked nf life and its
duties, its opportunities, its dangers, and its uncertainties. I quoted
to him a stanza from the writings of Letitia Barbauld:
"Life, I know not what thou art,
But know that thou and I must part;
Or when, or where, or how we met,
I own to me's a secret yet.
Life, we've been long together,
Through pleasant and through cloudy weather.
'Tis hard to part when friends are dear,
Perhaps 'twill cost a sigh, a tear.
Then steal away; give little warning;
Take thine own time;
Say not 'good night,'
But in some brighter clime
Bid me 'good morning.' "

"The just shall live by faith.'' If we have faith in God and immortality, if we have so ordered our lives that we may apply our hearts
unto wisdom, if, in our daily walk, we have exemplified the virtues
taught us in Freemasonry, we may reasonably hope that the separation
from our friends, our brothers, and our loved ones, will not be final.
Beyond the smiling and the weeping, beyond the mistakes and discords
of time, there will be an unbroken reunion in that Better Land beyond
the star-gemmed sky.
Full of years and honors, our brother has gone before us. His
noble virtues shall be recorded on enduring tablets, and his words
of love and kindness spoken here will be re-echoed in the Bright Beyond. With tottering steps he has passed adown that path where
life's evening shadows fall. Once again, and for the last time, he has
been brought from darkness to light. The glad "Good Morning" for
which he prayed has been given, and his great soul is now at rest
within the portals of the Supreme Grand Lodge above. Life's race
well run; life's work well done. How appropriate now the words of
Tennyson:
"And now he rests; his greatness and his sweetness
No more shall be at strife;
And Death has moulded into calm completeness
The statue of his life;
And round his grave are quietude and beauty
And the sweet heaven above,
The fitting symbols of a life of duty
Transfigured into love."

Nature's lessons are given to us in varied language. Life is
typified in the swelling bud, the opening blossom, the ripe fruit, and
the falling leaf. The footsteps of decay are everywhere. The sad word
"change" is written upon rock and tree and flower. We hear it in the
whispering breeze, in ocean's roar. We read it in the broad expanse
above us, where God has written in azure with letters of diamonds.
The music of the spheres as they wheel majestically into the grand
march of the ages is set to the words, "Passing away! Passing away!,.
All must fade and pass away. But a short time, and he who now
addresses you, and all present, especially those whose locks are touched
with the frost that never melts, must, one by one, pass down into the
dark Valley of Sjlence. But, my brethren, Masons are not materialists.
Something within our breasts implanted is ever whispering in unmis"
takable accents that beyond the visible veil of nature there is a hidden
Power that guides and governs all ; that
"* * Beyond the deep unknown,
Standeth God within the shadows,
Keeping watch above His own.''

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Bro. Wm. P. Jeffries, Chairman of the Committee on
Returns, presented the following report:
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee, to whom was referred the examination of the
returns of the Lodges for the current year, with the assistance of the
Grand Secretary, have performed that duty, and take pleasure in reporting that the returns of all the Lodges have been received by that officer;
that a very large majority of them were prepared correctly; that those
that were erroneous have been since corrected by the Secretaries, upon
notice thereof (in some cases more than once repeated); that the dues
have in nearly every instance accompanied the reports, and that all
the dues have now been paid.
The classification which follows shows the respective credits due
the Secretaries of the several Lodges.
The reports of the following two hundred and seventy Lodges
were transmitted within the period of time prescribed by the Constitution; were accompanied by dues; were in all respects correct, and were
handsomely prepared :

w:. Grand Lodge, P. & A. M., of California:

During the discussions held concerning the management of the
Masonic Home at Decoto, it has been stated that, for several reasons,
it is not practicable to continue the institution as a combined Home
for our widows, orphans and brothers; one of the reasons given is an
insufficiency of the water supply, "and another, the bad influence that
results from the old people being brought in too close contact with
the children; in fact, it is imperative that the two should be separated
at once.

I

.

Notwithstanding these statements, we believe that there is a
good and abundant supply of water on the property of the Home; and
that it only needs an additional reservoir, which can easily be constructed, and some enlarging and repairing of pipes, to make the water
system perfect. We further believe that as the property is over two
hundred and sixty acres in extent, buildings could and should be
built for the accommodation of our aged brothers; 't hus avoiding the
necessity of bringing them in contact with the children, and yet
keeping the whole institution under the control of one general management. Other matters could be regulated by a practical board of
trustees.
For the purpose of expressing our interest in this matter, also our
desire to pave the way for the maintenance of the Home on the most
practical and economical lines, to the end that it will best serve its
purpose to the fullest extent, we beg to offer the following resolutions,
to wit:

We recommend that there be one Board of Trustees, consisting of
1even in number, to be appointed by the M.". w:. Grand Master,

n successor or successors, as the case may be; each appointee to hold
' ffice for the period of 5 years thereafter.

'fa the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee, to whom was referred all matters pertaining to
the Masonic Home at the last session of the Grand Lodge, beg to submit this, our report, and recommend its adoption.
We believe that our duties cannot be better defined than to quote
the words of the "Committee on Distribution" at the last session of the
Grand Led,; e. see pages 90-91, Proceedings 1908:
"In cur judgment the matter fraught with the greatest importance
to this Grand Lodge and discussed by the M. W. Grand Master in his
address, was that relating to the Masonic Home at Decoto," and "The
reports of the Trustees relating to the future conduct of the Home."
"We think that a proper solution of the matters relating to the
Home as they are presented by the Address of the Grand Master and
as they are exhibited by the report of the Trustees, demands that the
whole subject in all its ramifications, shall be submitted to a special
committee of the Grand Lodge," etc.
In addition to the above recommendation, which was adopted,
several matters were referred to this committee, chief among which
was the appropriation of the sum of fifteen hundred dollars ($1500)
to the Southern California Masonic Home at San Gabriel, California.
In all our actions we have been guided by the sentiment which seemed
to prevail, that this committee would give to the various matters referred to it, the most extended and careful study and invistigation. This
we have endeavored to do to the best of our ability and have devoted
considerable time thereto.
In passing, brethren, permit us to say that each and all of the committee from the first, felt, and do now feel, our great lack of ability,
and we beg for this report of our year's work your kind and charitable
consideraticn, believing that whatever may be decided upon by the
majority of this Grand Lodge as the best, will be improved by time

100

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

and experience, ultimately developing a system of caring for our wards, .
the children and the aged who have fallen behind in the race of life,
that shall redound to the honor and glory of Masonry in California
for all time.
Immediately after the adjournment of the Grand Lodge last year,
we began our labors and up to the present time have continued our
investigations, in order that an intelligible report might be made of
all the affairs pertaining to this important branch of Masonic Charity.
We have visited the Horne at different times in order to study the •
situation thoroughly and determine, if possible, the best method of
conducting that institution; let us here premise by saying that the
present Board of Trustees have anticipated evefy important change
which we would feel it our duty to recommend, and by their earnest
and intelligent efforts have already brought about many reforms which
we think will make for the good of the residents of that institution,
as well as for the general welfare of those committed to our care.
We deem it proper at . this time to report the results of our investigations, which are hereby submitted for your information, and are not
intended as a criticism of the administrations, present or past, but sim- ,
pie statements of the condition of the Home as we saw them, and
existent at the times our visits were made.
At the time of our first visitation as a committee, during the latter
part of October, we found the place crowded with visitors, some of
them Masons, all expecting to be entertained and accommodated in·
the dining room; this entailed double work on the help, who already
had all they could attend to ; the day being Sunday, the usual Sabbath
day exercises were held in the Chapel, and was well attended by the
older people, as well as all of the children. Your committee spent
the day in the examination of the premises, talking with the residents,
looking over the farm and making such examination of the Home as
the limited time at our disposal would allow; we found the approach .•
to the Home, as well as the driveway and grounds, well kept and in
fine condition; the main building in fair condition, but still showing
the ugly scars of the earthquake of 1906. The cottages in which reside
the older brethren were very much in need of repair and paint, the
plumbing in the entire plant was in poor condition; the septic tank
was a source of much complaint from the residents, owing to the foul
odors arising from it. We were glad to find upon the occasion of
later visits that all of these matters had been considered and remedied by the Trustees, as their report will show. We were impressed
with the necessity of adequate fire protection at the Horne and upon
investigation found that little or no precautions against fires were taken.
One of the brothers resident there was acting as night watchman, but
beyond the simple act of inspection there had been no steps taken to
prevent a calamity which would inevitably ensue were a fire to break

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

161

out in the night time; it seems that two chemical engines had been
purchased and one of them only had been put in commission by being
charged and placed under the stairway leading from the main part
of the building to the dining room. Nobody had been instructed how
to handle the apparatus and no fire drills ever had; this was called to
the attention of the Trustees with a recommendation that some of the
older boys, as well as the men, be properly instructed in the matter of
fire drills, and that the matter of fire escapes be looked into at the
earliest possible moment; no fire escapes have ever been placed on the
buildings, and in view of the absence of an adequate water supply
with which to fight fires, we believe this matter ought to have the first
consideration of the new Board of Trustees.
The water question at the Home at Decoto is the greatest problem
with which the present and other Boards of Trustees have had to deal
and calls for prompt action in the matter of developing a sufficient supply for the needs of that institution; we earnestly request careful consideration of that portion of the Trustees' report wherein certain recommendations are made looking to a solution of the water problem,
all of which recommendations are concurred in by your committee.
The question of the "fa~n " was also investigated by your committee, especially the complaint u1at the farm was being conducted at.
a net loss to the fraternity approximating $2500 per annum, which state
of affairs had continued for the past ten years; we found this to be
an error caused by the failure to take proper credit for the produce
consumed on the place. For example, the poultry, eggs, milk, pork, veal,
etc., if charged at market prices, would have shown the farm to have
made a profit instead of a deficit; we were informed that only such
farm products as were actually marketed were ever credited up to
the farm, hence the im.pression that the farm was a source of loss.
We were forcibly impressed with the lack of room at Decoto, and
while the children's dormitories were sufficient for all demands made,
and were in admirable condition, clean and well kept in every respect,
the men's quarters in the cottages seemed to be crowded, and many
of them by the acts of the men themselves; were unclean and uncomfortable; the cottages were sadly in need of repairs and pai,nt, and
more room needed generally.
The dining room and kitchen were in admirable condition, the
service good and the food of superior quality; this we were informed
was the rule and not the exception.
The children we found happy, well contented and well cared for;
the Boys' Band and Girls' Orchestra were a great source of comfort
to the older people resident there, and a prolific source of entertainment to the visitors; this is a course of education which we will do
well to continue. We found some dissatisfaction existing among the
6

162

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

older' .people, but nothing which in our opinion was of a serious nature; in fact, we were thoroughly satisfied that the dissatisfaction was
solely the. result ~f idleness on the. part of these old folks. Many of
them havmg nothmg to occupy their time naturally fell into the habit
oi grumbling and fault finding. We sincerely trust that some system will
eventually be adopted and whereby all persons resident at the Home
~ill have some lit.tie duty to perform, however trifling it may be,
m order that their minds may be occupied with the idea that the
Home. is.· indeed their home and needs attention at their hands, if only
to a hm1ted degree. This should be a rule and extended to the children in order that they may grow' up to be self respecting men and
women, having the self satisfaction of contributing to their own support and education.
Many of the complaints were to the effect that the rules of the
Home were harsh and unnecessary, restricting the liberties of the older
people to an unwarranted degree; this we investigated and from our
conclusions find that the rules are the result of years of observation
and experience, of careful thought by able and unselfish Masor,s, made
for the good of all, and we believe that extreme care should be exercised in making any changes in these rules.
In the matter of visitation to the Home we were impressed with
the necessity of restricting the privileges enjoyed by the public. It was
the ~~stom for large numbers of pleasure seeking people on Sunday
to VISlt the ~~me. Many of these were automobilists enjoying rides,
who would VISlt the Home about the noon hour, expecting to be entertained at the small expense of twenty-five cents for dinner. These
were in many cases persons having no interests in the residents, the
Home, or even the fraternity, wholly dominated by selfishness. We
were pleased to learn that the Trustees soon afterward found it necessary to prohibit the serving of meals to visitors at any hour; we trust
this rule will be continued in future, except in the case of official visits
by Lodges or Officials of this Grand Lodge. There is every reason
why the help should be considered. It should be particularly observed
on the Sabbath day, whicH ought to be a day of quiet and rest for
all. W e do not mean that the custom of receiving visitors should be
stopped, rather that it should be regulated, but no dinners served on
Sundays.
We desire to r efer to the Christmas exercises which were attend~d
bY your committee on December 27th, at which time many visitors
were present and participated in the happy spirit of the day. The exercises were conducted by the children, the Girls' Orchestra rendering
the Christmas Cantata in a splendid manner. It was very gratifying to
all of us to note the spirit manifested, and a most enjoyable day was
spent. The Christmas tree was loaded with presents for all of the
residents ; none were overlooked or forgotten, and to your committee

the liberal manner in which the fraternity contributes to the Christmas

163

Fund for the residents of the Home is ample evidence of the interest
you have in this important branch of your charities. We were impressed with the careful training of the girls composing the orchestra.
They showed thorough preparation in their musical studies, and this is
but an indication of the general education which they are receiving at
the hands of those to whom they are entrusted, and if all else were
termed failure, we should still feel amply rewarded with the results
obtained with these young children, who are being educated and fitted
for a future career by the Masonic fraternity.
The Boys' Band contributed to the enjoyment of the day, and assisted materially in the entertainment of the visitors.
One of the resolutions referred to our committee for investigation and action was the matter of appropriation of $1500 to the Southern California Masonic Home at San Gabrie_I, California, (see page 169
Proceedings 19IB) : Early in December your committee was advised
by the M. W. Grand Master that a request had been made to him by
the Trustees of the Southern California Masonic Home, that this committee visit the Home at San Gabriel, and make an investigation of the
affairs of that institution in accordance with the resolution referring
the matter or advisability of the appropriation referred to, by the Grand
Lodge to this committee. In accordance with the request of the M. W.
Grand Master that we comply ·with the request made at as early a date
as possible, your committee made a trip to San Gabriel in the early
part of December, ancl spent the better part of a week making investigations of the affairs of the Southern California Masonic Home, meeting many of the prominent Masons of the southern portion of the State,
with whom was discussed matters pertaining to the 'Home, and it appearing that the appropriation was a just one, we so advised the M. W .
Grand Master, and upon, our return to San Francisco authorized the
payment by the V:. W:. Grand Secretary of the amount of the appropriation, viz: $1500. Owing to the crowded condition of the Home at
Decoto and the inability to accommodate an additional number desiring
to enter the Home there, the advisability of utilizing the Southern California Masonic Home was discussed with the M. W. Grand Master and
the Trustees of that institution, and after a thorough investigation and
discussion of the matter, and conference with leading Masons of the
State, all of whom were of the opinion that the situation at Decoto
demanded immediate attention in the way of affording more room, a
plan was formulated looking towards the tender of the properties of
the Southern California Masonic Home to the Grand Lodge of California; such tender was made and your committee recommended the acceptance of the same provided the transfer was made unconditionally
and free from debt. We understand that the transfer has been so made

164

PROCEEDI~GS

OF THE

and the properties placed in the hands of the Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Home of this Grand Lodge.
Your committee was influenced mainly in their recommendation to
the M. W. Grand Master by the following facts, viz:
The Home at San Gabriel is admirably located, it consists of ten
acres of valuable ground, upon which are two large buildings, the
largest of which was erected for a hotel and contained upward of fifty
bedrooms, besides offices, etc. ; the other building, which is one large
room, presumably erected for an auditorium, is in good condition, and
with some slight repairs can be made to serve the purposes of the fraternity in many ways for a number of years. The Home is lo~ated
near the town of San Gabriel, about twelve miles east of the city of
Los Angeles, on the electric car line, in the San Gabriel Valley; the
main building is three stories high and is handsomely furnished; the
dining room will accommodate nearly two hundred, and the kitchen
has ample capacity for all likely to reside there for years to come. The
grounds are in fine condition and afford room for expansion in the
way of cottages or additional buildings if required; your committee
place a conservative valuation on this property of $60,000.
The time has arrived when this Grand Lodge should undertake the
distribution of all Masonic charity pertaining to the maintenance of
Homes for the aged, the widowed, and the orphan wards of the fraternity. Owing to the crowded condition of the Home at Decoto as
well as the peculiar conditions existing geographically, the item of
traveling expense needs consideration in determining the question of
maintenance of one or more Homes, and the further advisability and
-desirability of encouraging visitation to the Homes by the fraternity
must enter largely into consideration; we are of the opinion that with
a Home at Decoto and a Home at San Gabriel, the interest of the craft
in the Homes will be largely increased and more attention will be
given to the matter of visits by Lodges and by individual Masons. At
the Home at San Gabriel the water supply is ample and adequate to
all demands and its coat reduced to a minimum. The facilities for the
care of the children in the matter of education a~e all that could be
reasonably required. The Home is within a half mile of the public
school, and we are of the opinion that it will be the pride and care
of the brethren of the south to see that everything is done for the comfort and health of the residents, and for the proper education of the
.children if entrusted to their care, which can safely be done. These,
brethren, are mainly the reascns for our recommendations to the M.
W. Grand Master regarding the Home at San Gabriel. We were also
governed by the fact that the Home at Decoto was too small to accommodate all who were entitled to entrance to the Home, for we
recognize the importance of caring for all, the aged members of the
craft, as well as the children, and believe that the time has arrived

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

165

w~en

all should have an opportunity of entering who are worthy;
this could not be done with the limited space available at Decoto, but we
are of the opinion that with the San Gabriel Home it will afford all
the room necessary for years to come.
Your committee has made a careful and exhaustive investigation
and study of the entire situation, and the recommendations submitted
herewith are the result of such study, and after consultation with
leading Masons of this jurisdiction, to whom we are indebted for
valuable suggestions and advice.
RECOMMENDATIONS.
We recommend that the two Homes now in the possession of this
Grand Lodge at Decoto and San Gabriel be µiaintained under the
following plan:
We recommend that there be one Board of Trustees consisting of
l!'IVE in number, to be appointed by the Most Worshipful Grand
Master, their term of office to be respecvvely ONE, TWO, THREE,
FOUR and FIVE years. Their tenure of office shall be determined by
lot; each succeeding Grand Master to appoint a successor, who shall
hold office for FIVE years.
We recommend that· at least two members of the Board of Trustees be appointed from Lodges in the vicinity of San Gabriel and two
from Lodges from the vicinity of Decoto, the Grand Master having
power to remove any or all of the Trustees at any time he may
deem it for the best interest of the fraternity to do so.
We recommend that the Board of Trustees when appointed shall
meet immediately thereafter and assume full charge of all matter•
pertaining to the conduct and maintenance of the Homes at Decoto
and San Gabriel; they shall organize and adopt such by·laws as they
may deem necessary, and said by-laws when adopted shall be in full
force and effect as if adopted by this Grand Lodge.
We recommend that the Grand Treasurer of the Grand Lodge be
the Treasurer of the Masonic Homes of California.
We recommend that there be created the office of Supervising
Secretary of the Masonic Homes, who shall be selected by the Board
of 'frustees, and whose duties shall be to supervise the affairs of
Masonic Homes under the direction at all times of the Board of Trustees, and to whom there shall be submitted daily reports from the
Homes upon such forms as may be required by the Board of Trustees:
He shall keep all records of said Board and make requisitions for all
supplies required :for the Homes, submitting same to the Board for
their ac.tion. He shall issue all warrants upon the Grand Treasurer for
the account of the Homes when so required by the Board of Trustees
and shall perform any and all things necessary to be done for the
conduct of the Homes under the direction of the Board of Trustees.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

He shall reside at either the Home at Decoto or the Home at San
Gabriel as shall be directed by the Board of Trustees. He shall have
general supervision of the Homes under th~ directio.n of t~e Board of
Trustees and shall receive such compensation for his services as may
be fixed by the Board of Trustees. He shall hold office at the pleasui:e
of the Board 'of Trustees.
We recommend that the Board of Trustees, if in their judgment
it be deemed necessary or advisable, employ a competent person at
each of the Homes at San Gabriel and at Decoto who shall act as
Assistant to the Secretary, and who shall in addition-to their duties
as Assistant to the Secretary, perform such other duties a~ may be
required of them to assist in the conduct of the Homes; they shall
receive such compensation as may be fixed by the Board of Trus~ees.
We recommend that the Board of Trustees adopt such regulations
for admission to the Homes as will embrace the following:
The present plan of representation in the Homes be continued, but
in the event any Lodge desires to enter more than the present allotment the said Lodge be re'l_uired to pay to the Board of Trustells the
actual cost of maintenance of such excess representation; such actual
cost of maintenance to be determined and fixed by the Board of
Trustees and be collected from the Lodge by the Grand Secretary of
the Grand Lodge in the same manner in which the Grand Lodge dues
of said Lodge is collected, such cost of maintenance not to exce~d

Many of our wealthier brethren would be moved to endow the

upon this subject, hoping to see it taken up by abler hands than

submit that its accomplishment would be a great and lasting evidence

If the path ahead does not look so easy as we could wish, let us
remember, brethren, that Masonry never failed to persist through vicissitudes and has always presented such a solidarity of purpose that
upon its altars the sun never sets. Let us not grow weary. of the
work we have undertaken; let no man compare California Masonry
with that of jurisdictions elsewhere, where they only pay one dollar
per annum lodge dues, whereas our Masonic charities amount to more
than double that sum. Because some of these ~·dollar' ' States have

great work, let us keep it up; but remember, "it is one thing to soar
on the wings of genera!itie!J and quite another to work out the mechanism of flight.'' Be charitable with our humble efforts. Help us to so
· improve and perfect the syetem that it shall round out a beautiful
whole to the honor of Masonry in this Grand Jurisdiction for all

we now possess, both perfect and complete within themselves, segregating the young from the old, male and female, but allowing them

Ma.on himself was taught to do.'' Not all will want to go to

lo all ways; let the Homes be but one of these, and never forget ''the
poor are with us always, and that life's highway i1 strewn with
lo11es,'' and the kinder Masonry is and becomes, the more it ftghh
the eternal law of nature, the survival of the fittest, by extending

do not fold your cloak around you and point to the Home; in1tead,
let him feel the strong grip; it may help him to his feet. Never allow
charity to take semblance of an abstract machine instead of a concrete

tlesf Because they so loved Masonry that night after night they have
worked till midnight and toiled over the complex problems, earnestly,
honestly and with great ability, all this "without the hope of fee or
reward.''

our jurisdiction unless satisfactory evidence be furnished by the action

certified, that the applicant is worthy and that his standing and character are such as would entitle him to affiliation in such Lodge. In
this case no such certificate accompanies the petition for restoration.

To the M:. w:. Grand Lod~e of California:
Your Committee, to whom was .tderred the trial record in the
case of Charles Wolf, expelled by El ~entro Lodge, No. 384, have
had the same under consideration and re•ctfully report as follows:
There was absolutely no legal eviderte heard by the trial commissioners. The accused was charged with defrauding brother Masons
in Colorado, Illinois and Virginia by drawing worthless checks and
securing money on the same upon his representation that he was a
Master Mason. The evidence introduced before the trial commissioners
consisted solely of letters written to the officers of El Centro Lodge
by the brothers whom he had defrauded. These letters were offered in
evidence without any showing whatever as to the genuineness of the
signatures, and were, of course, hearsay, pure and simple. In addition
to the brothers whose names are set out in the charges, Brother Wolf
appears to have obtained money in the same manner from a large
number of other brothers residing in various parts of the United
States whose complaints by letter were also introduced in evidence
before the trial commissioners. We have repeatedly decided that a
Mason, can only be expelled upon a fair trial and in a legal manner ;
it will be the duty of the Lodge to proceed to a second trial in this
matter and take the depositions of such of the victims of this brother's

OPERATIVE OR SPECULATIVE?
Emerson has said that "the kind of men the nation produces is the
true test of a nation's greatness." Whether it be an oligarchy or a democracy, whether it be based on constitutional liberty or be the product
of an absolute despotism, a nation's place in history is determined by
the men it gives to the world.
The same observation is peculiarly true of each and every of our
great fraternal organizations. All, so far as I am advised, are founded
upon enduring principles of equality, fraternity and morality. No one,
however, achieves distinction save from the character and class of men
who bear its banner forward. The particular lessons taught by its
ritual, if known, would be bi.:t a secondary consideration with an applicant for admission. There is no occasion for the individual who
desires mer ely to become acquainted with high ideals or great moral

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

truths, to pass the closely guarded portals of any secret society. The
best teachings of the best fraternity ever instituted among men cannot
compare with the simple lessons which fel! from the lips of the Man
of Nazareth and which today are the comfort, the solace and the
inspiration of enlightened manhood and womanhood everywhere. He,
however, who desires not only to be and do good, but also to be and
remain in constant touch and close communion with men who are
similarly inclined and who by the force of initiative, superior will
or friendly example may lead him on to higher and better things in
life, if he have any inclinations toward membership in a fraternal
society such as ours, will instinctively turn to that one whose roll of
membership comes nearest, in his opinion, to a roll of honor. He
will sedulously seek the fraternal companionship of those men who,
in their daily existence, in their social and business relations, in the
multitude of trivialities that go to make up this complex thing called
"life," give an outward proof of an inward determination to be of
benefit to their fellow man. He will knock at those doors that offer
the greatest assurance of opening upon men· whose ~haracter and
standing and deeds of high resolve have made for substantial progress
toward the betterment of humankind.
Fraternities, like unto nations, then, are gauged by their men. The
only fraternity that can be great is that fraternity which has or has
had great men to mould and shape its course-men great not because
they have acquired unusual wealth or attained unusual preferment,
but because of their extraordinary capacity to foresee man's opportunities to do good and because of their innate ability to "do noble
things, not dream them all day long." And as that nation that gives
to its citizens the best environment, the best government and the
least restraint compatible with the general tranquility, thereby serves
10 develop the best and the greatest of men, so that fraternity whose
·basic principles, teachings of morality and accepted standards of good
•conduct most nearly approach the divine attributes of God's Appointed,
furnishes the most sublime examples of fraternal loyalty and human
.endeavor.
Lord Brougham, one of the greatest of British statesmen, once
said: "All that we see about us, Kings, Lords and Commons, the
whole machinery of the State, all the apparatus of the system and
its varied workings, end in simply bringing twelve good men into a
box." By this he meant that governments are instituted among men, ·
constitutions are ordained, executives are clothed with power, congresses and parliaments are assembled, laws are enacted and tribunals
are set up simply and solely in order that society and every individual
member thereof shall be the recipient of that which is justly duenothing more, nothing less.

In the same way, fraternal societies have been organized, rituals
have been compiled, obligations have been administered, lectures have
been delivered, Grand and Subordinate Lodges have been constituted
and convened, in order that there might be caused to be written, in
1£tters of living light, along the horizon of the activities of every
human being, that phrase so pregnant with hope for humanity :-"I am
my brother's keeper."
Freemasonry has ever been noted for its men-men who have
been the leaders in the world's activities; men who have shed a bright
and enduring lustre on the kaleidoscopic page of history; men who
have brought solace and sunshine into the homes and hearts of the
widowed and orphaned and fanned anew the fires of fraternal love
in the breasts of the aged and incapacitated; yea, men who have seen
and felt in Liberty, Equality, Fraternity and Morality the touchstones
of human progress, the capstones of human achievement.
But again, just as it is true that no nation can live and thrive on
th<' record of its glorious past, so it is also true that no great frah:rnity can so live and thrive. The place that Freemasonry will
occupy in the world's estimation tomorrow is not the place that it
occupied yesterday, but the place that it is making for itself today.

176

177

"Over my head the stars, distant and pale and cold ;
Under my feet the world, wrinkled and scarred and old;
Back of me all that was, all the limitless Past,
The Futur~ waiting beyond, silent, untenanted, vast;
"Babylon lies in the dust; never a sentinel calls
With fear on his parted lips from any of Ninevah's walls;
Troy is only a name; Ca:sar is deaf to praise,
Back of me spreads the Past in numberless yesterdays;
"I stand at the end of the Past- where the Future begins I stand;
Emperors lij! in the dust; men may live to command ;
But greater than rulers unborn, greater than kings who have reigned
Am I that have hope in my heart, and victories still to be gained!
Under my feet the world; over my head the sky;H ere at the center of things, in the Living Present am I!"
Let it not, for any cause, be said of our organization that it
exhibits much in the way of promise but little in the way of endeavor,
"The waves of shame and sorrow roll over the ruins of many lives
that have found shipwreck in a sea of promises." Promises without
performance do not constitute fraternity, any more than great faith
and no works constitutes religion. In Masonry we want to think

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

well of a man not for having taken an obligation to do many things.
nor even for having taken many obligations t-Q do one thing, but for
having done a few things.
.
Our Ancient Brethren were workers. They wrought m woo.ct.
and stone and marble and brass, and they knew how to use to advantage the square, the level and the plumb. To. the~ alone,. partly .by
reason of a monopoly, principally by reason of their supenor att~m­
ments as practical builders, was entrusted the buildin&:, the squar.mg,.
the leveling and the truing of all great works of architecture. . Smee
the· reorganization of the craft in England, however, we'. their successors, have been content to describe ourselves as Speculative Masons,
and to refer to our Ancient Brethren whose garb we have put on a_nd
whos'e tools we employ, as Operative Masons. They were operative
Masons ; they worked; they builded-builded even better tha~ they
knew. The results of their endeavors were and are yet seen m the·
many imposing edifices of the Old World . We engage in no such
works ; our hands are strangers to the chisel and the mallet, and
it would be a most arduous undertaking, I dare say, for even our·
Most Worshipful Grand Master, primus inter pares, the first am?ng
us, to endeavor to apply the tools of architecture of o.ur Anc1~nt:
Brethren, now symbolically employed by us, to the uses for which<
they were originally intended.
We would do well, though, I apprehend, my brothers, were we to
take to ourselves· more of the operative characteristics that seemed'
to ennoble, and perpetuate the virtues of, our Masonic ancesto~s. T:'
be speculative is to be philosophical, meditative, contemplative; it
implies a condition of mere thinking-;thinking perhaps of ~h~t has
been done or thinking even of what ought to be done-but it is not
doing. O~r Ancient Brethren, the operative Masons, did not retire·
to the recesses of their closets, there to contemplate and reflect upon
the needs of . their time. Masonry, intended and regarded as the most
practical exemplification of the living, breathing principles of Fraternity that the world may ever know, is not, and never should. be·
permitted to become, the field for me~e Casuists. Works, pract1ca~
results, genuine successes along any Imes of endeavor, are secu~ed
only, if at all, by workers. We must become, once more, Operative·
Masons.
.
Masonry, in its every conception, ought to be esse~tiall~ act1v~,.
transitive, dynamic, energetic, operative, rather than passive, mt~ans1tive, static, inert, speculative. We must remember _that the.re is n:i
nobler sentiment than that of him who said: "There 1s a loftier ambition than merely to stand high in the world ; it is to stoop down and'
lift mankind a little higher. There is a nobler character than that
which is merely incorruptible; it is that character which acts as anc
antidote and preventive of corruption."

The genius of our Ancient Brethren lay in rearing Heavenward
those mightly piles, of Antiquity, dedicated and devoted to religious
uses. With them, as workers in wood and stone, Man's duty to God
and Man was best subserved by erecting those temporal buildings
wherein all might unite in rendering praise and thanksgiving unto
the ever living God. To us, since we no longer work in wood and
stone, is now entrusted the more ennobling duty of fitting our minds
as living stones for that spiritual building, that house not made with
hands, eternal in the Heavens. Ours is the duty of fashioning temples, as was theirs; not temples, however, of blocks and timbers,
adorned with gold and silver and precious stones, but temples of
flesh and blood, enriched and imbued with an immortal spirit-a
spirit which, reflecting the paternity of God, proclaims the fraternity
of man; not temples fashioned from human designs and plans, but
fashioned in the image of our Common Creator.
Each being with whom we come in contact is such a . temple.
Wherever that te~ple stands, so long as it is not wholly lost to the
intense divinity of man and the intense humanity of God, there is a
field for activity in Operative Masonry. And whoever labors on that
edifice with usefulness or distinction ; whoever plants its feet upon
the firm foundation of truth and virtue; whoever warms its heart
t:i a realization of the nearness of the ever-outstretched hand of
Charity and Brotherly Love, ready, willing and anxious to render
assistance; whoever guides its hands to deeds af charity and acts of
love; whoever contributes to instill into its mind pure thoughts and
honorable ambitions, has inseparably linked himself by a chain of
sincere affection to the immortal brotherhood of truly operative Masons. He, however, who fails, in Lodge or out, by day or by
night, through inadvertence or neglect, when travelling the path
either of prosperity or adversity, so to live up to the spirit of his
obligations, irrespective of the vows he may have taken, the lectures
he may have conned, or the promises he may have given, is not and
never can be an Operative Mason. He is in truth and in fact, at
best, only a mere Speculative Mason.
Our Ancient Brethren, as I had occasion to observe, and as the
early ~hroniclers testify, enjoyed a monopoly in the matter of building.
This monopoly-both benevolent and beneficent in its nature-resulted
naturally from their innate ability to carry to a successful conclusion
the work which they entered upon. We, their successors, however,
can expect, and should, in fact, desire, to participate in no such monopoly in the work in which we are engaged. Just as it is true that
there is no caste in morality, so is it also true that there can be no
monopoly of that the seeds of which God himself has planted in every
human heart. Masonry today welcomes, and has naught but words
of praise for, the efforts of all similar organizations. The State, the

178

li9

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

·Home and the Individual, the beneficiaries of that which we, as
Masons, hope and strive to accomplish, will be enabled the sooner to
profit, if to our efforts there be added the efforts .of others similarly
inclined and similarly engaged. It may be true, as existing contro·
versies would seem to indicate, that the North Pole is insufficient in
extent to accommodate more than one man ; but there can be no
doubt that in the broad domain devoted to Fraternity, Equality and
Morality, there are to be found fields of activity as boundless as the
shores of Time and as measureless as the sands of the sea, wherein
all who wish may till.
Temples such as those our Ancient Brethren contrived to erect,
beautiful and artistic though they were, were but cold and inanimate
objects whose existence was but ephemeral. The living temples which
it is our province to adorn are warmed by the breath of the Eternal
Spirit, which will never perish. On yesterday we wended our way to
the site of the new Scottish Rite Temple in this city and witnessed
the solemn and inspiring ceremonies whereby its cornerstone was lowered into place; in a short while the Craft of our entire great State
will unite in the erecting of a new home for this Grand Lodge and
it;, kindred bodies. The architectural splendor of these well proportioned edifices soon-to-be will no doubt bespeak the praise of men
throughout all time to come. The grandeur of the Temple of Solomon
on Mount Moriah, never excelled by human effort, a thing of the
past though it is, has been the theme and admiration of all successive I
ages. But the most enduring grandeur, next to that which flows
from the Almighty Throne itself, is the grandeur of a noble' and
well-spent life, wrapping itself in benediction round the destinies of
its fellowmen and finally reaching its eternal home in the blessed
bosom of the everlasting God.
Tradition tells us that when Cornelia, the noble Roman matron,
was called upon to exhibit her most precious possessions, she pointed
to her two sturdy sons, known in history as the Gracchi, the Tribunes
of the people, who gave their lives that Rome might not perish, and
proudly said, "These are my jewels.",
Let it be our ·constant endeavor, my brothers, so to live and act
as operative Masons that when we are called upcin to render an account
of our stewardship to our Supreme Grand Master above, we may point
with pride not only to the halls and temples and similar edifices •erected
under our direction and supervision, but also to a galaxy of mennoble men-whose hearts have been caused to resporft:l to the eternal
truths, whose tongues have been taught to proclaim the living principles, and whose hands have been guided to perform the glorious
deeds that go to make up practical, operative Fraternity.
Masonry, true operative ~asonry, is as enduring as it is universal.
Appealing to the better nature of man, divorcing him from his baser

instincts, it will last as long as Time itself. Though existing under
the ban of the Church, persecuted as an enemy by intolerant governments and denounced by untiring fanatics, "it still stands, like some
patriarchical monarch of the forest, with its vigorous roots riveted
to the soil, and its broad limbs spread in bold outline against the
sky," the first and foremost of its kind.
May its ideal exponent be described and depicted as one whose
good deeds outshine his aspirations, whose aspirations o'erleap his
obligations, and whose obligations mount up as high as the bounds
of human endeavor and reach down as low as the depths of human
necessity.
Nor think such an ideal too high. No ideal is too high merely
because it may appear to be beyond our reach, "else," as Browning
said, "why a Heaven?" Throughout all ages God has implanted in
the heart of man a yearning for the ideal, and man has ever best
reflected God's ultimate purpose by worshiping at its shrine. Ours may
be the materialistic age, but, as of yore, the idealistic will ever be
its goal.

"Mother Earth ! are the heroes dead?
Do they thrill the soul of the years no more?
Are the gleaming snows and the poppies red
All that is left of the brave of yore?
Are there none 'to fight as Theseus fought,
Far in the young world's misty dawn?
Or to teach as the gray-haired Nestor taught?
Mother Earth ! are the heroes gone?
"Gone? In a grander form they rise;
Dead? We may clasp their hands in ours;
And catch the light of their clearer eyes
And wreath their brows with immortal flowers.
Wherever a noble deed is done
'Tis the pulse of a hero's heart is stirred;
Wherever right has a triumph won
There arc the heroes' voices heard.
"Their armor rings on a fairer field
Than the Greek and the Trojan fiercely trod,
For Freedom's sword is the blade they wield,
And the light above is the smile of God.
So, in his isle of calm delight,
Jason may sleep the years away;
For the heroes live, ~nd the sky is bright,
And the world is a braver world today."
