To the M .". w:. Grand L odge of Californi(JJ:

Your Committee, to whom was referred the proceedings of Visalia
Lodge, No. 128, F . & A. M., in the matter of the trial for unmasonic
conduct of Bro. Daniel Osborn, of said Lodge, beg leave to report as
follows :
Brother Osborn was accused by the Junior Warden of said Lodge
with i.mmasonic conduct in that, as specified, he appropriated at different times to his own use moneys collected by him as conductor of
the Visalia Electric Railway. At the hearing, which was duly and
• regularly ordered, he admitted his guilt, professed penitence, showed
that he had been restored to his position by the superintendent of the
said railway company, himself a Mason, after full knowledge of his
offense ; but was thereafter discharged by said superintendent because,
as alleged, he had made statements derogatory of the character of
the said superintendent's wife. So far as these statements are concerned it is sufficient to say that Brother Osborn flatly and positively
denied having made them, and there is in the record, of course, no
proof that he ever did make them.
At the meeting on June 26, 1909, the commissioners by a unanimous
vote found the accused brother guilty both upon the charge and all the
s?ecifications save one. They refused, however, by the same vote,
either to expel or suspend him, determining only that he be reprimanded.
The Master announced to the Lodge the result of the trial
July 17, 1909. The Junior W arden, by the notice given August 17,
1909, appeals from the decision, on the ground that the penalty is contrary to Masonic law and inadequate.
An appeal must be taken in thirty days from the date of the announcement by the Master of the result of the action of the commissioners. This appeal was not taken within the time. However in
consideration of this matter, your Committee is disposed to disre~ard
this fact, particularly as it is not disposed to recommend that the
action of the Lodge be disturbed. It is true that the crime of embezzlement has uniformly been held justly and properly to be one of the
grossest. of Masonic offenses. It is true in this case the amounts
shown to have been embezzled were but small, almost trifling, but
this is little or no mitigation. Since, however, the accused brother
seems to have sincerely regretted and repented his misdeed, and since
his offense has been condoned both by the company for whom he
worked and by his Lodge, we do not think it advisable, notwithstanding
the inadequate penalty, to recommend a reversal of the action.
Respectfully submitted,
GEo. E. CHURCH,
H . M. Ow:tNs,
Committee.

Your Committee, to whom was referred the trial record of Bro.
Thomas Alexis Nerney, a member of San Diego Lodge, No. 35, who

Brother Nerney was charged with unmasonic conduct, as set forth
in the following specifications:
First: That on or about the 13th day of October, 1906, in the
City and County of San Francisco, the said Thomas Alexis Nerney,
as agent for the Pettibone Manufacturing Company, of Cincinnati,
·Ohio, rendered a bill to California Chapter No. 5, Royal Arch Masons,
for paraphernalia furnished said Chapter, in the sum of $987.95, the
receipt of which amount was acknowledged by him; whereas, the
amount actually received by him was only $750.75, thereby falsely
representing that the whole amount of $987.95 was the price of the
paraphernalia so purchased and paid for by said California Chapter,
No. 5, Royal Arch Masons.
Second: That on or about the 1st day of December, 1906, in the
City and County of San Francisco, the said Thomas Alexis Nerney, as
agent for the Pettibone Brothers Manufacturing Company, of Cincinnati, Ohio, rendered a bill to California Chapter, No. 5, Royal Arch
Masons, for paraphernalia furnished said Chapter, in the sum of
$1,862.25, the receipt of which was acknowledged by him; whereas, the
amount actually received by him was only $1,401.00, falsely represent·

In the Matter of Thomas Alexis Nerney.
Comes now the accused; Thomas Alexis Nerney, and for answer
to the charges filed with the M.". w:. Grand Master of Masons of
California by Henry Ascroft, admits that he, as the agent for the

that the whole amount of $987.95 was the price of paraphernalia purchased and paid for by said California Chapter.

R£lyal Arch Masons, for paraphernalia furnished said Chapter in the

only $1,401.00. Denies that he falsely represented that the whole amount

In addition to that above the accused testified that Brother Henning represented to the accused that he (Henning) wanted th~ bills
made out in full for the reason that Brother Henning wanted the
difference between the long bills and the short bills to be placed in an
entertainment fund, but because it was so seen after the fire they did ·
not want such items to appear.

any of the mcney the Chapter was supposetl to pay for the goods.

evidence in the records that he did receive a part of it, or knew that
Brother Henning was going to retain any portion of it and not report
the exact transaction to the Chapter. The accused also testified that
it was his custom to receipt both the long and short bills in the case of
allowing a commission. Taking the evidence as it appears, we are
satisfied that there was no criminal intent on the part of Brother
Nerney in doing this. Nevertheless, his action in tl:iis matter has been
grossly indiscreet.

M.". W.". Wm. S. Wells, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, reported as follows :
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee, to whom was referred the resolution offered by
Brother J. D. Tucker relative to Pacific Lodge, No. 822, under the
jurisdiction of Scotland and located at Honolulu, in the Island of
Oahu, Territory of Hawaii, have had the same under consideration and
report as follows :
The question involved herein was considered by the Grand Lodge
first in 1894 in the La Valle de France Lodge matter, where Past
Grand Mast~r Belcher, reporting for the Committee on Jurisprudence
said : "The question then recurs, can we receive this Lodge and its
members into our family, and if so, under what condition ? We
answer that with our present knowledge only we could not recognize
or receive the Lodge as a Lodge."
Stating various reasons why they could not, which reasons do
not apply to the case under discussion, that Committee then continue :
"Only one other way suggests itself to us for the accomplis~ment
of the purpose desired by the members of that Lodge, and t?at .1s for
them to surrender their charter to the Grand Lodge from which tt was
received. That being done, so many of its members as were made in
regular Lodges would be free to seek affiliation and membership ~n
other Lodges, and when a sufficient number had so placed thems~ves .m
good standing, to make application to the Grand Master for his dispensation for a new Lodge."
.
This was next considered in the matter of Le Progress L'Oceanic
Lodge, No. 124, A. and A. S. R. of Honolulu, Territory of Hawaii_,
and reported in Volume 26 of Proceedings at Pages 1080-1081.
This was a case where the Lodge had petitioned the Supreme
Council ·of France for permission to terminate its relation with that
body and requested this Grand Lodge to issue a charter or dispensation at once, with the proviso that it be delivered immediately upon
receipt of permission from the Supreme Council. This Committee at
that time reported :
"The proposition to accept as one of our family of Jf>dges a
Lodge chartered and constituted under another Grand Body is a new
one, as far at least as this Grand Lodge is concerned, and we doubt
whether under our Constitution any such procedure would be warranted Our Constitution provides in great detail the method by which
a Lod~e may be organized and the circumstances under which a dispensation or charter may be granted, and it may well be doubted
whether any other method can legally be followed. If twelve or more
Master Masons in Honolulu were to organize a new Lodge therein

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

199

under our jurisdiction, they may proceed under Section 2 of Article
I, of Part III, of our Constitution, and apply at any time to the Grand
Master for a dispensation."
With these decisions we are in entire accord, and considet it
Inadvisable to make any change in our Constitution relative thereto;
and are of the opinion that our Constitution now prohibits such
action. The same ruling applies to the communication in relative
to Mauia Lodge, No. 984, Grand Lodge of Scotland. The matter
1·1111 only be reached by an amendment to the Constitution and not
by resolution.
We therefore recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
Respectfully submitted,
WM.

M. H. Fr.INT,

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee to whom was referred the resolution offered
by Brother 0. M. Goldaracena, relative to waiver of jurisdiction over
aapirants for degrees who do not speak the English language, have
had the same under consideration and report as follows :
This is a matter which would require an amedment to the Constitution, the effect of which would be to permit a person, residing for .
ln1tance in Shasta County and speaking only the French language, to
make application to the French Lodge in San Francisco for the
degree without the necessity of any Lodge in Shasta County passing
upon his qualifications to become a Mason. This we do not consider
advisable. The Lodge within whose jurisdiction an applicant resides,
whether he speaks the language or not, is best qualified to pass upon
his petition. Of course in such a case it would be highly proper for
the Lodge within whose jurisdiction the applicant resided, to waive
Jurisdiction and to consent that the French Lodge con'f er the degree
without requiring any fee to be paid to them; provided they considered
him in all other respects qualified and good material, and it seems
Impossible that any Lodge in this jurisdiction would refuse such request under such circumstance.
.
We therefore recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
Respectfully submitted,
WM.
WELLS,
M. H. FLINT,
c. L. PATTON,

w:. Grand Lodg1 of California:
Your Committee, to whom was referred the resolution offered
by Brother J. W . Eddy, Junior Warden of Paso Robles Lodge, No.
l86, relative to receiving a petition for degrees from one engaged in
the manufacture or sale of intoxicating liquors, have had the· same
under consideration and report as follows :
This is a matter which cannot be reached by resolution, but must
be by an amedment· to the Constitution. Such an amendment was
offered in 1899, by which it was proposed to amend the Constitution
by adding as a final paragraph to Section 2 of Article III, Part III,
the following :
"Nor shall any Lodge receive such application from any person
who shall be engaged in the sale of intoxicating liquors."
f ,, the M.".

The Committee on Jurisprudence, consisting of Past Grand Masters
l'reston, Rucker, Johnston, Stevens and Angellotti, reported as follows:
"The proposed amendment, if adopted, would introduce class legislation into our Constitution-a thing that is repugnant to the principles
of Freemasonry. By one of the unchangeable tenets of our Order,
each Lodge is constituted the sole judge of the moral and social fitness
of any applicant who knocks at its outer door for admittance. Temperance is one of the cardinal principles of Freemasonry. Its precepts
are inherent in our ceremonies. They are unchangeable, and, therefore,
more permanent and just as obligatory as the mandates of our Constitution. The Lodge, or the individual Mason, who disregards the requirements of temperance to such an extent as to injure the good name
of Masonry, becomes, by the very force of our traditions, subject to
Masonic discipline. We, therefore, recommend that the proposed
amendment be not adopted."
This report was concurred in by the Grand Lodge. The resolution
under consideration is more drastic than anything yet offered. We are
in thorough accord with the decision of the Committee, and the Grand
Lodge, which has been the law of this jurisdiction since 1900, and we
think that the individual Lodges are in a better position to cope with
and handle this question as it may arise.
We, therefore, recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
Respectfully sub.mitted,
WM.

s. WU.LS,

M. H. FLINT,

c. r.. PATTON,
Tuos. FUNT,

To th e M." . w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee, to whom was referred the request for. a dispensation to hold a meeting of Hope Lodge on the brow of a hill near
the Lodge room, presented by Bro. L. H. Hughes, Master of Hope
Lodge, have had the same under consideration and report as follows :

· This matter was considered by Grand Master Perine in the case
of Mizpah Lodge, No. 378, and he held that the Constitution of the
Grand Lodge does not provide for a Lodge session at any other place
except in their Lodge room, and that it was improper to hold it in the
open.
This Committee and the Grand Lodge approved that decision.
In this case the Lodge room was destroyed by fire and they request
that they be granted a dispensation to hold the October 'stated meeting
in the open. We think this would be a dangerous precedent and one
not contemplated or permitted by the Constitution.
The Lodge should as soon as practicable arrange for a suitable
Lodge room, and until that is done no meeting should be held.
We, therefore, recommend that the request for a dispensation be
denied.
Respectfully submitted,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Bro. J. D. Murphey, from the Committee on Grievances, reported as follows :
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee, to whom was referred the transcript of the record
of the trial of Richard Walpole Kent, expelled by Tuolumne Lodge,
No. 8, and from which judgment of expulsion the accused has appealed,
have had the same under consideration and respectfully report as
follows:
The trial procedure was in accordance with the requirements of our
laws. The accused was charged with habitual intoxication. At the
outset of the trial, the accused filed the following written request for a
continuance:
"Sonora, California, Feb. 6, 1909.
"Brother Wm. L. Hood,
"Dear Sir and Brother: As Bro. F. W. Street is not in
town, and we have not had time to go into the case ( as the
papers were delivered to me eight days ago), will you kindly
postpone my trial set for February 6, 1909, for one week? By
so doing you will greatly oblige,
"Yours truly,
"RICHARD W. KltNT. "

Which request the master decided was not a sufficient ground for
continuance. This was a matter for the commissioners to decide, and
-0ne concerning which the Master should take no active part. The
Master in a Masonic trial acts in a judicial capacity and should act
upon the questions of law presented and remained absolutely neutral in
the matters properly directed to the commissioners for decision.
The grounds set forth in the request, the absence of the attorney
and the inability to prepare his case, when made in good faith, are
legitimate reasons for a continuance, and as this request was made at
the first meeting of the commissioners and only ten days after service
of summons, and as the time asked was reasonable, we think that the
trial commissioners erred in not allowing it.
Whatever may be the opinion of the commissioners and of the
Master as to the culpability of the accused and the necessity for weeding
him out of the Fraternity, they must not lose sight of the fact that
the Masonic trial must be beyond the suspicion of unfairness, and no
vrinciple of our laws is more firmly established than that the accused
shall not be forced to trial until he shall have had a reasonable opportunity to prepare his defense.

We recognize the right of the accused to appear by attorney, and
when a proper showing is made of the absence of the attorney he has
1r1lected to represent him or his inability to be present at the trial, no
11111umption of bad faith should be indulged in; on the contrary, when
the request is reasonable on its face, as it appears to be in this case,
It ahould be granted.
As a new trial of this case must be had, we shall call attention to
the fact that the record bristles with improper testimonr. Nearly ~very
witness is asked whether in his opinion the accused is a "disgrace to the
Fraternity ;" each is asked as to the general reputation of the accused
In the community in which he resides for drunkenness. Generally the
witnesses frankly admit that their information is purely hearsay, but
nevertheless they were permitted to state that in their opinion the conduct of the accused was a reproach to the Fraternity.
'
In view of the numerous decisions of the Grand Lodge as to the
lnndmissibility of this character of testimony, it is earnestly to be hop~d
thnt trial commissioners will sometime find it convenient to adhere to
Its plain admonitions. Witnesses ought not to be called upon for their
conclusions. They should detail the facts and not usurp the functions
of the judges, whose duty it is to draw the conclusions.
It may "not be amiss to notice one other matter in the record:
The attorney for the accused questions the propriety of calling as a
witness a physicia~ who attended the accused when suffering from the
effects of one of his alleged indiscretions. We think there is no merit
In this contention. We have held that the statutes governing State
courts in relation to confidential communications should govern in
Masonic trials, and that, therefore, the attorney cannot be compelled
to disclose facts communicated to him as such, but the same rule does
not apply as between physician and patient. The State statutes make
such communications confidential in civil actions only. As the trial of a
Masonic offense is in the nature of a criminal proceeding, we see no
good reason for extending the rule to cover such cases in Masonic
tribunals.
'

We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
R esolv ed, That the action of Tuolumne Lodge, No. 8, in expelling
Richard W. Kent be and the same hereby is reversed and a new trial
ordered.
Respectfully submitted,
J. D. MURPH!lY,
H. M. 0w:£Ns,
Gto. E. CHURCH,
Committee.

Which was adopted as read.

That Section 11, Article III, Part III, .be amended to read as
follows:
Section 11. No Lodge shall expel a member for the non-payment
of dues ; but, in case any member shall have refused or neglected to
pay his regular dues during a period of twelve months, he shall be
notified by the Secretary, either by registered letter deposited in the
United States post office addressed to him at his last known address,
or by actual service of notice, duly certified by the Tyler, that unless
at the next stated meeting either his dues be p~id, or sickness or inability to pay be shown as the cause of such refusal or neglect, he will
be suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
If neither of these things be done, he shi;ill, ;i.t such stated meet·
ing, be declared by the Master to be suspended; but any Mason thus
suspended who shall, at any time prior to the expiration of two years
thereafter, pay the arrearages due at the time of his suspension, together with such further dues as would, had he retained his membership, have ac~rued against him to the date of such payment, shall be
restored.
Any Mason who remains suspended for more than two years, and
thereafter shall pay the amount due at the time of suspension, together
with such further dues as would have accrued during the said two
years and such further dues as would, had he retained his membership,
have accrued against him to the date of such payment, or such less
sum as the Lodge shall, by vote, decide to accept, which shall not be
less than the amount due at the time of suspension, together with the
dues accrued during said two years, shall, by such act, be restored to
the rights and privileges of a non-affiliate; and a certificate under seal
of the Lodge, signed by the Secretary, setting forth the facts, shall
have the force and virtue of a proper dimit accompanying an applicati on for membership.
Any Secretary failing or neglecting to comply with the requirements of this section relative to notifying delinquents shall be subject
to discipline by his Lodge for neglect of duty.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.
MASONIC HOME. .

Probably the foremost question now under consideration by the
various Grand Jurisdictions of the United States is that which has
relation in some of its aspects to the general proposition of Masonic
Homes, either acquiring plans for adjuncts of this character by .jurisdictions that have them not, or problems of administration by those
that have; and we believe it is the deliberate judgment of those who
have had comprehensive experience in both departments of this great
question, that the initial achievement of getting the Home is but a
triflins- circumstance in comparison with the difficulties of succes.s ful
and satisfactory administration; and yet it is undoubtedly true that
even in those cases where Homes have been prolific of vexatious and
well nigh unbearable conditions, and where the expenses of administration have largely exceeded estimates, and have, in consequence,
imposed unlooked-for burdens upon the membership, there has been
no regret at the steps taken, and no thought of turning backward in
the work of making our institutions of this character real' homes,
where the atmosphere shall be sweet, and pure, and wholesome, and
where all suggestions of "Man's imperfect state by nature" shall be
removed.
The Grand Lodge of California imposes a per capita tax of .$1 upon
its. membership for the support of its Masonic Home, and this is in
addition to other Grand Lodge dues, amounting to a dollar more; and
never in the fifteen or more years since the project of the Home was
first entered upon has there been an adverse vote cast in the Grand
Lodge upon any question involving the imposition of a tax, the assuming of a burden, or the expenditure of money for the benefit of our
institution at Decoto; and the spirit of California Masons is such that
if a contribution of one dollar each for the support of our Home
should not prove adequate, two dollars would be voted.
California is upon the outer rim of our continent; the flag of
empire halts here in its westward course. California manhood is
formed from a blending of the brave and venturesome, the strong and
virile of all the other States of our Union.
California Masonry is as big as California manhood; it recognizes
that good is measured not by what one gets but by what one gives;
that one is raised by rais.i ng others. This is the spirit that supports
the great monument of Masonic Love in California, the spirit that
animates American Masonry, wherever it is found, for, whether on
the hills or in the valleys of our own broad land, or on the shores
of the frozen ocean, or in the islands of the tropical seas, wherever
there floats the Stars and Stripes, the truest type of Masonry is foundthe type that asks not "what can we get," but "what can we give."
Alabama, overflowing with soul and sentiment, distinguished always by pride and patriotism, with a people generous and genial, and

3

actuated by the moving spirit of fraternal kindn.ess, has ~etermined
tt · found a Masonic Home, and the consummat10n of this purpose
I he foremost work of Alabama Masonry today.

l'OREIGN CORRESPONDENCE.

The Foreign Correspondence report was rendered by the capable
and learned Chairman of the committee, W.'. Brother William Y.
Titcomb. Preliminary to the review of the various jurisdictions there
are special reports from the committee, which reports were duly
adopted, the substance of which was as follows:
First. Declining to grant request of the Grand Orient of Brazil
for r\!cognition, on the ground that it is not a Sovereign Grand Body;
and, secondly, postponing the decision of similar requests from the
Grand Lodge of Paraguay, and Guatemala, and the Grand Lodge "Cosmos" of Chihuahua, Mexico, until replies could be received to sev,ral
questions which had been propounded to the official heads of the several
jurisdictions covering certain fundamental qualities which must needs
exist as conditions precedent to recognition. The essential and necessary qualities are, without doubt, correctly enumerated by the committee as follows: First, that the Body seeking recognition confine
itself to the practice of the Three Degrees of Symbolic· Masonry; that
it hold itself bound to 'keep inviolate the Ancient Landmarks, and that
it is a Sovereign, Independent Grand Lodge, acknowledging no superior,
such as Supreme Council, thereby entitling it to be regarded as the
peer of all other Grand Lodges.
The general report of the committee reviewed sixty jurisdictions
in a comprehensive manner, affording a fund of information, critical
and otherwise, of exceeding value.

ALBERTA, 1908.
Third Annual Communication.
Edmonton, Province of Alberta.
May 27, 1908.
Three Special Communications of the Grand Lodge were held
during the year-the first for the purpose of adopting the new Constitution, and the others for the purpose of laying the corner stones
of public buildings; one, the Alexander Taylor Public School, at
Edmonton, and the other the new Masonic Building at Pincher Creek.
The Third Annual Communication of the M.'.
Grand Lodge
of Alberta, Ancient, Free and Accepted Masons, was opened in the
Masonic Hall, at the city of Edmonton, Province of Alberta, on Wednesday, May 27, A. D. 1908, A. L. 5908, at the hour of 10 o'clock a. m.,
M.'. W ;'. Headley C. Taylor, Grand Master, presiding.
The Grand Lodge of Alberta has only in very recent years taken
its place among the Sovereign Grand Lodges of Free ·and Acc<;1>ted
Masons of the world. Its growth during the past few years has been
marked, and especially during the year closed with the present Annual
Communication has the percentage of growth made phenomenal, the
actual net increase in membership during the year being 555, giving
the jurisdiction a total membership at this time of 2,225, the membership at the last Communication having been 1,670.
The jurisdiction at this time has twenty-five chartered Lodges and
fourteen under dispensation. The total income of the Grand Lodge
during the preceding year was $3,436.55, and the cash on hand in the
hands of the Grand Treasurer $1,847.08.

Dispensations during the preceding year were grante.d to for'?
thirteen new Lodges, charters for all of which were authorized at this
Communication.

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

The Grand Master in his address extends congratulations to the
Grand Lodge upon the great prosperity existing throughout the jurisdiction and voices a caution that in the rapid growth which the jurisdiction is now enjoying, great care should be exercised in the selection
of material for membership, this care being especially needful in a
new and growing community such as Alberta.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

In Arizona there is, naturally, no Masonic Home, although a Masonic Widows and Orphans' Fund is in process of accumulation and
is recruited each year by dues of 50 cents per member. It already has
reached the substantial figure of $10,161.25, and in a comparatively
brief period of years will be of sufficient proportions to permit the
establishment of a Home, if this should be in accordance with the
pleasure of the brethren, which, judging from the broad spirit of
benevolence characteristic of Pacific Coast Masonry, may be safely
predicted.
~RAND MASTER' S ADDRESS.

The Grand Master sets forth certain correspondence between him·
· self and the Grand Lodge of Texas, concerning the failure to reimburse
one of his Lodges by a Texas Lodge for expenses ii:icurred in caring
for and bringing back to health of a member of the Texas Lodge, who
was desperately injured. Perhaps the decision of the Grand Lodge
of Texas that it could neither undertake to compel one af its subordinates to make good expenditures of. this kind, if it professed inability
to do so, nor assume the task itself, may be good Masonic law, and
in accordance with the Golden Rule, but on the Pacific Coast the
weight · of opinion is otherwise, and concurrence would be .voiced in
the following expressions from the report of the committee to whom
the Grand Master's Address upon the subject was referred:
"Whatever the Grand Lodge of Texas may think of the 'Wisconsin' plan does not alter the fact that the Lodge at Yuma cared for a
Mason from a Texas Lodge, who was desperately hurt. After much
help from individual Masons, there still remained a balance of cash
paid by the Lodge of $155. There seems to be no doubt but that,
through the efforts of the brethren of Yuma Lodge, the life of the
brother from Texas was saved.
"With the facts in view, it seems to this commi~tee, and reme1.nbering that Yuma Lodge is a young Lodge and not m good fin~nc1a l
circumstances, that the letters from the Texas Grand Officer.s s1mp~y
offer an ex cuse fo r the subordinate Lodges of Texas not paymg their
just debts.
"Notwithstanding the resolution of the Grand Lodge of. Texas,
we are of the opinion that every· Lodge should take care of its owp
members and that each Grand Lodge should see that they fulfill their
obligatio~s."
·
California expends yearly through its Boards of Relief in 'its
principal cities, for the relief of distressed soj ourning brethren from
other jurisdictions drawn hither because of the healing qualities of its
air and sky, and its never-failing sunshine, more than thirty thousand
dollars only a fraction of which is ever returned, and the relief is
disbur;ed regardless 'of probability, or improbabilitr, of reimbursement; the only questions considered being the Masonic standing of
the applica nt, the worthiness, and the distress ; but after distress has
been relieved and the home Lodge of the sojourning brother has been

9

1·eminded of th e fact, for that Lodge, or the Grand Master of that
Jurisdiction to assume the air of superior virtue, and in a high and
holy manner talk about Masonic charity being above a "contractural
baRis," that it attaches to individuals, not to Lodges or the Grand
1,odge, that it ought to be a pleasure to relieve distress, that charity,
like virtue, is its own reward, etc., is tiresome in the extreme.
An Ohio Lodge, not many years ago, as a manifestation of its
11ltruism and broad spirit of Masonic love, remitted the dues of an
ill and indigent member who was living in California, and who had
been suspended for ten years, and restored him to full standing,
without asking so much as a farthing for their beneficent act, seemingly actuated only by a lofty purpose to do good: the derelict that
had been drifting aimlessly for so many years on the sea of Masonry,
1lftcr being recovered, immediately applied to the San Francisco Ma1onic Board of Relief for assistance, and the Ohio Lodge, located in
the classic town of Oberlin, the town that was the northern terminus
of the Underground Railroad before the war, where obedience to the
"higher law" was taught, said, "Go ahead, sure; do your duty!" And
after the San Francisco Board had expended several hundred dollars
in repadding the Mason's honey frame and getting his blood once
!)lore into circulation, they advanced the suggestion to Oberlin Lodge
that co-operation in caring for the frayed piece of humanity to which
they had given Masonic life and standing, would be appreciated;
whereupon the hands of Oberlin Lodge were, figuratively speaking,
lifted aloft and the ghostly exclamation escaped her, "Co-operation !
reimbursement! Perish the suggestion! Our dues are only three
<lollars a year, what can we do?" Our ~ction in restoring this decayed
remnant to our Masonic fabric was only to afford you the opportunity
of applying the well-known Masonic maxim that "Masonic charity
attaches, as an individual responsibility," and the Grand Master of
Ohio, t o whom the matter was referred, wrapped the drapery of his
long-tailed co~t about him, and, with a pitying inflection in his icy
tone, replied that Ohio Masonry could not recognize anything that
looked like the contractural relationship in the application of Masonic
charity.
This utterance put forth by the Grand Lodge of England or of
Scotland, from whom nothing is expected, would not be surprising,
but in America one naturally looks for something else. Wisconsin also
is quoted, and one is constrained to say that what Wisconsin does not
know about Masonic charity, considered from the financial aspect, is
not wo rth mentioning. The annual per capita contribution fixed by
the Grand Lodge of Wisconsin for charity is ten cents, and if any
advice is needed as to how to spread the syrup so that its flavor may
be detected and at the same time have it cover the whole loaf, Wisconsin ~ill fur~ish it : in fact, does f~rnish it, and that gratis, for in a

BRITISH COLU~BIA, 1909.

Thirty-eighth Annual Communication.
Vancouver.
June 17, 1909.
During the year an Emergent Communication of the Grand Lodge
was held for the purpose of attending the funeral of the late R. '. Worshipful Brother Rev:. B. Kelley, Past Senior Grand W~rden; and two
Special Communications-one for the purpose of laymg the corner
stone of the new public school building at Nelson, B. C., and the other
for dedicating the new Ma.sonic Hall at Fernie, B. C.
The Thirty-eighth Annual Communication of the M.".., w: . Grand
Lodge of Ancient, Free and Accepted Masons of the P~ovmce of
British Columbia was opened in "Ample Form" in the Masonic Temple,
Vancouver, on Thursday, the 17th day of June, A. D. 1909, A. L. 5909,
at the hour of 10 :30 a. m., M.". W:. W. K. Houston, Grand Master,
presiding.
GRAND MAST1'R'S ADDR1'SS.

The Grand Master's address is a straightforward, business-like
statement of his official acts during the year. He refers in feeling
terms to the loss during the year of two prominent members of. the
Grand Lodge, the Right Worshipful Brother R. B. Kelley, and Right
Worshipful Brother C. C. Fisher.
Dispensations were granted to form seven new Lodges.
.
Four of the five so-called "decisions" were upon questions of
physical qualifications, and are of no importance' beyond the ~~mediate
jurisdiction in which they were rendered. The fifth dec1s10n was
elementary in character and all of the decisions were approved by the

"Qucstio~: Is a Lodge (under Section 219 of the Constitution),
after suspendmg a member for non-payment of dues bound to reinstate him in the event of him tendering his arrea~s and all other
amounts owing the Lodge, irrespective of his conduct in the meantime Has the Lodge no voice in the matter whatever?
"Answer: If a member suspended for non-payment of dues tenders
the amount of arrears and all other amounts owing the Lodge, he
must be restored. B~t charges may be preferre~ agai!lst him for any
other offense of wl11ch he may have been guilty either before his
suspension or during his suspension, when he ma/ be tried just as if
he had never been suspended."
'. ' Has a Lodge the power. ~o pass a .motion disqualifying from
holdmg office those who solicit votes or resort to electioneering
methods? No. No Mason can be deprived of any of his Masonic
rights or privileges except after charges have been regularly made and
the brother has been duly convicted of a Masonic offense.
"Is is proper to give a Masqnic funeral to a deceased brother
who at the time of his death was under suspension? No. Suspended
members are deprived of all their Masonic rights anaprivileges."
The ruling of the Grand Master upon the question of physical
defects of proposed candidates was as tallows:
"A number of requests have reached me for rulings as to physical
defects of proposed candidates. These I have declined to give. The
Grand Master cannot properly judge of the nature or extent of a
defect from a written description; and in some cases it would not be
expedient to give written reasons for a ruling. Section 181 of the
Constitution is very plain; and every Master of a Lodge is able to
determine from a careful reading of that section the extent of a defect
which ought to disqualify a man from becoming a Mason. If a
candidate can comply literally with all the ceremonies of the work of
Grand Lodge, a minor physical defect does not cause his rejection.
If he cannot comply with all those ceremonies he must be rejected."
This is in harmony with the general policy of the Grand Lodges
of both England and Scotland, to refer the question of physical disabilities largely to the decision of subordinate Lodges, the only general
requirement being, that the candidates are able to conform literally to
the requirements of the several degrees.
Extreme activity marked the administration of Grand Master A. T.
Freed. Dispensations were issued by him to form eight new Lodges;
a number of Lodges were consecrated in due form; and a large number
of Lodge rooms dedicated, and corner stones were laid by the Grand
Lodge, with Masonic Ceremonies to at least six public buildings.
The Grand Master offers a mild criticism to the effect- that the
contributions to the so-called Semi-Centennial Fund, being in effect the
Charity Fund of the Grand Lodge, are not as liberal as he had expected.
The additions during the year having amounted to something in excess
of $10,000, making the principal of the fund now about $45,000.
The reports of the various Grand Officers, including the Grand
Secretary, and Grand Treasurer, the District Deputy Grand Masters,

"A member of a Lodge who has been granted a <limit, but did not
receive a certificate of his dimission, is nevertheless a dimitted Mason,

a ;esolution restoring the Brother to membership the same as if no

"A Worshipful Master of a I,odge has not the right to call a Past
Master to preside over a Lodge during a Masonic trial wherein .the
Worshipful Master is a witness. The Senior Warden must preside.
In case of his absence, the Junior Warden must preside."
One decision was reported upon adversely by the Committee on

"The M. ·. w. ·. Grand Master decided: 'A Brother applying for a
<limit cannot withdr<1,w his application after the same is before .the
Lodge for action.' In the opinion of your committee, such an application may be withdrawn at any time before the same has become final.

hindr·ance. As the brake is applied to the wheels of a car to lessen its
speed, or to bring it to a full stop, so is the principle of friction in one
form or another applied to every moving object. Even the tornado
that sweeps on its devastating course is in a short time worn out by
opposing currents, and its force scattered and dissipated. The rushing
waters of our mountain streams find their course impeded in rocky
barriers that throw their impact back in angry swirl and foam. The
utmost ingenuity of the skilled engineer is- exerted continually to overcome the retarding force of friction . So amidst the surging conflict
that has ever beat with mighty force along the lines of man's intellectual
development, there has entered as hindering forces the strongest powers
of human nature. Envy, hate, and avarice combine to dwarf and
belittle our better natures, paralyze our higher faculties, invite sickness
and shorten our lives. Not one of all the children of men are immune
from their blighting effects. Man imbued with their most pronounced
form, becomes the center of his own blindness. In the darkness of his
life, crime has its opportunity, villainy its chance, and infamy its fullest
scope. Were it not for counter forces, man would be driven off the
field of every conflict in defeat, and ruin.
"These forces are Faith and Hope, with Love as the mighty alkaloid that kindles and keeps the fire of both burning in the human heart.
How slowly mankind comes to the knowledge that love is the one allpowerful focce in the economy of creation. How loath men are to
make use of the most potential factor in our existence for the upbuilding of every interest we have, mental, physical and financial. Befoce
its magic influence the passions subside; imbruted man and savage
animal yield to its gentle sway. It permeates all nature in a mulfitude
of forms, and its voice is heard whenever and wherever our ears are
turned to listen. The greatest exemplar in all history of this mighty
force in whose life the flood-tide of love reached its highest point, was
He who trod the hills and valleys of Palestine; everywhere in the
name of this mighty alkaloid, bidding the blind to see, the deaf to hear
and the lame to walk; at the mention . of whose name, after nineteen
hundred years has passed, millions of the sons and daughters of men
bow in adoration. Would yon know something of this power to
soothe the passions of men ? I stood a few years since in a crowd of
the lower element gathered in a large hall in one of our Eastern cities.
Between the numbers on the program, pictures were thrown on the
screen. The whole performance was so worthless, that the disapproval
of the rabble was soon evidenced by a pandemonium, during which
chairs were thrown at the stage and the vilest oaths and epithets hurled
at the performers. Suddenly the lights were lowered and the features
of the "Man of Sorrow" was seen on the curtain. Then occurred a
scene seldom witnesed. Instantly the clamor ceased and an indescribable
feeling 's pread through the hall, and a perfPct quiet settled over the
audience.
"No. great movement to uplift the race has ever failed with love
as its incentive. No nation is great and strong and endurable without
a love of its citizens that will give their life for its honor. There has
never been a great man without he has loved much. Read the history
of a Lincoln, then look on his face and see the shadow of a great love
that found in youth a longing in his heart that finally ripened into traits
of character that makes him the greatest type of American citizenship.
The strong, masterful love of President .McKinley always succeeded
when arguments failed, and a~ depicted in the tender care of an invalid

wife blessed and strengthened every home in. the land, and will be
handed down by our Order as an heritage from a Brother Mason, to
our children and to our children's children forever.
"There is no religion but the religion of love; all sacred hist~ry
proclaims it, and it is written that through the power of l?ve to him
that overcometh the forces of error, 'all things that are hidden shall
be made plain.'

The following decisions of the Grand Master are quoted :
"Question : 'When a candidate having been regularly voted for,
has been declared duly elected, can a demand for a new ballot be made
within a few minutes thereafter, by a Brother who was present at the
ballot, and voted favorably?'
"Answer: 'Yes.' A Brother can call for a new ballot at any time
previous to the administering of the obligation in the Master Mason's
degree. The matter of its being only a few minutes after the ballot is
<leclared, makes no difference."
"Question: 'What standing in a Lodge has a Brother who having
presented his· <limit, has been duly elected, but has allowed several
months to elapse, without attending the Lodge or signing the By-Laws?
We have now found that we do not want this Brother in our Lodge.'
"Answer : 'Although the Brother has been duly elected to membership in your Lodge, he is not a member until he has signed your·
By-Laws, and at any time previous to his signing them, you can at the
request of any Brother of your Lodge, or of your own volition as
Master of your Lodge, call for a new ballot.' "
And the action of the committee and Grand Lodge thereon as
shown by the proceedings to have been as follows:
"Your committee endorses all of the Grand Master's decisions with
one exception. We hold that the signing of the By-Laws of a Lodge
is a mere matter of technicality and custom; that the act of acquiring
membership by a non-affiliate is complete by the consent of the Lodge
expressed by a unanimous ballot which cannot otherwise be revoked,
and by the deposit of a regular <limit by the bro'ther."

2&

"The ~econd section after animated discussion was adopted with
the exception of that part of the same referring to requirements for
membership. It was voted in relation, thereto, that the signing of the
roll of membership, should be, is, shall be and shall continue to be a
requisite to membership in the Lodge either by affiliation or by rec~iv­
ing the degrees within that Lodge." '
An instance of the Grand Lodge overruling the Jurisprudence Committee is something of rare occurrence. There is a marked distinction
between a Mason made in a Lodge and one who seeks to affiliate therewith; the former is a member unquestionably, even though he fails to
sign the By-Laws, and notwithstanding the fact that at the conclusion
of the ceremony of the M. M. degree~ he is told that to sign the ByLaws is the last act needful to constitute him a member; but the act
of affiliation, it would seem, is scarcely consummated until the roll is
actually signed. The first decision, quoted above, may be good law
where a ballot is taken for each degree separately, but it does not represent the practice in California where but one ballot is taken for all the
degrees, and, where after a candidate is elected, but before initiation
a simple verbal objection spoken to the Master without disclosing to
the brethren the identity of the objector, and without requiring of him
the assignment of any reason whatever, for this action will stop a candidate; whereas after initiation, while it is not necessary to prefer
charges to prevent a candidate's advancement, it is necessary in order
to accomplish that purpose, to file written objections with the Master,
which after due investigation and report by a committee appointed by
him must be supported by two-thirds of the members present at a
stated meeting._

The third Stated Communication was the last meeting of the
Grand Lodge assembled at the old . Temple which had been the scene
of so many notahle Masonic gathe'i-ings in the bygone years. It was
largely a leave-taking of the old halls that held so dear a place in the
hearts and memories of so many, and their sentiments were fittingly
.and eloquently expressed by the Grand Chaplain Brother Joseph Dawson, who was called upon to say the farewell words.
There were two words that came to the mind of the speaker, about
which there clustered the thoughts induced by the leave-taking, the
words, "sentiment and sacrifice." Sentiment is the main spring of
man's loftiest and most heroic actions. "Sentiment," said the speaker,
"is the basis of patriotism." "The materialist will tell you," said he,
"that a country's flag is composed of so many colors and so much material, but this fluttering emblem means more: it means inspiration, consecration and is followed with cheers through the din and tragedy of
battle, and to die enwrapped in its tattered folds becomes an elysium
·Of joy." To win the Victorian Cross, of iron, men willingly, nay,
joyfully, face almost certain death. It is sentiment that rules the
world, sentiment rooted in a soil of sacrifice.
At this session also there was passed a resolution requesting the
-Commission appointed by Congress to erect in the District' of Columbia
a statue of Admiral John Paul Jones. who was a brother Mason, to
-place the statue in the triangular space in front of the New Masonic
1'emple.

"The religion of Moses prophesied a Messiah who woufd be a

.111<1 the only way to uplift humanity; and the followers of the crescent
111 Id it to be the basis of their faith. ·I say, then, man knows no higher
ldcul, he can have no holier religion, than the brotherhood of man.
"Throughout the past other methods have been tried to lift men
ll ' higher life, but all such efforts have failed.
"Egypt sought to build a strong civilization, that would last always.
>\1~ ignorant populace and an educated priesthood was her plan. She
thl)ught mystery would frighten ignorance. Her policy was to govern
11wn by fear.
"Greece built her hopes for a higher civilization and a lasting
arnvcrnment upon the development of the mental faculty alone. Her
pln11 was to educate the human mind. She thought both sin and frailty,
too, were the result of ignorance. She dedicated her temples to the
Onddess of Wisdom.
"Rome scoffed at Egypt and Greece, and said, I will build a
civilization that will last. I will govern men by force, by the clash
•>f ringing steel, by fortress, castle and tower.
"For awhile Egypt flourished with her ideas of control by mystery,
but her power vanished and her dynasties died.
"For a time Greece grew becau:;e edt!cation advanced the moral
life, but life as cheerless and cold as the marble statues which their
l'hisels cut.
"Rome attained a grandeur in her imperialism that startled the
world. But it all was soon 'as a tale when it is told.' Her rulers perl~hed and the ruins of their country crumbled over their dust. Failure
has marked every effort of nations and of men who have adopted any
other basis for higher life than the basis of a universal Brotherhood,
having its origin in the universal Fatherhood of God.
"This is true because you can only govern the hearts and wills
of men by love. You can lead, but you can never drive either the
heart or the intellect. They tried that when Antiarchus leveled the
walls of Jerusalem, sacrificed swine on the altars of 'Jehovah, the
God of the Jews, and undertook to enforce with the sword the wor'Ship of Jupiter Olympus upon God's chosen people, in the temple built
by their hands.
"They tried that when Titus took by storm the Holy City that
would not yield ~o siege, and sent her sons and her da··,ghters to the
-stone quarries of Egypt and the slave markets of Rome.
"They tried that on that early morning in May; when Tancred
and Raymond and Godfrey and the Saxon Knights, with the army of
the first crusade, mounted the walls of the sacred city and the army
of the Christ butchered the army of the Prophet.
"In our own land. they tried that when British oppression undertook to force the colonists to believe in the justice of taxation witl1out representation; and they tried that in the valleys and on the hills
of Blue Ridge, where Stuart'.s sabres flashed against the steel of
Sheridan's cavalry, and gallant men who wore the blue fottght under
the Stars and Stripes for universal freedom of person, against noble
men who wore the gray and followed the Stars and Bars for universal
freedom of thought.

"No! You can never drive men to change of thought. This is
true because the human will, the real personality of man is as divine
and as free as the God who made him.
"But why the need of such an organization as this of ours?
"If God indeed the universal Father, why not men so strongly
knit togethe; that u~iversal Brotherhood exists as a matter of course?
"It is because man though with a will like that of the Divine,
is still imbued with e~ery instinct of animal life, its appetites, its
desires, and its passions.
"In his blood is the flood of the tiger
And the claws of its hate and desire.
"We know what would happen if only natural law was sought for
human guidance. What a terrible time would come! You would
see the rich with grasping greed enter the homes of the poor and
take the bread from the hungry children and the couch from under
the cripple. You wou!d see the discontented .and desperate poor lurk
with dagger drawn, thirsty for the blood of his ?ppressor. You. would
see the libertine with lascivious lip lure the mnocent to rum, and .
the despoiler take the pure in his lechero?s clutch and drag them to
his lair. You know this would be the qmck result of a surrender to
the law of man's nature.
"To help in counteracting this result, is the task to which our
Craft has set itself, and there is sore need that the task be done.
"Obedience to moral law can never do it. If man were required
to live only a life of rigid righteousness, of even-handed justice only,
what would become of the weak and the frail and the outcast?
"Something greater, higher, nobler, better. than justice is demanded
of you just because some men are weak, while some are strong, some
are po~r and some are rich, some are fortunate and some .fail, so~e
seem always to stand firm in the blast of every temptation, while
others falter and fall.
"If the world is to grow better, the rich must not stand on his
rights; he must yield to the touch of pity; th~ strong must give a. hel~­
ing hand to .the weak; the man who stands 111 the storm must hft his
fallen brother and give him a new chance.
"It is for such teaching that our Craft stands; it is such work that
it has set itself to do.
"By what method has she sought to te.ach it? By symbols and
signs, the square, the level, and the plumb lme.
.
"Do you imagine that because they are simply symbolic that they
have no power to teach and to lead men t-0 higher thought and nobler
deeds? Go ask the scarred veteran to tell you the story of hi~ count'ry's.
flag. A ·s ymbol? Yes, but with power to bind men together and to
lead them on to danger and death.
·
"And now, how has Masonry done its task-,the t~sk to ~hich it
set itself so many centuries ago? The ~orld a.sks this question. It
has a right to demand an answer. We still see 111 the world about us
so much of greed that grasps only for self, so much of wor~hip that
bows only to the god of gold, so much of human want un.sat1sfie~, s_o
many pitiful appeals unheeded and m;1he~rd.. But I submit that 1t ts
incontestibly true that because of the mstttu~ton of M~sonry the world
is less selfish and cruel and hard and unkmd, than 1t would be had
the work of Masonry been left u~done. I maintain that by its power

88

rur good to men, the fallen have been lifted, the weak strengthened,
I contend that hearts are warmer
,rnd homes are purer because of its vital force among the children of
,411tl the strong made stronger yet.

mrn.

"I have likened Masonry to that current in the world of waters
as the gulf stream, having its source in the Gulf of Mexico,
rounding the coasts of Florida, and flowing on its northern way through
the deep and the wild and the storm of the ocean. That current is
1111t always distinctly defined. It does not save every ship from storm
1111d tempest ; it does not take the chill from every blast of the northern
: one; but it does help to stay and still 'the blasts; it does speak a
1 on1mand of partial peace to every storm that blows in its wake;
It does temper and soften the clime of every coast by which it flows;
it does cause the flower to bloom and the fruit to come on many a
lonrrcn coast where thorn and thistle would be except for its temper1111( power.
"And so with our noble order. It has not completed its task,
hut it has done it in part. Wherever its influence has been felt, in
every land where it has flourished, it has made lighter the burden of
the widow and the orphan; it has responded to the appeal of pity
for the poor and the unfortunate; it has quelled the anger, and driven
the hate out of many a human heart; it has helped the tired toiler
nnd the traveler on his way; it has sheltered the homeless; it has
~hielded the innocent; it has given strength to the frail; it has lifted
the fallen; it has helped to cleanse the atmosphere of social life; it
has protected, it has fostered, it has sanctified, it has hallowed the
purity of the home; the home, the very warp and woof of domestic
JOY, the corner stone of our liberties, the bulwark of our civil 11:overn111cnt, and the type of all the joys which humanity hopes will come
when this life is done.
"You have done well, then, my brother Masons, to build this
beautiful Temple, here in the heart of your nation's Capital, and you
do well to meet together tonight, in solemn, but joyous, assembly to
dedicate this house-not to the Goddess of Beauty, though in very
truth you have a right to boast of its beautiful architecture; not to
the Goddess of Wisdom, though true wisdom will be learned in the
~ecret conclaves that will he held within its silent chambers; not to
the glory of your ancient order, of whi,eh you are justly proud; but
you and I now dedicate this Temple to that which your order has
stood in the annals of the past, that to which it pledges itself as its
future task. We dedicate this house to a broader, cleaner view of
God, the universal Father, and to a holier love among men!"
At the Annual Communication, the first one held in the new
Temple, the Lodges were very fully represented, and the business
transacted was of a routine and mostly local character, only one decision was rendered, and that a question touching physical disability.
A decision rendered by the Jurisprudence Committee on a case
previously referred to it, holds that the right of appeal from the verdict of acquittal by a Lodge lies in the accusing brother, the same
as in the brother accused, in case of conviction, which is confirmation
of the oft repeated statement that "Masonry is a law unto itself."

The purpose of Florida Masonry t o establish a Masonic Home has
not yet been consummated, although the fund to that end is in pro. cess of accumulation, and now amo~nts to $14,955.91.
The Order of Eastern Star has pledged its active and zealous

ultimate participation of that institution in the management of the home.
One of the notable achievements of the fraternity during the year
was the completion of the Masonic Temple, costing upwards of $150,000,
at Jacksonville, and its dedication at this Communication. Funds
for the purpose were obtained principally by the issuance oi bonds,
secured by a lien upon the property, although the Grand Lodge's
available cash was employed, and the credit of the Grand Lodge
pledged to provide for the deficiency.

MASONIC HOME.

Georgia has a Masonic Home, the reward of years of sacrifice and
effort. Concerning the Home, the Grand Master speaks as follows:
"Yonder upon that hill, above the winding river, stands .the Mecca
of Masonry. The place toward which every eye is turned, the place
where every Mason feels he has an abiding interest, a sacred trust.
It is our Home. The home whose foundations were laid in love of
humanity, whose walls were erected by the sacrifices of the hands of
pity, whose capstone· was placed with songs of rejoicing, and whose
dedication was baptized by the sympathetic tears of the great family of
Masonry of Georgia.
"No Mason looks toward it without an emotion of joy at its completion; no Mason thinks upon it without a swelling p·ride that he,
'in part, is responsible for its existence; none meditate upon it without
a sense of gratitude to the thoughtful minds, the loving hearts, the
willing harids and ready purses that gave it to the Craft-a home of
refuge, a shelter of peace for the wayworn and weary, the destitute
and helpless, the fatherless and the widow."
The beneficiaries of the .Home now number thirty-four, divided
as follows: 9 women, 5 men, 11 boys, 9 girls. The Home is maintained by appropriations from the Grand Lodge and donations from
Lodges, Chapters, etc. The per capita cost for each beneficiary last
year of the Home was $211.90. The Home is in sound financial condition; it is the purpose to enlarge its accommodations, so that a greater
number may be provided for and the scope of its usefulness thereby
enlarged.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

The Grand Master's Address is luminous and comprehensive, and
it sets forth an immense amount of work performed, as may be understood from the consideration of some of his official acts. His official
visitations numbered over forty, the record for his jurisdiction ; he
traversed the length and breadth of the State, traveling more than
5,000 miles; he constituted personally and by proxy twenty-four new
. Lodges; he laid the corner stones personaHy and by proxy of sixteen
public buidings, half of them himself; hi issued dispensations for ten
new · Lodges; he rendered decisions, conducted an extensive correspondence, appointed representatives and displayed wonderful activity
in every direction, and with his address reporting his official acts to
the Grand Lodge he eloquently portrays the character and aspiration
of Free'm asonry :
"'Excelsior' is the battle cry of Masonry. With her mighty hosts
marshalled urider the banner of Truth, she is an intrepid army which
neither the evils within nor the foes without can deter.

a pioneer of California, having arrived in the State in 1854, locating
at Fort Jones, Siskiyou county, and affiliating with the North Star
Lodge, No. 91. He left California in 1866.
The work of the year was represented by several Special Communications for the purpose of laying corner stones, etc., and by dispensations to form two new Lodges, and by a general activity shown in a
net increase of about 10 per cent. in the membership.
Idaho has, notwithstanding the obligation taken by every E. A.,
expressly authorized the use of a key, or cipher, to the unwritten work.
This is certainly contrary to the spirit and teachirigs of our institution,
and should everywhere meet with the strongest reprobation. Kansas,
Idaho, Montana and Rhode Island are all offenders. It is true in
Idaho and in every jurisdiction where ciphers are permitted that they
are frequently lost and fall into unauthorized hands, and it is not a
difficult matter for the uninitiated to decipher any cipher that was
ever invented. That these telltale booklets are going astray may be
judged from the following taken from t,he Grand Secretary's report:
"There are eight of the Worshipful Masters who have not sent in
the receipts. Who has the Cipher or what has become of it is a
matter of conjecture, and not what is intended by the law. I will only
add, if the information received by this office is correct, the restrictions
imposed by the certificates are not adhered to by at least one Lodge.
The particulars will be given if desired."
Among the "decisions" of the Grand Master, which were approved by the Jurisprudence Committee, were the following:
"September 12, received a communication from Brother C. F.
Pike, of Boise Lodge No. 2, stating, 'At the annual election of Masonic
officers a brother moves that Brother 'A' be instructed to cast the
unanimous vote of the Lodge for Brother 'B' for Treasurer for the
coming Masonic year. T_he motion is seconded, put and carried, and
Brother 'B' is elected and installed in accordance with the above motion.
Is such a procedure proper in a Masonic Lodge? Is it in harmony with
the teachings of Masonry respecting the sacredness and secrecy of the
ballot?'
"Answer: No. Such procedure in my opinion would be a violation
of the letter and spirit of the constitution and contrary to the teachings
of Masonry respecting the sacredness and secrecy of the ballot."
"July 19, received a communication from Brother A.' L. Fowler,
Worshipful Master of Gr0ve City Lodge, No. 33, requesting a dispensation to perform the ceremony of unveiling the Jason Lee Memorial
Window, which was recently installed in the Methodist · Episcopal
Church at Blackfoot.
"Request denied, for the reason that the Grand Master has no
power to grant a dispensation to any Past Master or Master of a
Ledge to convene a Grand Lodge except for the following purposes
alone: To lay the corner stone of some public edifice, to dedicate and
consecrate Masonic Halls and to constitute new Masonic Lodges. Our
official Monitor contains no ceremony• for unveiling memorial windows, etc., and to do so would, in my opinion, be contrary to the
customs, rules and regulations of Masonry in this jurisdiction."

MASONIC HOMES.

Illinois has two Masonic Homes, the Orphan Home at Chicago and
.the Illinois Masonic Home at Sullivan, Illinois, for aged and indigent
Masons, the wives and widows of Masons. One of the distinctive
features of the Orphans' Home is the policy of placing children so
far as possible, in desirable families, where they may be reared i~' the
pure and wholesome athmosphere of the real home, and this policy has
met with a considerable measure of success. At the Orphans' Home
there has been an average of fifty residents during the year, the average
.cost per capita for maintenance was $192.36.
There has just been completed at the Sullivan Home a new main
building, which it is believed 'will be adequate for the accommodation
for a long time to come of all that will need its sheltering protection.
E ighty-three residents are enrolled at the Sullivan Home and the yearly
.cost per capita for maintenance appears to have been $260, considerably
above. the average cost of other Masonic Homes, and more than twice
the per capita cost of the Kentucky Home, which affords one of the
best examples in our country of economical management. The Homes
are supported by direct appropriations from the Charity Fund of the
Grand Lodge Treasury, and not by a fixed per capita, although the
-cost of maintenance of the Homes amounts to a per capita of about
thirty cents. The Homes are in excellent condition, and some of the
features of management, especially of the Orphans' Home at Chicago
are worthy of the thoughtful attention of other jurisdictions.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Amorlll the dispensations asked for and refused by the Grand
Master was one requested by a Lodge to attend services on Easter
Sunday at a church. The Grand Master's reasons, which are very
convincing, for refusing the qispensation, are set forth in the following
language:
"For a Mason or any member of Masons separately or collectively,
in procession or otherwise, to attend religious services at any church,
is highly commendable in them and they ought to be encouraged to
do ·so. But religious services on Easter Sunday are commemorative
of events wh~ch do not appeal to many thousands of Masons in this
Grand Jurisdiction. For a Masonic Lodge to attend religious services.
on Sunday at a church, wearing the clothing and bearing the jewels
and pharaphernalia of a Lodge, is largely a matter of mere parade.
The church service is not in any sense a M<tsonic ceremony or ser1Vice,
·and is in no wise necessary that organized Lodges should participate
therein. The Lodge does nothing. Its members merely sit still arid
"listen. If Lodges may determine to attend religious services at some
denominational church, it inevitably leads to a discussion and choice
'between churches, in which those favoring · one church would urge
that the Lodge attend services at that church, and those favoring
other churches would insist that the Lodge attend services at such
other churches, and that if the Lodge had attended services at one
church last year, it ought in fairness to attend services at another
church this -year, and thus Lodges might easily become distracted
by a discussion of purely denominational matters in no wis·e pertaining to Masonry."
It is remarkable in a jurisdiction of the character and standing
of Illinois that the Grand Master should be called upon, as appeared
to have been the case, to answer such questions as to whether a Lodge·
could appropriate funds from its treasury for the purpose of aiding
in proposed repairs upon a certain church, or to aid in the establishment
of a shoe factory in the city where the Lodge is located.
Practically the only question of Masonic law decided by the Grand
Master was one in reference to the restoration of a member suspended
for non-payment of dues, the Grand Master holding (in which he was.
sustained by a majority of the Jurisprudence Committee), that under
the Grand Lodge By-Laws, which provide that a member suspended.
for non-payment of dues may, upon payment or remission of same,
and upon a favorable ballot of two-thirds of the members present at a
Stated Communication, be restored to membership, that is, to good
standing in the fraternity, leaving him non-affiliated, it was not competent for a Lodge to provide, through By-Laws of its own, for payment of an affiliation fee as a consideration precedent to restoration
to membership. .
A dissenting opinion was filed by one of the Jurisprudence Committee that a Lodge by-law prescribing the payment of a fee in addition to a unanimous ballot, as condition precedent to restoration te>
membership, was not in contravention of th~ law of the Grand Lodge.

The Grand Master is commended by the committee to which his
address was referred "for the kindly and masterly manner" in which
he has governed the Craft during his year in office, and for the credit
reflected by him upon the fraternity.
The oration by R.'. W.'. Brother Elmore E. Beach, Grand Orator,
upon the subject of "International Brotherhood" claimed the attention
of the Grand Lodge during the second day of the Communication, and
at its conclusion, upon motion duly made and seconded, the thanks
of the Grand Lodge were extended to the Grand Orator, and he was
requested to furnish a copy of his address for publication in the Pro·
ceedings.
He forcefully maintained that notwithstanding thirty
thousand years of evolution of the human race along material and
intellectual lines, there still remains unsolved the stern problems of
man's avarice and ambition that there yet remains to be overcome
that cruel spirit inherent in· mankind that, for the aggrandizement of
self, will trample underfoot and crush beneath the heel of tyranny
the rights and liberties of others. Figuratively, .the speaker hears
man's cry for light; man knows that beyond the clouds of oppression
that gather and have gathered in darkness, above and around him,
there shines the effulgent light of altruism and love. The speaker
reads in history mart's efforts, often blind efforts, to push back these
clouds and get at the sunlight of truth shining behind them, and while
the speaker confesses that the coming of the day of universal peace
is long deferred, he yet discerns the faint breaking of the tlawn. He
points out the fact that in Ancient Rome, the Temple of Janus,
always open in time of war, was closed but twice, and then only for a
brief period of six years, from the reign of Romulus to Augustus
Caesar, a period of seven hundred years, and then for hope looks to
America, our own beloved land, where in a century and a third the
years of war to those of peace bear the relation of one to thirteen,
whereas, <for a period of three thousand years prior to the Civil War
in America the world knew only two hundred and twenty-seven years
of peace, thirteen years of war to one of peace. All signs point, he
·aftirrns, to an ultimate era of ·universal peace, and Masonry, with its
foundation principles of benevolence, and Brotherhood of Man, is
destined to be a potent and most powerful influence in lifting humanity
to thfs hjgh level. Ame~ica, with its host of more than one million
Masons, is the :vanguard in the Army of Progress. The keynote of
the Orator's splendid effort is struck in the following quotation, which
is introdu.:ed midway between the beginning and the end of the oration:
"As one stands on the mountain top and sees the valleys running
down to the plain below, and through the trees the silver streams
trickling, and knows they lead on to some mighty river, so we look
through the history of the past two or three hundred years and see
how material civilization, political progress, national history, indus-

The Lodges chartered at the preceding session were duly and regularly

on petitfons were granted and nineteen refused. Of the nine granted,
the Grand Master states that he required a showing on the part of
the petitioner that there was reasonable ground to think that a mistake
had been made. While there is a well-grounded feeling that dispensations for reballot shall be granted only in extreme cases, limited practically to such as will correct, what amounts to an admitted error, yet
it is probably true that in many cases when a petitioner has been
carefully investigated by a competent committee, and unanimously
recommended and is afterwards rejected in the ballot, that this result
is either because a committeeman has been loath fo disclose his adverse
report to the friends of the candidate (which is a cogent argument
for the secret report, such as is the law in California, Illinois and
some other jurisdictions) and casts the black ball himself, or because
some brother is influenced by motives other than Masonic; for it is
a fact that cannot be gainsaid, our lectures to the contrary notwithstanding, that the obligation does not make a man a Mason, and if he
is devoid of genuine principle before he takes his obligation (and
there are plenty such), he is not materially changed after, and it is
the: admitted experience of more than one . Masonic Lodge in every
jurisdiction on this continent that sometime in its career it has been
put to shame by some one within its fold abusing his high Masonic
prerogative and casting, with his secret ballot, humiliation upon some
of the truest and best of men.

MASONIC HOME.

There is no Masonic Home in Iowa, although the Grand Master
in · his address refers to a visit made by him during his incumbency
in oif•ce to the Eastern Star Home at Boone, Iowa. As a business
propc~ . tion Masonic Homes undoubtedly present an expensive method
of dispensing Masonic charity, but they are, nevertheless, very properly
approved by the Fraternity, and are maintained in most jurisdictions.
The care and maintenance of these Homes tend to the development
among the ,:raft generally of the virtues· of patience and toleration, of
consideratk\ and kindness, which virtues are above a money value.
In lieu uf a Masonic Home 'the Grand Lodge of Iowa has a Charity
Fund, which receives an annual appropriation from the Grand Lodge,
and from which certain needy and indigent Masons, their widows and
'orphans, are assis· ed. The principal of this fund is now about $20,000,
and the amount u •nsferred at this session of the Grand Lodge to its
credit was about ~,000, which represents practically the amount disbursed from the fund during the preceding year.
Iowa and California are almost identical as to membership. California appropriates not less than $10,000 each year toward the support
of its Boards of Relief at San Francisco, Los Angeles and Oakland,
etc., every dollar of which, and as much more in addition thereto,
contributed by the local Lodges, members of the several Boards, is
expended for the relief of r ~edy sojourning brethren and widows and
orphans from other juri~di., ;ions; and in addition to this, California
expends each year upon its I 'ome, for the benefit of its own needy,
approximately $40,000. These 'igures are mentioned not for invidious
comparison, because it has b~en affirmed, with unquestioned truth,
that the Iowa Masons are among the best in the world, but simply to
show that, notwithstanding the liberality of California in its appropriation · for charity and the care of its Home it has still maintained
itself upon a sound financial basis.

DECISIONS.

Of his five reported decisions the following may be of interest:
1. Is it a violation of Masonic law for a Mason to engage in the
saloon business, provided he operates strictly and in absolute compliance with the so-called mulct law? Yes.
2. Can a young man whose duty is that of a bookkeeper only for
a brewery petition a Masonic Lodge, and may the Lodge legally receive the petition? Yes.
3. A brother Mason who is a druggist is indicted for keeping a
¥iquor nuisance, pleads guilty, and is fined. Is it the duty of the
Worshipful Master of the Lodge to order an information filed against
the brother charging him with a Masonic offense?
A. No more so than in any other Masonic offense.
4. A brother residing in lowa moves to another State, taking a
<limit from the Iowa Lodge. He neglects, or for some reason fails, to

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

affiliate with a Lodge in the jurisdiction of his resic,lence. May he~
while still a non-resident of this State, return his dimit to the Lodge
isrning it and be reinstated? No.
The Committee on ] urisprudence, sustained by the Grand Lodge,
approved the Grand Master's decisions Nos. 1 and 4, disapproved
No. 2, and modified No. 3, by adding to the Grand Master's answer
the words · "of like magnitude and importance." It will throw some
light on these decisions to know that, under the Iowa Masonic Code,
it is unlawful for a Lodge to knowingly receive or act upon a petition
of a profane who may at the date of petition be engaged in the liquor
traffic. This being true, the decision of the Law Committee in sustaining the Grand Master on No. 1 was correct, but it seems like a
forced construction to overrule him on the second. The bookkeeper
of a powder company would not appear to be any more engaged in
the manufacture of explosives, and thereby, for instance, a prohibited
risk for life insurance, than the bookkeeper of a brewery, engaged
in the liquor traffic, and ther.eby a prohibited aspirant for the degree
of Masonry.

Master and others, and the ceremony of dedication was most. impressively performed.
In conclusion a reception was tendered to
the Grand Lodge and Masons generally, their families and friends,
by the Temple Association, attended by not less than six thousand
pleased and delighted guests.
