REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The larger portion of the Grand Master's report is devoted to an
elaborate expression of his views on the subject of what he calls "The
Nationalization of Free and Accepted Masonry." The occasion of 'his
frrvent and ambitious outburst being the receipt by him of a communication from the M.'. W.'. Grand Master of Pennsylvania, inviting
him and other Grand Masters east of the Mississippi River to attend
a meeting of Grand Masters to be held in the city of Philadelphia at
the time of the Quarterly Communication of the Grand Lodge of · ·
Pennsylvania, on June 1st of this year, "to consult with regard to the
general interests of Free and Accepted Masonry." A careful reading •
of the letter of invitation from the Grand Master of Pennsylvania fails
to make clear that "Nationalization" of Masonry in the United States
is intended, but possibly the Grand Master of Indiana has some sidelights that ·do not appear in the text of the letter. In any event, he
attains an exhilaration of spirit in espousal of what he calls "Nationalization" that suggests the. necessity of oil on some of his mental ·
bearings. "All other orders," observes the orator, "of which I have
any knowledge are nationalized." Unfortunately, unlike Deity, his knowledge is limited, but even if it is imperfect, as it is in this
case, one may grant him that Freemasonry is different from "other
15rders." To nationalize Freemasonry would be to belittle it. The
world is its r ealm and the landmarks of Masonry, notwithstanding
-disagreements and differences of opinion on the subject, are n_evertheless, in essentials, everywhere the same and serve to identify the
institution and by means of a genuine knowledge of these landmarks
a Mason, no matter where made, can prove himself such to any Lodge
of Ancient Craft Masons on earth. A "General Grand Lodge" for
the UniteC! States? Never in a thousand years. There would probably be no objection from any source of a convention of representative
Masons from different Grand Lodges for an interchange of views on
questions of policy, such as duration of penal jurisdiction over rejected candidates for degrees, reciprocal arrangements for adjustment
of jurisdiction over applicants residing near State lines, the character
of committees of investigation, the nature of their reports, the status
of un-affiliates, Masons suspended for non-payment of dues, and numerous other like questions; and the conclusions of such convention, or
conventions, if held at stated intervals, could ·be communicated to the
various Grand Lodges with such recommendations touching legislation
as seemed advisable, without presuming to touch the sovereign right
of each Grand Lodge to legislate for itself. To such a plan as this
there could be no reasonable objection, but the idea of a "Supreme
Council" or a "General Grand Lodge" in Ancient Craft Masonry, to
be invested with the prerogative of sovereignty, even if limited to the
minutest detail, is repugnant to the very nature of Freemasonry, and
if adopted would, under the iaws governing recognition, place every

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCR
Grand Lodge in the compact under the ban of non-intercourse of every
other Grand Lodge of Ancient Craft Masons in the world. Yes, it is
true the scheme was discussed very fully forty or fifty years ago by the
Grand Lodges of the United States, as recorded in the early history
of the Grand Lodge of California, but it !Ilade no headway, and it is
safe to predict that it never will.
The Jurisprudence Committee to whom was referred that portion
of t~e Grand Master's address concerning "The Nationalization of
Freemasonry," evidently entertain an exalted opinion of the prowess
of the Grand Master, and their admiration finds expression in a quality
of metaphor peculiar, one must believe, to Indiana. Here is an excerpt from its report:
"The honor of laun.c hing this great ship of accomplishment on the
vast ocean of opportumty must perforce belong to him. Would that
we were pptimistic enough to believe that he 'a lso could stand on the
bridge as she safely sails into port. The rocks, the shoals and the
storms that may sweep across the path of this course never safely
travel~d before, bring misgivings to the minds and h~arts of your
committee."

There is in what was Indian Territory, under the jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge of Indian Territory an Orphans' Home. It was
formally opened on the first of January, 1908, at Atoka, Oklahoma.
There are at present 36 children in the Home, and the cost of
maintenance is estimated at $180 per year per capita. The Home is
maintained by the interest received upon the Endowment Fund, yielding about $3,500 annually, and in addition to this 25 per cent. of the
Grand Lodge receipts are devoted to Home purposes, providing a
maintenance fund of about $7,500 per year.
The following concerning the children of the Home is copied from
the printed proceedings of this Annual Communication:
"The first public appearance of the children of the Home was a
memorable event of this Communication. At 1 :JO o'clor,k of the second day about thirty boys and girls, clean, bright-eyed, happy and
enthusiastic, were introduced from the stage, where they rendered some
excellent musical numbers. In the evening they appeard in uniform
and gave an elaborate and beautiful drill. The children were the
pride and delight of this Annual Communication."
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

The Grand Master in the opening of his address apostrophizes
Truth and holds it up as the supreme ideal of Masonry. He sets
forth, elaborately and in detail, the ancient legend of Hafaz, the
Egyptian, seeking the grand object of existence, and finally finding it
upon the brink of the grave, as Truth.
The Grand Master, in his reference to the fraternal dead, mentions John Dillon Seaman, for many years identified with the Grand
Lodge and Chairman for a number. of sessions of the Committee on
Education.

The principal business transacted at this Communication was the

with the Grand Lodge of Indian Territory, with the view of arranging •
a basis of amalgamation of the two Grand Lodges, so that in future
for the new State of Oklahoma there shall be but one Grand Lodge.
The Committee from the Oklahoma Grand Lodge was received in a
broad and fraternal spirit, the animating purpose of both jurisdictions
being to arrive at a satisfactory and honorable basis, whereby the
identity -of the two old Grand Lodges might be merged into one grand
organization which should embrace all of the Masons of the new State
of Oklahoma. under one jurisdiction. A satisfactory basis of agreement was reached, and it may be stated that the new Grand Lodge of
the State of Oklahoma has since been formed, and the present Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge of Indian Territory is the last
and final one of that particular jurisdiction; and that the next Annual
Communicatlbn of the membership comprising the former two Grand
Jurisdictions will be the first Annual Communication of the new Grand
Lodge.

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

The work of the year is found in the granting of dispensations to
form ten new Lodges; in the constitution ~f three new Lodges to
whom charters were granted at the last Annual Communication, and
in a number of Special Communications of the Grand Lodge for the
purpose of laying corner stones, etc. The Grand Master refers to
efforts that are being put forth to secure by means of additional State
legislation, if necessary, the exemption from taxation of Masonic property the income of which is devoted to charitable purposes. If any
property is to be exempt from taxation, such property should be thus
favored, but it is the opinion of many thoughtful economists that
property of every description should be taxed, and taxed for its full
value, and that there should be no exemptions whatever.
'fhe Grand Master refers to the loss of official ciphers t:hrough
carelessness of Lodges. It is incomprehensible how any Grand Jurisdiction in this country, noted for its enlightenment and intelligence, can
not only countenance but deliberately authorize a cipher; nor is it
plain to the ordinary understanding how the use of a cipher can be
reconcil!!d with the obligation taken by every initiate before he is
permitted t o see even the form of the Lodge into which his desire
for light has led him.
Only three decisions were rendered during the year by the Grand
Master, and were all promptly approved by the Jurisprudence Committee. One of therp may be of general interest :
"The fact that a member has been convicted of a public offense
.
m the State courts does not in and of itself constitute a ground for
charges against him, but is such strong evidence of his guilt of the
wrongful act forming the basis of his conviction as ordinarily to be
practically conclusive against him."
·

observes:
"No society, however strong in numbers, however. moral in its
precepts, can live upon the record of its past alone. Progress is as
necessary in societies as in a nation or an individual, and the future

MASONIC HOME.

As its Masonic Library is the distinctive feature of Iowa Masonry,
so are its Masonic Homes the pride and glory of Kentucky Masonry;
and as Iowa is able to point the way to success in the assembling and
management of a Masonic Library, so is Kentucky able to show to
the Craft the development of the best along the lines of homes for
our orphans and widows, and for the dependent aged among our
brethren. Kentucky has two homes; the Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home, and the· old Masons' Home. The Craft throughout the
jurisdiction takes an especial interest in these institutions, and in
addition to the regular assessments for their support, much in the
way of voluntary action, such as the equipment of dormitories on
the part of Lodges and individuals, is done to promote the welfare of
the institution. An Endowment Fund for the Widows' and Orphans'
Home, amounting now to $314,259.13, has been accumulated, and it
is the hope of the fraternity that this may soon be augmented to half
a million dollars, through an appeal, which has been formulated and
presented to the fraternity, asking members to make the Home the
beneficiary under their wills to the amount of $1 and upwards, and
to be known as the "H. P. Barret Fund."
The income from the Endowment Fund amounted last year to
·$14,640.51, which income was supplemented by assessments upon the
membership (about one dollar per capita), yielding $29,645.65, making
a total of $441286.16, which also was increased by receipts from printfog office, shoe shops, etc., at the Home to the extent of several
thousand dollars additional, ma.king a grand total income for the
Home of $47,444.92.
The Home is administered with marked economy and skill; the
annual per capita expenses being $127.55, about one-half the cost of
our California Home. Departments of Manual Training for the boys
and Domestic Science for the girls are about to be introduced to the
end that the graduates from the Home may be adequately equipped
to assume the battle of life.
·
When results such as are being accomplished by our Kentucky
brethren thr°ough the Widows' and Orphans' Home are considered,
all criticism as to the expense of an institution of this character should

but how many characters may be saved, how much of an uplift may

The Old Masons' Home appears to be managed with the same
ability as characterized the administration of the Home for the children, and both reflect the utmost credit upon Masonry in Kentucky.

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

The Grand Master's address discloses a year of marked prosperity
and usefulness. Dispensations to form twelve new Lodges, certainly
an enviable record, were granted. On account of the losses of theii;
charters by fire, dispensations were granted to two Lodges to continue·
work, etc. This would hardly seem neces·sary, even though the parchment were actually destroyed. Constructively the charter still exists,
and the chartered character of the Lodge was not interrupted any
more than the marital relation of husband and wife are disturbed by
the loss of the marriage certificate.
A large number of corner stones were placed during· the year,
mostly by p·r oxies, for the Grand Master, and permission issued to
various legitimate purpose. Visitation, owing to untoward cireumstances; was somewhat limited, only three Lodges being thus favored ..
In California this . would be considered rather unusual.
Most of the "decisions" of the Grand Master, and also of the
Deputy Grand Master, who officiated while the Grand Master was
absent from the State, pertain to reinstatement, and questions relative·
thereto, of members suspended for non-payment of dues, and the
Grand Master was not in any instance overruled by the Committee.
Some of his decisions were as follows :
"Can a brother who has been suspended for non-payment of dues
for a number of years, presumably over two, and who is now engaged
in running a whisky house, be reinstated in his Lodge?" Answer
"No."
"Can a Lodge remit the dues of a brother who has been suspended for non-payment of dues for over tw·o years and receive his
petition as if his dues had been paid?"
Held, "Yes." In the exercise of a sound discretion this is within
the right of the Lodge.
"A member has been suspended for non-payment of dues for over
two years. He petitions in the regular manner, and the amount of
his dues for which he was suspended accompanied the pefition. .Petition being rejected upon ballot, should the money be refunded to him?'"
Held: "It is ntcessary for the suspended brother to first pay aU
dues before it would be proper for the Lodge to even receive his
petition. The dues for which he was suspended stand as a just debt
from him to the Lodge which he owes, and should pay whether he be
reinstated or not."

Under the heading of "'Necrology" the Grand Master expresses
the profound regret experienced by the whole jurisdiction in the
"passing onward" during the year of Past Grand Master L. C. Allen
nnd Deputy Grand Master Fred C. Marsh, and he briefly outlines their
careers, rich in devotion to duty and manifestations of genuine unselfishness and worth.
During the year a district of considerable extent in Louisiana
was visited by a cyclone, devastating the country, killing and wounding many and leaving hundreds without shelter. The Grand Master
took prompt action and forwarded without delay to the stricken section money needed to provide the necessary relief. California, fortunately, is not afflicted with hurricanes, cyclones or tornadoes, and
except for the unpreparedness of the water company in San Francisco
three years ago the temblor which tarried here for about forty-five
seconds at that time would have left fewer traces behind than any
one of a dozen cyclones or hurricanes or tornadoes that have caressed
other portions of our fair land during the last two decades.

the larger portion of which (about $160,000) consists of investment in
the Masonic Temple at New Orleans.
MASONIC HOME.

There is no Masonic Home in Louisiana, although a small fund is
listed in the Grand Lodge balance sheet as "Widows' and Orphans'
Home Fund," from which it would appear that the ultimate establishment of a Home is contemplated, and that the creation of a fund
for that purpose has commenced.
GRAND MAST"ER'S ADDR"ESS.

The acting Grand Master refers to the circumstances which occurred during the year, whereby he was unexpectedly advanced from
Senior Grand Warden to acting Grand Master, and says:
"Wh9 knows the possibilities of a day? The present only is in
our keepmg. Let us avail ourselves of the opportunities it offers and
remember that the reward of one duty is the power to perform
another."
In Louisiana, in the formation of new Lodges, it is not necessary
that charter members shall sever their connectiori with their old
Lodges until after the new Lodge has actually been constituted, a
certificate of good standing having the same effect as a <limit; confusion has arisen from this practice owing to the frequent failure of
Secretaries of new L odges to notify Lodges to which charter members
formerly belonged of the severance of their membership therein, which
has resulted, in certain cases, of Masons appearing as members of
both the old and the new Lodges, and to avoid the recurrence of this.
apparent dual membership, the Grand Master recommends that dimits.
only be accepted in connection with petitions for dispensations for
new Lodges.
The work of the Order in the city of New Orleans was, during
the early part of the year, disturbed by the attempted introduction ·of
Cerneauism into the State; the Grand Master took prompt action in
exposing the spurious character of the alleged Masonry. In doing
this the name of the promoter of the clandestine brand was mentioned
by the Grand Master, so it was affirmed by this individual, in an
indelicate manner, and to show that he was a man of no mean parts,
he forthwith commenced action against the Grand Lodge, alleging
damages in the sum of $50,000. It is surprising to learn that neither
the apprehensions nor the dues of the Grand Lodge have been raised
in consequence of the threatened seizure of the Grand Lodge treasury.

D"ECISJONS.

The Grand Master decided that an E. A. who has lost a foot and
been supplied with an artificial pedal extremity could not be passed
to F. C. In Utah the Grand Master permitted the passing and raising
of one who, in an accident, had lost both legs, one below and one
above the knee. In Texas the loss, after initiation, of the nail from
the little toe of the left foot would, it may, with great confidence be
affirmed, act as a bar to advancement.
The Grand Master properly decided that a Lodge U. D. could
not issue a dimit, ruling that such Lodges are strictly limited to the
performance of such acts as are delegated to them in the instrument
which gives them life-that is, to initiate, pass and raise candidates
for admission into Masonry.
'
A decision of the Grand Master that in spite of an objection to
the installation of an officer-elect, the installation should, notwithstanding, be proceeded with, the right being preserved to the objecting
brother to make known his reasons to the Master at the conclusion
of the ceremony, is thus commented upon by the Jurisprudence Committee:
"We regret to be compelled to express the opinion that there is
error in the ruling of the M.'. W.". Grand Master. permitting an
officer-elect to be installed over an objection to the installation, but
reserving the objector's right to make the reasons known after the
installation to the Master.
"We are of the opinion that the objection should be heeded, the
ground stated, unless the accused brother withdraws, and the question
settled before the installation can proceed."

In his concluding remarks the Gr8.nd Master pays this tribute
to the memory of the earlier workers of the fraternity in Louisiana: .
"The years of the Grand Lodge of Louisiana are rapidly approaching the century mark. Its struggles for existence in the early years
of its life are now matters of history. Planted in a community almost
wholly antagonistic to its teachings, at a time when Masons cotild
hardly publicly acknowledge their allegiance to the institution, then
through the dark days of the Civil War and the depression which followed, it had to be carefully nurtured and tended while awaiting more
favorable conditions. We revere the memory of the faithful workers to
whose energy, and fortitude we are so deeply indebted. Their persistence and faith are well worthy of our sincerest emulation."

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

. The Grand Master's Address is a businesslike statement of the
work of his administration. He states that he has answered a great
many questions during the year, but does not wish to designate any
of them as "decisions,'' as nothing new was involved in his rulings.
In conclusion the Grand Master says :
"Now as I am about to lay down these duties, I can say to you
with all sincerity that my appreciation then of the honor has nQw been
increased a hundred fold, and my knowledge of the magnitude and
extent of the work in a much larger proportion. I did not then know
Masonry as I know it now. I had iust completed a short excursion
along the shores of that great ocean whose tides rise and fall upon
every land. I have since sailed a little further out on that ocean,
though not beyond familiar capes, yet far enough to catch a glimpse
of the commerce conveyed upon its surgin~ breast, not a commerce
whose object is wealth, but brotherly love.'

MARYLAND, 1908.
One Hundred and Twenty-second Annual Communication. Baltimore.
Nov. 3, 1908.
The M.". w:. Grand Lodge of A. F. & A. Masons of Maryland
commenced ·it~ One Hundred and Twenty-second Annual Communication on the third Tuesday of November, 1908, at 8 o'clock p. m.
The Grand Lodge was opened in due form by the R. W . Deputy
Grand Master, Brother James R. Brewer, with prayer by the Grand
Chaplain, the other Grand Officers occupying their respective ?laces.
By order of the R.". w:. Deputy Grand Master, the Grand Director
oi Ceremonies, the Grand Sword Bearer, and other members of his
staff, proceeded to the apartments of the Most . Worshipful Grand
Master and escorted him to the Grand Lodge room.
His entrance was proclaimed by the Grand Marshal, the Grand
Honors were given and the M.". w:. Grand Master took the gavel
tendered him by the R.". w:. Deputy Grand Master and assumed the
duties of the Grand East, which illustrates a custom prevailing in th.e
Grand Lodge of Maryland which does not obtain in other Grand
Jurisdictions in this country, and because of the dignity and impressiveness of the ceremony having much to recommend it. Another custom of the Grand Lodge of Maryland distinctive in that jurisdiction
is that of holding two semi-annual Communications, the one of equal
importance with the other, and that instead of annual reports fror;i
officers and committees there are semi-annual reports. At the Semiannual Communication held May 12, 1908, the Grand Master delivered
a brief address, dealing almost exclusively with matters growing out
of the destruction of the Masonic Temple by fire, and at the so-called
Annual Communication held in November no address whatever appears in the proceedings as having been delivered by the Grand Master,
although it is briefly stated that the Grand \.faster made an address
touching work done toward reconstruction of the Temple.
The
address, however, must have been extremely ·informal in character.
At the semi-annual Communication in May, 107 out of the 114
chartered Lodges appeared to be represented, and at the Annual Communication 113 Lodges. The total membership of the jurisdiction at
the Annual Communication was 12,828, a gain over the previous year
of 528. No recommendations whatever touching the aff~irs of the
Craft are made by .the Grand Master at either of the Semi-annual or
Annual Communications.
No decisions are reported by him, and not only is there no report
of Jurisprudence Committee, but in fact not even does there appear
to be any such committee of the Grand Lodge.
.
The Grand Lodge dues collected from members durmg the year
appear to have been $35,415.95, all of which was turned over to the

MASSACHUSETTS, 1908.
One Hundred and Seventy-fifth Anniversary. Stated Communication.
'Boston, Dec. 29, 1908.
Four Quarterly Communicatioll'S are held by the Grand Lodge
each year, one each in March, June, September and December; and
the so-called Stated Communication on St. John the Evangelist's Day,
at which the installation of officers takes place, and at which time the
Festival of St. John the Evangelist is held.
At the Quarterly Communication, held in March, 1908, the Grand
Master, M.". w:. John A. Blake reported the deaths of Past Grand
Masters Charles A. Welch and Percival L. Everett, and others.
Recognition was refused to the so-called Grand Lodge of Greece
and so-called Grand Orient of Argentine. The application for recognition on behalf of Greece was presented by a person calling himself
Ange Romeos, and becoming impatient at the delay in receiving the
recognition craved, it appears that he, in connection with sundry
others "notorious, spurious and pretended Masons," started a concern ~hich they called Haramon Lodge, No. 143, under the jurisdiction
of the Grand Orient of the Argentine Republic. Romeos appears to
have been very active in . soliciting recognition from various Grand
Lodges, but with little or no success, and the warning to the Craft
put forth by the Massachusetts Grand Lodge against this personage,
and what he represents, is hardly needed.
It was determined at this Communication to cause to be prepared
and published a history of Freemasonry in Massachusetts from Colonial
days to the present time, and the brother chosen by universal cons~nt
as the best qualified for the position of Historian was the Recordmg
Grand Secretary, Sereno D. Nickerson.
The June and September Quarterly Communications were ~evoted
chiefly to the consideration of reports from the Committee on Masonic
Home, showing the accumulation of funds and the gradual progress
toward the acquiring of the Home, which remained to be consummated
later in the year.
At the December Quarterly Communication there were presented
the -usual annual reports of officers, from which the following statistical
information is obtained:

MASONIC HOME.

.·

The Masonic Home idea in Massachusetts has become an accomplished fact, and this large and important jurisdiction has been added
to the number of American Grand Lodges that consider the Masonic
Home as an absolutely necessary adjunct to the proper administra·
tion of Masonic charity.
At the Feast Of St. John's Day the retiring Grand Master, M.". W.".
John Albert Blake, in his banquet address, made these felicitious
remarks:
" I am glad to inform you that today we have comi;>leted an
agreement which makes us the actual owners of :i M~somc Home.
'I'his agreement has been signed today, and I consider 1t one of the
happiest moments in my life; when I affixed m)'. name to the document
as the M.". W.". Grand Master of Masons m Massachusetts. (Applau!>e.) Tms was my last official signature.out of some three thousand
or four thousand."
A special fund, actually in hand, and pledged, al'l)ounting to
probably a hundred thousand dollars, fifty thousand of which has
been used to purchase the Home property, has been raised, and with
Past Grand Master Blake as Chairman of the Home Board, no one
can doubt the beneficent succes, of the institution from the very start.
An exhaustive report was made by Past Grand Master Charles
'I'. Gallagher upon the application of the so-called Grand Lodge of
France for recognition. He had visited Europe during the previous
year and had examined, on the ground, the conditions surrounding
French Masonry, and from personal knowledge was able to give the
Grand Lodge a comprehensive statement of all the facts needed to
form a most intelligent judgment. Recognition by English-speaking
Grand Lodges of the Grand Orient of France was withdrawn it1 1877,
because of a full realization at that time of the atheistic character of
French Masonry, and of an absolute disregard of the fundamentals
of Ancient Craft Masonry. The Grand Orient of France was then,
and still is, atheistic, and is not even tolerant in its attitude toward .a
belief in God; belief in God is denied; .and it is, therefore, mamfestly true that the Grand Orient of France is not in any possible
sense Masonic.
In 1894 there was organized the so-called Grand Lodge of France,
which claims to recognize Deity and to conform to the Ancient Landmarks,. and it is the Grand Lodge of France that is seeking recognition of English and American Grand Lodges. Brother Gallagher,
however, was forced to report adversely to the pretensions of this

Recognition was, of course, denied.
The Grand Master during the year made a large number of officiar
visits; he presided at ten Special Communications of the Grand Lodge,
three for the purpose of lasing corner stones, five to assist in fiftieth
anniversary celebrations of various Lodges, and one to participate in
the celebration of the one hundred and seventy-fifth anniversary of
St. John's Lodge.
The Grand Master is opposed to all sorts of innovations in the
conferring of degrees, such as the use of robes, the stereopticon, etc ..
He refers to the action of the Grand Lodge in 1896, which voted 1'that
the Grand Lodge order the discontinuance in this jurisdiction of the
costuming of the Fellow Crafts," and the Grand Master further expresses himself upon the subject as follows:
"The strength of Masonic work and its peculiar characteristic is
found in its impressive simplicity, and that our attempt should be to
endeavor to inculcate the moral precepts rather than to exhibit our
dramatic abilities; to cultivate the substantial rather than the superficial elements and possibilities of our work."
There was, up to two years ago, one Lodge in California that had'
for a number of years assumed the right, without asking, to costume,
and felt sorely aggrieved because the Grand Lodge refused to admit
that the Lodge had acquired, by sufferance, the privilege of continuing this innovation, and becau.se the Grand Lodge ordered its subordinate to come down off its perch and conform its work to the
standard adopted for all.
Through the efforts of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts a law
was passed by the Legislature of the State against the use of the name
"Masonry,'' or in fact that of any other legitimate fraternity, by bogus
peddlers of degrees, and a conviction following a test case was obtained, so that Massachusetts is likely to be quite free in the future

A similar law was passed by the Legislature of California last
winter, but it failed to receive the Executive's approval, because it
was not, in his judgment, drawn upon constitutional lines.
The Grand Master reports no "decisions,'' and there appears to
be no Jurisprudence Committee and no Foreign Correspondence
report.

for the next ensuing year were elected, and at the Stated Communication on St. John the Evangelist's Day, following, were duly installed

MICHIGAN, 1909.
Sixty-fifth Annual Communication.
Detroit.
May 25, 27, 1909.
The Grand Officers, Past Grand Officers and Representatives of
the constituent Lodges of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of
Michigan assembled in the Masonic Temple in the city of Detroit, at
high twelve, on Tuesday, the 25th day of May, A. D. 1909, in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution and By-Laws, for the
purpose of holding the Sixty-fifth Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of Michigan.
M.'.W.'. Herbert Montague, G. M,, presiding. A distinctive
feature in the practice of the Grand Lodge of Michigan is the calling
by the Grand Secretary immediately after the formal opening of each
Annual Communication crf the "Roll of Honor,'' bei.ng the list of the
Past Grand Masters of the jurisdiction who have passed beyond the
shadows of earth and have entered into the radiance of the eternal
dawn. This list contains many honored and historic names, including
those of Cass, and Fenton, and Coffinbury, and McCurdy, and many
others, only one name, that of McCurdy-"the grand old man of
Masonry"-having been added to the roll since the last assemblage
of the brethren. Fourteen, all but three, of the living Past Grand
Masters were present at this Communication, and out of a total of
412 Lodges (chartered and under dispensation) in the jurisdiction, 403
were represented, a circumstance that denotes a wonderful degree
of enthusiasm in Michigan Masonry and augurs well for the future
of the Craft in that State.

MASONIC HOME.

The Masonic Home proposition has been approved by the Grand
Jurisdiction of Minnesota and funds for the purpose of founding a
Hoine have been in process of accumulation in Minnesota for a number of years past, and under the provisions of the Constitution of the
Minnesota Masonic Home Association, the sum of $100,000 must be
raised before any measures are inaugurated for the location or con·struction of a Home. The funds thus far accumulated, while of a
substantial amount, are very much short of the stipulated sum, and
consequently the adoption of definite plans for the construction of a
Home are deferred to a somewhat indefinite date in the future.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

The Grand Master presents a voluminous report of his official
actions and rulings during the year; two Lodges, to which charters
were voted a year ago, were duly constituted; dispensations were
granted to form three new Lodges; corner stones were laid to five
-public buildings; dedications of three Masonic Halls .w ere made, and
a number of official visitations are recorded.
Under the heading of "decisions" the Grand Master states that
while he has been able to answer a great many of the questions propounded to him by simple reference to the Masonic Constitution and
Code, he yet has found it necessary to promulgate a few "decisions,"
and he then proceeds to take a birdseye view of Masonic Law and
Jurisprudence in eighty-three so-called decisions. His "decisions,"
however, were over well explored ground, and without changing a
letter or a punctuation . mark were unanimously approved by the Jurisprudence Committee.
Fraternal recognition was extended to the Grand Lodge Valle de
Mexico.

MASONIC HOME.

For more than thirty years in Mississippi there has 'been a movement looking toward the acquirement of a Masonic Home, the first
suggestion along these lines having been made in Grand Lodge as far
back as 1874, revived again in 1877, and sefious work toward the
acquisition of an Endowment Fund commenced in 1890, when Past
Grand Master Rev. E. H. Bartley, who is considered the father of the
Masonic Home, offered a strong and carefully prepared paper urging
the Grand Lodge to action.
·

In this connection the Grand Master states in his address:

be remembered by the Masonic fraternity in this Grand Jurisdiction.
Many of our old brethren who have gone to their reward worked and

·

Speaking of the children which have already been gathered within

clothed and under the influence of a splendid, courteous management.
The children who are large enough attend our public schools, which

The Grand Master refers also to the encouragement and assistance rendered to the Haine project by the members of the Order of
the Eastern Star, and ascribes much of the success which has been

·
The Board of Trustees in rendering their report of the Home
use the following language :
"Every Mason has a direct and personal interest in the Home,
and every Mason's orphan can there find a home when bereft of a
father's love and a mother's care. When the rich Princess of Rome
showed with pride her glittering jewels to Cornelia, who had no glittering gems to show in return, but drawing to her bosom her two
noble boys, the proud, noble Roman mother replied, "These are my
jewels." So may the Masons of Mississippi draw together within
this Home the orphans of their departed brethren, and let it be the
casket in which will ever be found jewels more rare than ever graced
the Monarch's crown, wh'ere they will be kept, polished, and formed,
and sent forth, perfect gems to adorn Masonry's· crown of rejoicing."
In addition to tlie value of the Home property, conservatively
placed at something like $50,000, there is the Endowment Fund invested in gilt• edge securities, which reaches the comfortable total at
this time of about $70,000; and it is the purpose of the brethren to
increase this endowment fund to at least $100,000, and as an evidence
of the willingness of the Mississippi brethren to submit to taxation
for the benefit of the Home the following resolutions were unanimously adopted by the Grand Lodge :
"Resolved, That an assessment of 25 cents per capita be made
upon the Lodges for the ensuing year for the Maintenance Fund of
the Masonic Home ;
"Resoh•ed, That an assessment of 50 cents per capita be made
upon the lodges for the ensuing year for the Maintenance fund of
the Masonic Home."

Since the opening of the Home sixteen children have been received within its sheltering arms, and it is the intention of the Craft
in Mississippi to provide, as rapidly as it can be done, accommodations
for decrepit Masons and the aged and infirm widows of Masons.

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

At the opening of his address the Grand Master, speaking of
Masonry, refers to it as
"Founded upon the purest principles of morality and virtue, its
strong and beneficent influence in joining in the good work of helping
to make our common country better and greater, and the conditions
of mankind happier and more useful. The work of our institution is
to relieve the distress of a worthy brother, to provide for the destitute
widow and care for the helpless orphan; to disseminate light and
truth. As early as 1840 this Grand Lodge went on record in favor of
free education, and since its' early history has fostered and encouraged
enlightenmel'lt. In fact, every public movement for the betterment of
our people, morally, socially and intellectually, when not of its direct
instigation, has had the hearty support of this institution. The spirit
of Masonry, its religion, has always been that wherever one hand meets
another helpfully there is the true spirit, there is the true. religion.
And, after all, the spirit of confidence, of trust and, above "all, the'
spirit of love and helpfulness, is the only true religion which eve!' was
or ever will be.'.'
He also adds that
"The large annual gatherings of Masons that come together from
all parts of our country are doing much towards making our people
understand and know that we are one people and are spreading the
cement of brotherly love and affection that has and will continue to
reunite our country into one band of friends and brothers."
The Grand Master refers in eloquent language to the noble and
exalted qualties of a number of the fraternal dead in other jurisdictions, mentioning especially Hugh McCurdy of Michigin, the "Grand
Old Man of Masonry ;" to Martin H. Rice of Indiana, Past Grand
Master of that jurisdiction and editor for thirty years of the Masonic
Advocate; to John H. Barlow, Past Grand Master and Grand Secretary, at the time <>f his death, of the Grand Lodge of Connecticut; and
to others.
The activities of the Grand Master during the year were represented by numerous dispensations granted, among them ten to form
new Lodges, to eight Lodges constituted, charters for which were
issued at the last Communication; to the laying of corner stones of five
public buildings; to the dedicating of three Masonic Halls, and to the
direction of emergent relief occasioned by a cyclone which on April
24, 1908, visited a portion of Mississippi and devastated a section of
the country, killing 83 persons and wounding 340. A special fund of
about $3,000 was promptly contributed by the Masons of Mississippi
and distributed by the order of the Grand Master for relief of distressed members of the Craft.
The Grand Master reports having attended 120 Lodge meetings
during the year, certainly a wonderful .record. He also states that
he personally officiated upon all Special Communications of the Grand

·REPORT ON CORRESPONpENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Lodge called for the purpose of laying corner stones, dedicating halls,
etc., adding that he performed these duties in person and not by
proxy, because he believed in doing his duty and not delegating it to
someone else.
As an evidence that the bitterness engendered in the dark days of
the war between the States is rapidly passing away, the Grand Master
offered the following .recommendation, which met the prompt approval of the Committee to which it was referred, and was unani'mously adopted by the Grand Lodge. This recommendation is couched
in · tbe following language :
"The veterans of the Civil War are growing old and feeble, and
most of them now, worn by many years, are poor and needy. They
served their country in the days of their youth, and made our country's hi~tory glorious. We have many of these old veterans, citizens
of our State, who fought on the other side. They, too, are old and
·unable to make a living by manual labor.
"I recommend that the old veterans, whether of the Southern or
Northern armies, who were soldiers and did service in the Civil War,
be exempt from the further payment of dues in this Grand Jurisdiction."
That the Grand Lodge of Mississippi has no use for negro Masons, whether they belong to the Prince Hall Grand Lodge variety or
are of the regular kind, such as are initiated in Scottish Lodges and
Alpha Lodge, No. 116, in New Jersey, is revealed in the following
excerpt from the Grand Master's address, and it may be added that
the action of the Grand Master was very promptly and emphatically
endorsed by the Grand Lodge :
"I received a letter from R.". w:. J. M. Whitehead, stating that
a member of Olive Branch Lodge, No. 34, had visited a negro Lodge,
and asked me what should be done. I replied instructing him to have
charges preferred against the offending member and put him on trial.
After some correspondence Olive Branch Lodge did prefer charges
against him. April 11th he was put on trial. When he came before
the Lodge he said that he visited the negro Lodge, sat with them
until the Lodge was closed, and that he did not know it was a Masonic offence to visit a negro Lodge. After this confession the defendant retired, and Olive Branch Lodge, No. 34, by ballot acquitted
the defendant. The action of the Lodge was reported to me by the
Worshipful Master, who was also a District Deputy.
"I removed the District Deputy, arrested the jewel of the Worshipful Master, and arrested the charter of Olive Branch Lodge, No.
34. I now submit the case to you for your consideration.
"Certainly it is time this Grand Lodge should take a de~ided
stand against the visiting and conversing with clandestine Masons,
whether they happen to be negroes or whites."
It is the 'opinion of the fraternity of Mississippi, and this opinion
is stated to be an open secret, "that virtue and .morality, which are
indispensable essentials to· the membership of Masonry, are foreign
to the negro race." This is rather strong language, but perhaps no
one in the world is better qualified to speak of the true character of

the negro than the Masons of Mississippi, for more than one-half of
the population of that State belong to the colored race, and opportunities
for observing them and acquiring a true knowledge of their real characteristics are unsurpassed.
The Grand Master was not called upon to render any decisions
touching Masonic Law and Jurisprudence, but all of hjs rulings concerning dispensations, jurisdictions, etc., were approved by the' Law
Committee, and it appears to be the ·practice in Mississippi to refer
to the Committee on Masonic Law and Jurisp~udence all questions of
law, instead of presenting these questions in the first instance to the
Grand Master, as is the usual practice.
.
The Masonic Law and Jurisprudence Committee rendered quite
an extensive report, but the legal questions discussed were, almost
without exception, of a local character.
One of the most competent Grand Secretaries in the United
States is. M.". w:. Frederic Speed, Past Grand Master of Mississippi.
The statistical tables prepared by him and the arrangement of the
subject matter of his report may well be considered as an example of
intelligence, neatness and comprehension.

ll!ASONIC HOll!Ji.

Missouri has one of the best equipped and managed Masonic
Homes of any of our American jurisdictions. It is a home for aged
Masons, Masonic widows and orphans. The number of residents
at the Home is now 156: 39 men, 40 women, 38 girls, and 4-0 boys.
The Home derives its support from various sources, the principal
source at present being a per capita tax of 50 cents upon the membership of the jurisdiction; this is supplemented by a per capita tax from
the Eastern Star, about one-tenth as much in the aggregate as is·
contributed by the Lodges; also certain appropriations from time to
time from other Masonic Grand Bodies-the Grand Chapter, R. A. M.,
of Missouri, for instance, having during the past year given $5,000,
and in addition to these various sources of revenue there is the income from the Endowment Fund, which amounts now to $115,261.83.
The total income of the Home last year was $39,265.93, and the
expenses of management $29,938.36, making the yearly cost of maintaining each resident about $190. The Masonic Henne assets are as

The Grand Master's Address, as stated by the Committee to which
it was referred, is not long, being, as it were, a very brief summary
of his acts, although his administration was a successful one, and his
official acts such as to redound to the honqr of the Fraternity. He
feelingly refers to the work of the "Grim Reaper" in removing, during
the year, three of the honored Past Grand Masters of the jurisdiction,Brothers Noah M. Givan, Joshua B. Thomas and William R. Stubblefield. Brother Givan was President of the Masonic Home Board, was
greatly beloved, and was characterized by the Grand Master as a
"grand, good man and Mason." Brother Thomas, evidently, was.
likewise a man of generous and noble instincts, and his passing was.
an occasion of much grief and sorrow. Brother Stubblefield is spoken
of by the Committee on Necrology as unostentjltious, of sterling worth,.
and deserving of all the honors that were placed upon him.
It is also mentioned as an incident in Brother Stubblefield's career
that Capt. U. S. Grant petitioned the Lodge in which Brother Stubblefield was raised (Occidental, No. 163, St. Louis), and was elected at
the same time with Brother Stubblefield, but did not present himself
for initiation. General Grant would have been an honor to Masonry,
and it is pleasing to know that he thought so well of our institution
as to subscribe to the necessary declaration of approval and belief,
and no doubt circumstaF1ces over which he had no control prevented
the consummation of his desire. His life is an illustration bf the·
truth that in the body of a free people, like our own, there always
reside men of great character who, under ordinary circumstances, are.
known only in the small circle, usually the very small circle, in which
they move; but through the great crises in the world's history are·
brought forth and are made to assume a high place among the honored names of the earth, and except for these crises they would have
been unknown beyond those with whom they immediately came in
contact. Among such names is that of Oliver Cromwell, who, until'
after middle life, was a man of comparative obscurity, and who had
actually embarked on board a ship in the Thames for the purpose of
sailing for America, where there came "Order In Council" •forbidding
the ship to sail; and it was after this event that the great career qf
Cromwell opened, which led him, step by step, until he became the
Great Protector of the British Commoi;iwealth and the foremost man
of his time, who lifted his country to a positio11 of power and prestige
among the nations of the earth; and through him and by him the
idea of the ''divine right of kings" was forever banished from the·
Anglo-Saxon race.

Likewise, Ulysses S. Grant, trained in his earlier life as a soldier,
but who had given ·u p that ~ailing, and as an humble citizen, just
prior to the opening the Civil War, moved in and out among his
neighbors and was unknown, it is said, even to the Congressmen of
the district in which he resided, yet he became, through his geniu·s
and his grim determination the foremost General of the greatest war
in history, and was regarded as almost the savior of his country.
Yet it is a fact in all these cases that circumstances which appeared to make the man served only to disclose the man, whom preparation had made ready-as the sun dispels the mist that hangs upon
the boulder. It is to the honor of Masonry that General Grant, before whom and iri whose presence kings and the descendants of
kings stood uncovered, should have entertained so high an opinion of
Masonry as to have voluntarily sought to have enrolled himself beneath its banners; and who was only prevented from doing so by
untoward circumstances.
The Grand Master reports no decision, but states that he ha!
answered every communication sent to him, and on all matters pertaining to questions of law has been able to dispose of them by refer·ence to the By-Laws or decisions of the Grand Lodge. Here is an
instance of a Grand Master who is ~bsolutely honest, and it is the
0pinion of many who have served as Grand Masters, and are therefore competent to give expert testimony, that many of the so-called
decisions of the Grand Masters are not in any true sense decisions
at all, but are inventions: they do not represent genuine cases, but are
put forth simply for the purpose of exploitin'g opinions. It is inconceivable, for instance, that in a jurisdiction in one of our Southern
States there could have been propounded, as was reported in a recent
year, nineteen actual cases involving questions of physical defects
alone, and such questions !-"the loss of a big toe," "one who is hair1ipped," "the fleshy part of the end of a finger mashed off,'' "one joint
of the little finger of left hand gone," and fifteen more of similar
import, all of which were held to disqualify, and all of which were
probably "men of straw."
The Grand Orator, Brother I. N. Evard, delivered a most instructive oration on the subject of "Freemasonry of the Present,''principle, patriotism, belief in and reverence for God; study of His
word, character. These, according to the speaker, are the true qualities underlying Freemasonry of today. The Grand Lodge of Missouri is certainly not lacking in fluent and impromptu talkers, for if
the records are not in error, the learned effort of the Grand Orator
was" followed by equally erudite and eloquent addresses, rendered

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

The Grand Master refers in fitting terms to the death of Past
-Grand Master, Henry L. Frank, of the jurisdiction of Montana, who
was in his day a prominent figure in a business, political and Masonic
sense in Montana, and his 1.-ss is deeply mourned.
The activities of the Grand Master were represented by dispensations granted to form four new lodges; by the constituting of the
several Lodges, charters for which were granted at the last Annual
Communication; by various special dispensations granted; and
especially by the official visits of the Grand Master, he having, during
his official term as Grand Master, visited all the Subordinate Lodges
-of his jurisdiction.
When it is considered that Montana geographically is one of
the greatest states in the Union; that to accomplish the visitation of
all of the Lodges in that jurisdiction must of necessity involve an
immense amount of traveling and inconvenience, it will be understood how great must have been the efforts of the Grand Master to
have honored with his personal presence all of the Lodges of his
State.
In addition to the official visits to the Lodges of his own jurisdiction, he made a trip throughout a number of the Grand Jurisdictions
in the eastern portion of our own country, he having been received
by the Grand Lodges of New York, Pennsylvania, District of Columbia and Virginia.
In conclusion, the Grand Master expresses his deep appreciation
of the honor con~rred upon him in the following terms:
"The year past has been one of the pleasantest of my life, and
I wish to thank you for the great honor conferred upon me one year

The brethren of Montana do not hesitate to assess themselves
for what they consider worthy objects of their benevolent consideration, and their willingness to pay $1.00 each in support of Masonic
charity as exemplified in a Masonic Home, is well worthy of emulation.
The Order of the Eastern Star is co-operating most loyally in the
Masonic Home project and the Official Head of that order was
welcomed to the floor of the Grand Lodge during this Annual Communication and uttered high and exalted sentiments in some wellchosen words.
The tendency of the great majority of the Grand Masonic Jurisdictions throughout the country to taboo liquor selling and liquor
sellers was reflected in the attitude of the Grand Lodge of Montana
at this Communication in the adoption of the 'following resolutions:
"Resolved, That any memb~r of a Lodge in this juri~diction who
shall engage in the saloon busmess or act as barkeeper m a saloon,
shall be considered guilty of un-Masonic conduct, and it shall be _the
duty of the Junior Warden of such Lodge to prefer ch~rges agamst
any such member; but it is understood that this resolution shall not
be retroactive."
The "Signet Ring," intended as a special mark of distinction, and
a special honor to the Grand Master during his incumbency in office,

1887, and since that date passed on from one Grand Master to another,

MASONIC HOME.

One of the distinctive features of Nebraska Masonry is the 'large
expenditures made by the Grand Jurisdiction on account of charity.
There are three distinct funds from which disbursements are made on
account of charity, viz: Nebraska Masonic Home; the Orphans' Educational Fund; and the Grand Lodge Charity Fund.· The Masonic
Home Fund and the Orphans' Educational Fund have in a sense bec9me merged and the Orphans' Educational Fund, amounting to
$50,000 has become a permanent endowment for the Home. Seventy- .
five per cent of the income from the Orphans' Educational Fund, or
Home Endowment Fund, is used for the benefit of the Home and
in aid of the education of Masonic Orphans. The Grand Lodge dues
.in Nebraska are $1.25 per member, borne upon .the rolls of the
Subordinate Lodges and 50 cents of each $1.25 of the· Grand Lodge
dues is appropriated for the benefit of the Home, and the Home also
receives other appropriations from the Grand Lodge, and from other
sources.
The Masonic Home in Nebraska is the especial pride of that
jurisdiction and was founded by Past Grand Master George W.
Lininger, considered, probably, up to the time of his death, as the
foremost Mason in Nebraska.
There are now at the Home about forty beneficiaries. Half of
them are aged Masons and the other half made up of the widows
of Masons and several children. The cost per capita of maintaining
the Home last yea~ was $230.30. The Grand Master in speaking of
the Home reports the same as in most excellent financial condition.
He refers to the fact that most of the beneficiaries are old people
upon whom infirmities of age sit- none too ·lightly, and that the
management of these people requires on the part of the Superintendent
an infinite amount of patience and tact. He further states that thanks
to the generosity of the Craft, there is no lack of funds to meet
every legitimate want.

!H

At the opening of his address, the Grand Master remarks that
"Masonry is an institution peculiar unto itself. It follows none,
patterns after none, and competes with none. It is an institution
founded for the purpose of impressing upon the minds of its members
lessons of morality, obedience to law, and the leading of just and
upright lives. Every lesson in Freemasonry is intended to impress
upon the minds of its votaries the duties they owe to themselves and
to others ; and the work of th~ several degrees should be done so
as to make the impressions of the sublime lessons and principles as
deep and lasting as possible."
The first official act which Grand Master Kink was called upon
to perform after he had assumed the Grand Master's Chair, was to
call an Emergency Communication of the Grand Lodge for ·the purpose of conducting the funeral of Past Grand Master, George W.
Lininger. His death came suddenly and unexpectedly and was a
shock not only to the jurisdiction of Nebraska but throughout the
Masonic world, Brother Lininger being regarded as one of the foremost Masons in our country. He made a deep impression upon the
Craft in his own jurisdiction and his loss is sincerely and profoundly
mourned. The memory as stated by the Grand Master, of his "generous philanthropy, his wise counsels, his inspiring enthusiasm, his
beautiful and blameless life will remain as an inspiration to Nebras~il
Masons for all time to come."
The activities of the Grand Master during the year are shown in
dispensations granted for six new Lodges; in the laying of a number
of corner stones; in the dedication of several Masonic temples; in the
constitution of Lodges to whom charters had been previously granted;
and in a large number of official visits during the year by the Grand
Master.
The "decisions" of the Grand Master were ten in number, all of
which with one or two slight modifications, were approved by the
Jurisprudence Committee, and of the ten the following are quoted :
"A brother applying for a <limit for the purpose of enabling him
to join another Lodge, who is found free from all charges and cleaF
of the books, is entitled to receive a <limit, without any vote by
his Lodge.
"A Lodge of Master Masons opened for the sole purpose of conducting a Masonic funeral should not be called from labor to refreshment before leaving the lodge room. A Lodge is at labor while
conducting the burial service.
"A member of a Subordinate Lodge in anot}ler jurisdiction, before
being examined for the purpose of visiting a Lodge in this state,
must present documentary evidence, not over one year •old, attested
by the seal of the Grand Lodge of the jurisdiction whence the visitor
comes."
The reports of the Grand Secretary and Grand Treasurer disclose a sound and wholesome condition of Nebraska Masonry from a

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE
business and financial standpoint; and, as previously stated, from the
st<tndpoint of Masonic Charity, Nebraska is preeminent.
The report of the Grand Custodian shows a most careful attention to the ritualistic standard and from it is gathered the impression
that the charter of the work in Nebraska is of a high order.
By virtue of the recommendations of the Committee on Foreign
Correspondence, fraternal recognition was extended to the new Grand
Lodge of Saskatchewan and was denied to the United States Lodge
-0f Mexico, -Grand Oriente d'Italia, to the Grand Lodge of Chili, and

On the evening of the first day of the Annual Communication
W. Brother Roscoe Pound, Grand Orator, delivered an oration upon
the general theme of the tendency of the world toward Universal·
Peace and International Justice, and of the important part which
has been played and will continue to be played by Freemasonry in
the attainment of these ideals.
The thanks of the Grand ·Lodge were returned to him for his
masterful effort and a request was made to him to prepare a copy
of his address for insertion in the proceedings of the Grand Lodge.
Several important amendments to the laws of Nebraska were
prepared by the Committee on Codification of the Law, and were by
the Grand Lodge unanimously adopted. One of the amendments,
which may be considered of general interest, is as follows:
"No Lodge in this jurisdiction shall receive a visitor from any
Lodge outside of this State, unless a Master Mason, known as such
in the Lodge, shall vouch for the visitor as a Master Mason in good
standing, or until the visitor, after strict examination, shall prove
himself to be a Mason in good standing; and no such visitor shall
be examined until he produces to the Worshipful Master of the Lodge,
or to the committee of examination appointed by him, a certificate
under the seal of his Lodge, authenticated by the seal of the Grand
Lodge of the jurisdiction whence the visitor comes, which certificate
must show that he is a member of said Lodge in good standing.
And the Master and committee must be satisfied that the Lodge giving
the certificate is a regular Lodge, working under the jurisdiction of
a regular Grand Lodge recognized by the Grand Lodge, A. F. &
A. M. of Nebraska. And unless such certificate is dated within one
year prior to the date of such examination, the visiting brother must
also present some receipt or other documentary evidence from his
Lodge, bearing a date not to exceed twelve months prior to the date
of such examination, showing that he remains a member of said
Lodge in good standing."

"It is emphatically the Masonic event of the year in our little

degrees. They perfect themselves, bring along their own candidates,
hold a special Communication of their own, a matter of their own
Lodge record, work their degree, and are then criticised by our State
Lecturer, who has had the assistance of his Deputies. It is New Hampshire's School of I1;1struction, though we name it something else. To
this we add a yearly visitation to every Lodge by the District Deputy
Grand Master and by the District Grand Lecturer, the degree work
being criticised or commended by the latter officer. The tw o together
have brought about a perfection in work throughout the State that
cannot be surpassed-astonishingly so."

MASONIC HOME.

The Committee on Masonic Home reports the affairs of the Home
in an entirely satisfactory condition, the number of beneficiaries at
date of report being 81 ; divided as follows: 40 men, 19 women, 10
boys, 12 girls. The financial condition of the Home is sound and
solvent, the Home having twice during the year been remembered in
the wills of departed brethren, one bequest being for $15,000 and the
other for a smaller amount. The Home is supported· by a per capita
tax on the membership of 30 cents, fees for initiates, interest on investments, etc., these various sources of revenue during the year producing $19,735.50. The total expenses were $18,910.96, making the
annual expense for each beneficiary $230.44.

The Grand Master's Address is a scholarly production, and proclaims its author as a man of mental attainments, and high moral
qualities. At the opening of his addfess, in speaking of Masonry, he
says:
" It has been well said that history scarce furnish.es its parallel. ~ts
traces are to be found in the remotest ages and m the most vaned
conditions of the human family. It exists where other worthy orders
have not successfully penetrated, and its claims are respected even

Masonry justifies its existence not by antiquity, but, by principle,
which, doubtless, accounts for its antiquity. Its supreme object is to
develop character."
The work during the year is represented by the constitution of
three new Lodges, charters for which were authorized a,t the last Annual
Communication, dispensations to form two new Lodges, and a net
gain in membership of nearly 1,500.
New Jersey must be a paradise for the maimed, the halt, the lame,
and the blind, for the Grand Master reports that 102 cases of visible
physical defects were submitted to him for decision during the year.
I Ie passed eighty and turned down twenty-two.
Of "Decisions" the Grand Master makes the following report :
"Frequent applications have been made to me for the interpretation
·if our laws in particular cases, but as each question was, in my
opinion, covered by the existing law, I did not find it necessary or
advisable to formulate any new decisions."
New Jersey in the more than 120 years of the existence of its
Grand Lodge had up· to the present Annual Communication claimed
perpetual penal jurisdiction over rejected candidates for degrees, being
one of the fourteen Grand Lodges in this country still adhering to
that discredited doctrine, and during the year this question was pressed
upon the attention of the Grand Master in the consideration of cases
that had arisen, and in his report he makes a strong and logical argument for the abandonment of this pretension, and offers a recommendation that action to this end be taken by the Grand Lodge of his State.
The Jurisprudence Committee reported ·against his recommendation
and advocated the wisdom of holding to the position so long regarded
as sound law by the Jurisdiction. The arguments of the Grand Master,
however, prevailed and the fellowing resolutions were adopted:
Resolved, That penal jurisdiction shall be retained over rejected
petitioners by the rejecting Lodge so long as the rejected petitioner
continues to reside within the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge, and
penal jurisdiction shall be terminated only by a bona fide removal
·
from the State or the consent of the rejecting Lodge.
"Resolved. further, That all sections in the present digest referring
to penal jurisdiction are hereby annulled or susperseded."

The conclusion of the Grand Master's address is of a high orde.r,
and there is abundant justification for this liberal quotation therefrom:
"Brethren, I want the end of this address to be logically consistent with its beginning. In opening I justly extolled Masonry,
its history and principles. In conclusion, I would emphasize our
personal responsibility as members of so privileged an institution and
as custodians of so priceless a charge.
"Unless I misread the signs of the times, there is writ large upon
the face of this century that impelling word SERVICE. It would
seem that institutions are to be judged in this twentieth century, as
never before, upon their ability and willingness to be of use to mankind. This is to be the humane age, as distinguished from the theologic, scientific, analytic, all of which terms have characterized certain
past ages. If this contention is right, now is Masonry's great opportunity, her accepted time, her day of salvation.
"Mark well, Masonry has not come to the age, but the age has
come to Masonry. She anticipates just such an era. It is what
Masonry has stood for, theoretically at least, all through the past.
First and last, Masonry is committed to the cause of humanity. Herein
lies our solemn and great responsibility. To ·excite in man noble
aspirations; to develop in him practical charity ; to make him keep in
·s ubjection rude and impure passions; to make lying, cheating and
grafting more difficult ; truth, candor and fair-dealing more easy and
popular; to maintain high ideals in the home, in the State and in the
nation; to deal bread to the hungry, comfort to the afflicted; 'to
break every yoke and let the oppressed go free,' all this to fulfill
the missiort of Masonry.
"The old historian Livy, could find no.thing better to express his

gentium, the salt of the nations.
"May we, as Masons, in our individual practice and influence, rise
to the call of the age and justify for our beloved Craft the encomium
of Livy."

During the year seven Special Communications of the Grand Lodge

Preceding the report of the Grand Master, there was a report

the year a suitable ornamental iron fence had been placed about the

Montezuma Lodge at Santa Fe, whose Lodge register bears his signature April 21, 1861. He was a distinguished pioneer and did much for .
Masonry, and for New Mexico. Montezuma Lodge, it is stated, is the
p~oud possessor of his rifle, and the Grand Lodge of New Mexico is
the owner of his Masonic Apron through the gift of Past Grand Master

A chaste and lofty diction is manifested in the introductory clauses
of the Grand Master's address. He amplifies the idea of change, "the
evolution upward, the transition from bad to good, from good to
better." Of this universal truth, as applied to Freemasonry, he says :
"In form . and ceremony Freemasonry has changed, as changes ·
all earthly thmgs. In the underlying tenets which have given it
ccntinued life and virility it changeth not.
"The great verities of "human life never change; the great. principles of Freemasonry are, likewise, immutable.
"Belief in God, love for our fellow beings, loyalty to all that
becometh a man, the practice of manly virtues, and the giving in
full measure, not of alms, but of human charity, from the beginning
until now have been its foundation stones.
"Upon these has been built the superstructure, every change in
the form of which has but given opportunity for greater usefulness.
"As the world has grown better, Freemasonry has kept step with its.
march of progress; and fully abreast with the day, it is now as ever
a mighty power for good.
'
. "As. changes in. life and nature are bµt a preparation for something higher and ncher, so the changes in our Fraternity have but
opened the way to us for higher endeavor and richer fruition."
· He refers with feeling, and in fitting terms to the "Fr~ternal
Dead," and recounts the virtues and sterling qualities of many of those
of his own Jurisdiction, who, during the year, had answered the last

as gradually becoming less troublesome, the exposure of its spurious·

Dl(CISIONS.

The report of the Committee on Jurisprudence, which was adopted,
on the Grand Master's Address covering dicisions were as follows :
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom was referred so much
of the Grand Master's Address covering decisions, find but one decision,
which is as follows:
"A brother, who has been unaffiliated for non-payment of dues,
tendered to his Lodge the amount owing, which, after some hesitation,
was accepted and receipt given. He then applied for reinstatement,
but was rejected.
"Question. Could he apply to any other Lodge for membership ?
"I held that, having paid in full his indebtedness to his Lodge,
his status thereupon became the same as that of one who had paid
his dues and been, at his own request, dropped from the roll. That
having discharged his obligation to his Lodge, his punishment could
not be longer continued; and that if the Lodge did not care to
restore him to membership he was free to apply to any other Lodge
for affiliation and could be lawfully received.
"This is so manifestly in accordance with former decisions and the
Constitution that the Committee heartily approve, and ask the Grand
Le dge to confirm this report."
This is not in accordance with the law in California, where the
vote that restores to good standing in the fraternity, restores also
to membership in the lodge; but it is the opinion of many in this Jurisdiction that a modification of our law ought to be made, whereby in
restoring a member suspended for non-payment of dues, a distinction
should be drawn between restoration to good standing in the fraternity,
giving to the member the standing of a non-affiliate, which might be
<lene upon payment of arrearages, and by a majority or two-thirds
vote; and restoration to membership in the Lodge, which should be
accomplished only by unanimous ballot.
The beneficient operations of the Grand Lodge of New York
a re multifarious. The reports of the various committees, especially
that of the Grand Historian with historical sketches of various Lodges,
full of interest and most valuable information.
The principal burden of the Grand Master's address was an
elaborate exploitation, from his point of view, of differences which
had arisen during the year between himself, and the Trustees of the
Hall and Asylum Fund, as to the proper policy to pursue in relation
to the improvement of the Masonic Hall 'property at 6th Avenue, and
23rd Street in connection with the so-called annex, just completed,
(or practically so) on 24th Street.
The Trustees are in a sense independent of the Grand Lodge, or
of the Grand Master; are created by act of the legislature for certain

108

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

purposes .in connection with the management of the properties of the
Craft, and are vested with certain powers, of which they may not be
divested except by additional act of the legislature. This board is
composed of the selected men of the fr<1ternity, six in number, chosen
because of their knowledge, business sagacity, and training. It was
the belief of this Board that, acting in the line of what they considered the clearly indicated wishes of the Craft, as shown in the
proceedings of the Grand Lodge, during the three previous Annual
Communications, steps should be taken at once to replace the old
poorly designed building (at least, for income purposes), on 23rd Street
with a modern eighteen story commercial building; and, to this end,
it appeared to the Board that they were justified in taking such preliminary action as might be needed to accomplish this purpose, especial!y
the embracing of an opportunity to purchase, at what they considered
a 'favorable figure, a long lease held by the Garfield National Bank,
upon a large portion of the ground floor. And in opposition to ·the
wishes of the Grand Master, the purchase of the lease was consummated. Notwithstanding the unquestioned power of the Trustees of
the Hall and Asylum Fund to proceed with the project of the proposed new building, they preferred to refer the entire matter to the
Grand Lodge for action, and the majority of the Hall and Asylum
Fund Committee, and the Grand Lodge, by vote of Lodges, sustained
the Grand Master and the project has been, seemingly, for the time
being . arrested, and the Trustees discredited; which illustrates how
difficult it is to overcome the prestige which a Grand Master holds
with the Craft, sin:iply by virtue of his office. For, in this case the
weight of the argument was clearly on the side of the Trustees. The
Frafernity is in possession of one of the most valuable corners in the
city of New York, upon which is an antiquated building, almost tenantltss, but with suitable improvement, the property could, in the judgment of disinterested experts, be made to pay a large return, especially
in view of the great advantage it enjoys in the fact that the entire
property is, by virtue of a law of the state, exempt from taxes, so
long as the net revenue is devoted to charitable purposes, which of
course it is, and the purposed million dol!ar improvement would not,
therefore, have added one dollar to the outgo for taxes. It is astonishing that the combined judgment of .the six Trustees, undoubtedly
among the foremost men of the Fraternity, thoroughly trained in the
matter of finance, acting wholly from unselfish motives, and influenced
only by a desire to promote the good of the Craft, should be overthrown, simply because it r.an counter to the opinion of a man, who
for the time being, wore the regalia of the Grand Master. The sentiments appealed to by the partisans of the Grand Master were, judging from the arguments, that the Trustees were presuming to arrogate
to themselves an importance above that of the Grand Master, or even

the Grand Lodge, that they were attempting to belittle that august
personage, that they were endeavoring .to plunge the Craft hopelessly
into debt, and that the Grand Master was the only bulwark that stood
between tlie Fraternity and financial chaos. The circumstance that
the Grand Master when he becomes such, wears an elaborately embroidered collar, and an' apron bordered with gold, and sits among
his brethren with his hat on, does not invest him with any mental
qualities that he did not previously possess, and the quality of his
gray matter is not at all enhanced thereby. In the consideration of
a business and financial question, such as was this building proposition, the Grand Master should have counted simply as one man among
others, and just such weight should have been given to his judgment
as his training, and business experience entitled it to receive, and no
more. The eminent Towersend Scudden, Past Grand Master, Judge
of the Supreme Court, and President of the Board, in his report tersely
expressed this idea when he said:
"The Trustees have the greatest respect for the Grand Master,
and reverence for the office. · Judgment. however, emanates from men
as individuals and not from officials. The matter under discussion is
a business and not a Masonic proposition."
The soundnes!f of the judgment of the Trustees will without doubt
be proven within a very brief period of time.
A certain city was once threatened with a visitation of bubonic
plague, incipient manifestations having already developed. The Board
of Health, made up of medical experts, as a means of conserving the
welfare of the city, recommended the adoption of certain adequate
steps of regeneration and purification, together with the destruction
of the rodents that carried the disease, which measures necessitated
the expenditure of a large sum of money, but which would put the
city on a plane of safety. The Mayor of the city, having been chosen,
not because he possessed medical skil!, but from other considerations,
insisted that the measures proposed by the board of medical experts
were wasteful and il!-advised and altogether useless, and that no real
necessity existed for any such extravagance, impeded by virtue of his
official position and the authority incident thereto, the action of the
Board, and finally by reference of the question to the Electorate, who
were even Jess qualified than himself to judge of the impending danger
that threatened, overthrew entirely the measures recommended by the
Board, and for a season there was great rejoicing because the threatened
avalanche of expenditure had been stayed. In the meantime, however, the rodent carriers of the disease had been multiplying, the conditions for the outbreak of the dread malady had been ripeping, and
finally the plague burst forth with appalling virulency, and before its
ravages ceased, one fourth of the entire population had been tol!ed off
as victim of the destroyer.

This was not the fateful outcome of the visitation of bubonic plague
with which San Francisco was threatened three years ago. It might:
however, easily have been the outcome, if the Chief Executive of the
city had not co-operated, as he did, with the medical experts, who
insisted, in face of the strong opposition of the uninformed public,
that the expenditure of a large sum of money was needed to safeguard the health and welfare of the city.
It may be possible to discover an analogy between the conditions surrounding the health situation in San Francisco three years
ago, and conditions involved in the financial situation of the Fraternity
in New York today, although the analogy ceases at the boundary line
where recommendation merges into action.

The report on Foreign Correspondence is by M.'. w:. William
Sherer, P ast Grand Master. His survey of the Masonic world is exceedingly comprehensive-49 American, 8 Canadian, 59 foreign jurisdictions are considered-although his views as a rule are quite brief.
Many Masonic bodies that are not recognized as peers by our Grand
Lodge are noticed by him, no doubt upon the theoty that information
concerning many of these is frequently desired, and may very properly
be given without thereby according any implied recognition. Concerning Italy, he expresses regret that absence of proof that that country
is organized under the jurisdiction of symbolic Lodges prevents recognition at this time.
Requests also for recognition from Chili, San Domingo, Greece,
and San Salvador were refused because these so-called Grand Lodges
were not legitimately organized and are not the sole rulers of Masonry
in their respective countries, and hence, in accordance with the American idea, not entitled to recognition.
