MASONIC ORPHANS' HOME.

North Carolina was early among the fraternal or religious institutions of this country in the establishment of Orphans' Homes, or
Asylums, as they are called. To Kentucky probably belongs the honor
of being first, but North Carolina, also a pioneer, has made its Orphans' Home pre-eminent above all others, unquestionably the foremost
institution of its character in the United States. Its success and usefulness have been so marked, and its work of such general and widespread beneficent a ·n ature that the Home long since assumed the
character of a quasi public institution, and · has received annual appropriations from the State for many years towards its support. This
Nor th Carolina Orphans' Home was established nearly forty years
ago, at a time when only one State in the Union-Michigan-had a
State Orphan Asylum; it has given shelter and a start in life in the
right direction to more than three thousand orphans, and now holds
within its protecting arms 325 little ones, bereft by fate of a parent's
love and care. Not only does the North Carolina Home give to the
orphan moral teaching and mental discipline, but, what may be of
almost equal importance in the strife for existence, manual training,
so that when the child leaves the Home he is, in a measure, prepared
to withstand the rude jostling which awaits him amid life's surging
crowds.

REPORT ON .CORRESPONDENCE.

113

More than one industrial department of the Home is made to
show an exc.ess of income over disbutsements, and the singing class
returned a net profit last year through concert tours, etc., of over
six thousand dollars. The per capita cost, above the earnings of the
institution, of maintaining each child for the twelve months, was approximately $66, and the combined cost of education and maintenance
about $79, a most unusual and praiseworthy record.
North Carolina Masonry is proud of its Orphans' home, nor,
one is constrained to believe, will it take kindly to the suggestion contained in the address delivered at the Annual Communication by the
Grand Orator, Past Grand Master Robert Bingham, that in the onward
march of humanity the Orphan Asylum will likely become as an abandoned derelict, something in comparison with which the progress of the
race may in future be measured, and while it is undoubtedly true that
the ideal atmosphere in which to rear the orphan is found in the
family relationship, and that the trend of modern effort is to find
families in which to place the waifs of society, yet the high function
of the Orphans' Home will never cease and the time will never come
in North Carolina when the music of children's voices at the Oxford
institution will be supplanted by the toothless whisper.ings of age.
A home for the aged and infirm is beyond question among the expectations yet to· be realized by the Masons of North Carolina, but one
may be sure that this will not be done, as intimated by the Orator,
through the conversion to such a purpose of the present orphanage
at Oxford, the very apple-of-the-eye of North Carolina Masonry. ·

involved in its acquirement.

NORTH DAKOTA, 1908.
CERNEAUISM.

Cerneauism has at different times for more than fifty years been
a source of· perplexity and trouble to the Grand Lodge of North
Carolina, and during the past year renewed efforts were made by that
alleged form of Scottish Rite Masonry to establish itself within this
jurisdiction. The Grand Master refused to render an opinion favorable
to claims of this organization to legitimacy, but also reserved condemnation, preferring, as he stated, to refer the entire subject to the
consideration of the Grand Lodge. The committee of the Grand Lodge
to whom the matter was referred reported adversely to the pretensions
of the so-called Cerneau Rite, and reaffirmed the previous rulings of
the Grand Lodge, declaring that rite clandestine. This report was
adopted by the Grand Lodge, and it is unlawful for Master Masons
in North Carolina, as is true in most of our American jurisdictions,
to receive the Cerneau brand of the so-called higher degrees. It
might be a serious question as to the province of a Grand Lodge of
Ancient Craft Masons to undertake to decide between the conflicting
claims of rival Supreme Councils · of the Scottish Rite, both of which
are of decidedly modern origin, if it were not for the fact that the
so-called Cerneau Rite Supreme Council has not hesitated in this
<;ountry to presume to charter symbolic Lodges, where, in being denied
access to regular Blue Lodge members, a body of Masons was needed
from which to draw recruits to fatten the treasury {Jf the body conferring the alleged higher degrees.
The Supreme Councils of the '.fhirty-Third Degree, A. and A.,
Scottish Rite, of the Northern and Southern Jurisdictions of the
United States-the brand that is esteemed regular-has not undertaken
to, charter Symbolic Lodges in this country, and has preserved its
good standing in consequence, but it is not denied that it has assumed

of Mr. A. was received and referred. Regular meeting February 25

1?08, 1t was understood that Mr. A. would present himself for initiat10n. Lodge was opened and the order of business proceeded with.
When the order of business 'Work Conferring Degrees' was announced
by the Master, Brother F. moved as follows :
"'Worshipful Master, I have been informed that at our last regular·
meeting an illegal ballot was taken. I now move that the Master
appoint a committee of three (Past Masters, if possible) , to whom I
may report in private what has been told to me, the committee to
report to the Lodge.' The motion was seconded by Brother G. and
was carded by the Lodge. - The Master appointed as such committee
Brothers B, C, and D, to whom Brother F. reported as follows : 'I
have been told by Brother B, who acted as Senior Deacon at our
meeting of February 25th, that he saw, when removing the balls from
the box, that an unfavorable ballot had been cast.' Upon consulting
the code, the committee ruled that the candidate stood elected. Brother
B. then sta.ted to the committee that he had himself cast a black ball,
was sure that he had done so, and sure that he had seen it in the box
when removing the evidence of the ballot. The Master and Wardens
were then called, who stated that they are well satisfied that the
ballot was clear. The Master then postponed the conferring of the
deg ree until the ruling of the Grand Master should be obtained.
"Question.-Is the candidate elected and entitled to the degrees ~
if not, how shall we proceed?
''Answer.-No. We must take into consideration the intent of
the brother who stated that he cast the black ball. The very fact that
he stated he did so showed his intention, even if he might have made
the mistake and picked up a white ballot when he inrended to use a
black one, which, no doubt was the case, else the officers who examined
lhe ballot could not !;ave found it clear. The brother, however, having
declared that he cast a black ball, his intentions must govern my
decision, a nd I must declare the candidate rejected and he must wait
for the expiration ·of the statutory time befo re he can renew his.
application for the degr,ees.
·
"This decision is disapproved. The ballot once spread, inspected
and declared is final. It cannot be attacked at a subsequent meeting
by collateral evidence. It is the duty of the Maste r, upon declaring
the ballot, to destroy it; and upon the declaration of the Master, after
the inspection of the ballot, the candidate is elected and entitled to
the degrees, if the ballot is clear."

regalia, which can have no purpose except that of display. Ancient

Concerning physical qualifications, the Canadian Grand Lodges,
as a rule, follow the lead of the Grand Lodge of England in construing
liberally the question of physical qualification, the Grand Master of
Nova Scotia ruling this year that the loss of an eye did not disqualify
nor the fact that an applicant was "club-footed" did not disqualify.
Upon the question of dual membership the Grand Master held that
while dual membership in Lodges in the same jurisdiction was not
permissible, there was no objection to an applicant acquiring membership in a Lodge in Nova Scotia while retaining his memJ>ership in a
Lodge in another jurisdiction, and this decision was held to be good
law in Nova Scotia.
The Grand Master returns his thanks for the cordial support given
him during the year and for the honor bestowed upon him in his
re-election to the exalted station of Grand Master.
The reports of the Grand Secretary and Grand Treasurer show a
sound and wholesome financial condition of the jurisdiction, and the
reports of the various District Deputy Grand Masters disclose a con<l.ition of general prosperity.

for the degrees or for affiliation of any person engaged in manufacture

Ohio, 'which has been the storm-center in times past of clandestinism, is gradually emerging from that malignant visitation. The

Lodges in other jurisdictions against the danger of receiving <limits
issued by any of these extinct fraudulent Lodges, Grand Secretary
Bromwell in his report gives a complete list of these spurious organizations, to which list reference may easily be obtained.

The address of the Grand Master opens with felicitations upon the

the State ; its influence for good, its magnificent achievements and
present proud position amid the jurisdictions of the earth. He recalls
the names of Putnam, Corwin, Cass and Garfield; of Pattison, Hoadly, Hanna and McKinley, historic characters, each one of whom, clad
in the rough raiment of humility, had stood in darkness at the outer
door and craved permission .of a Lodge within that jurisdiction to be
brought to see the light.
A large number of dispensations for various legitimate purposes
were granted, and a large number refused for improper purposes.
New Lodges in Ohio are not formed with the speed and celerity that
is characteristic of many of our Western and Southern jurisdictions;
in twenty years, from 1889 to 1908 inclusive, but twenty-six new
Lodges were added to the list, although the membership of the jurisdiction more than doubled during the same period, advancing from
34,184 in 1889 to 72,339 in 1908, and as an example of the strength
of proposed new Lodges, the Grand Master states that the petition for
dispensation for Brenton D. Babcock Lodge at Cleveland. came to him
bearing an even hundred names, and Euclid Lodge, chartered in 1908,
has now 162 members.
Ohio enjoys a thorough system of Lodge supervision, the Grand
Master stating, as a result of a careful examination of the reports of
District Lecturers, that every Lodge in the State had been officially
visited and inspected during the year. Numerous proxies were issued
by the Grand Master for the purpose of placing . corner stones, and
m any special Emergent Communications of the Grand Lodge were held

MASONIC HOME.

There has been a movement looking to the acquisition of a Masonic
Home in Oklahoma, which was inaugurated several years since, and
while the establishment of the Home has not been actually consummated, the fund represented by cash in hand and securities and pledges
amounts now to about $45,000. In view, however, of the amalgamation of the two Grand Jurisdictions of Indian Territory and the Territory of Oklahoma into one Grand Jurisdiction, to be known as the
Grand Lodge of the State of Oklahoma, . it is reasonable to presume
that the Masonic Home funds heretofore belonging separately to the
two jurisdictions will be consolidated, with the result that there will be a
strong Endowment Fund for the support of one Home for the combined jurisdictions.
0

be said to hold the record. Five Special Communications of the Grand
Lodge were held for the purpose of laying corner stones of public
buildings.
Numerous special dispensations were granted for the conferring
of degrees without regard to the statutory time.
The Committee of Jurisprudence, in referring to this portion of
the Grand Master's address, states that the Grand Master should be
very careful in granting these special dispensations, and expresses
its opinion that the Grand Master should state in his address the
reasons for granting these dispensations. If there is any prerogative
that belongs clearly to the Grand Master, it is that of granting special
dispensations for conferring degrees out of 'time, and it is presumptuous of any committee of the Grand Lodge to question this prerogative
of the Grand Master, or to suggest to him the wisdom of his stating
to the Grand Lodge his reasons for the ex.ercise of this prerogative.

MASONIC HOME.

There is, as stated, a Masonic Home in Pennsylvania, incorporated
by Act of Assembly in 1871, and it has been in successful operation
as a Home for twenty-four years, and the Elkins Orphanage for Girls
has been in operatfon since 1906. The Masonic Home owns real estate
and funds of an aggregate value of more than a million dollars, and
it provides now for 92 men, 24 widows and 14 girls. It is supported
by do;,ations from individuals, from subordinate L edges and from the
Grand Lodge, the contributions from the subordinate Lodges and the
Grand Lodge since 1900 aggregating $68,630.35; and in addition to
this, it is worthy of mention that the charity dispensed by the Grand
L odge during the last eight years aggregated $76,204.75, and the
cha rity disbursements during the same period by the subordinate
Lodges, o f which records have been kept, amount to $215.339.10,
certainly a noteworthy achievement. But the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania is not satisfied with what has been accomplished, and now
that the indebtedness against its great Temple property at Filbert and
Broad streets, in Philadelphia, has been paid, and the income therefrom, which has for many years been devoted to the liquidation of
that obligation, released, it is .the purpose and intention to establish
a Central Home for the care, maintenance and education, and this
without fee o·r charge of any kind whatever, of a ll who are entitled to
the charitable regard of the fraternity in Pennsylvania, which Home
shall be under the direct supervision and exclusive control of the
Grand Lodge ; and about this Centfal Home, in which shall be merged
th(' present Masonic Home, to be located at some beautiful spot, some
rolling landscape, of which Pennsylvania can boast so many, it is the
intention ultimately to group the great charities of the Craft in the
Keystone State, including finally the Thomas Ranken Patton Masonic
Institution for Boys, when the fund for that purpose shall become
available in twelve yea rs from the decease of the founder-about ten
years from now-and when it will then amount to probably a million
and a half or two millions of dollars. ·T he project ha!! already been
approved by the Grand L odge, and the initial steps have already been
taken in what will probably become the greatest and most comprehensive Masonic charity in the world.

The Thirty-third .Annual Communication of the Most Worshipfu.l Grand Lodge of the Ancient and Honorable Fraternity of Free and

111 Freemason's Hall, in the town of Summerside, on Wednesday, the

The membership of the Grand Jurisdiction of Prince Edward
Island, is as large as a good sized Lodge in one of our American
cities. The total member~hip at the date of this Communication was
678, and at the Communication one year ago the membership was
668, showing a net gain during the year of 10. There are fourteen

is small, and the total membership less than 700, still the ·Lodges

has not summoned, durins the year preceding, any of the office;s of the
Grand Lodge, and that out· of the entire Jurisdictiou, only six have
been called to their last reward.
The Grand Master, during the year, personally visited everyone
of the Subordinate Lodges with a single exception, and his failure to
visit this Lodge, was the result of circumstances for which he was
in no way responsible.
Only three dispensations were issued during the year and no
decisions upon the Masonic law were asked for.
A substantial Benevolent Fund has been · accumulated, sufficient
to provide for the needs of the Jurisdiction. The income of the Grand
Lodge during the preceding year, amounted to about $1,200 and the
total assets to about $2,500. Reports are rendered by the various
District Deputy Grand Masters; by the Grand Lecturer; and by other
officers .from which it is gathered that the jurisdiction generally is in
prosperous condition.

Under the heading of Fraternal Dead, the Grand Master feelingly mentions the "passing onward" of John Rice Bellinger, Past

142

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Grand Master, which occurred on August 27, 1908. Brother Bellinger
was one · of the best and most favorably known Masons within the
jurisdiction of· South Carolina. He was a man of strong and decided
personality, fearlessly honest and uncompromising in all matters of
principle. The Grand Master also refers to the death during the year
of Rev. James Henry Thornwell, Past Grand Chaplain, and a man
greatly beloved throughout the jurisdiction.
The distinctive featt:re of Grand Master Michie's address is the
statement by him cf the position taken by all of the Grand Jurisdictions in the United States upon the question of "physical qualifications." South Carolina, as is well known, demands of her applicant
for initiation absolutely perfect physical qualifications, standing in a
class in this respect almost alone, although Texas may be placed
practically in the same category with South Carolina. Brother Michie's
purpose in assembling and placing before the Grand Lodge the law
and practices in all of the American jurisdictions is evidently to obtain a substantial modification of South Carolina's unreasonable insistence upon absolutely perfect physical qualifications. In other Words,
to conform in practice to the rule followed in most American jurisdictions of demanding only such a degree of physical perfection as will
permit the candidate to conform literally to all of the requirements of
the several degrees and to· be free of such maim or defect in his body
that may render him incapable of learning the art.
The laws of a few of our American jurisdictions upon this subject may with profit be quoted:
CALIFORNIA

"The person who desires to be made a Mason must be a man
having no maim or defect in his body that may render him incapable
of learning the art; and physically able to conform literally to what
the several degrees respectively require of him."
NEW YORK

"To earn his liviqg at manual labor, if necessary, without the
assistance of artificial limbs; and to perform all things necessary to
the receiving or giving cf work of Freemasonry," is all that is
required.
OHIO.

"A candidate for the degree of E. A. should be able physically,
as well as intellectually, of himself, and without external aid or assistance from another, to receive and impart all of the essentials of
Masonic. recognition.
"No one in this world is perfect in physical, or intellectual, or
moral qualifications. What degree of excellence in either or all of
these will fit ·a candidate for the degree of Masonry must be determined by the subordinate Lodge."

'PENNS YI, VANIA.

In a conversation which Grand Master Michie had with the Grand
Master of Pennsylvania, the latter personage informed Grand Master
Michie that he did not consider Pennsylvania quite so strict as South
Carolina. For instance, he stated that "the loss of a small piece of a
joint of the finger or toe" would not disqualify nor "a small sli~e off
the lobe of an ear."
UTAH.

Utah goes somewhat to the other extreme and may be considered
a "loose constructionist" of the Landmark concerning physical qualifications. This is what the Grand Secretary of Utah reports as the
law of his State upon the question of physical qualifications:
"We are broad-minded as to physic~! qualifications. Our Grand
Lodge, ever since its organization, did not take any stock in the old,
long. woriicut Landmark, which even the Premier Grand Lodge of
England has long since thrown in the rubbish of the Temple. With
t:s the heart counts, not the limb."
ENGL .~ND.

"The general rule in this country is to consider a candidate eligible
for elettion who, although n ot perfect in his limbs, is sufficiently so
to comply with and go through \he various ceremonies required in
the different degrees."
SCOTLAND.

Resolution of Grand Lodge, "physical disqualifications: the utterly
blind, and the deaf and dumb. Lodges are allowed to exercise their
own discretion as to the initiation of candidates who are mutilated in
or minus a limb."
Almost 'any old thing' looks good to Scotland.
Jn America the majority of the Grand Jurisdictions occupy a middle
ground of reasonable requirements, insisting that the candidate shall
he, to all intents and purposes, a physically sound man, but waiving
such technicalities as the loss of parts of certain joints and other
trifling defects that do not in any way interfere with the ability of the
candidate to gain a livelihood, if necessary, by physical toil, nor with
his ability t~ conform literally to the requirements of the several
degrees; . and the law of California expresses this middle ground as
succinctly and judicially as the law of any jurisdiction in America.
At the extreme position of st rict constructionalists are found the
States of South Carolina and Texas, and somewhat less so, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, and at the other extreme among the loose constructionalists is Utah, which has permitted the advancement of an Entered
Apprentice who, after initiation, met with the loss of both legs, one
·
above the knee and the other below the knee.

MASONIC HOME.

There is a Masonic Home in Tennessee for Widows and Orphans,
one of the most capably managed in the country. On January 1, 1909,
the beneficiaries numbered 131, divided as follows: 30 widows; 47
boys; 54 girls. The total expense of conducting the Home in 1908
was $12,558.01 and the average annual cost for each beneficiary was
$96.71, the lowest of any Home in the l.Jnited States. A school is
maintained at the Home, three teachers being employed therein, and
the instruction is as· advanced as the grammar grades of the ordinary
city schools. The Home has been able to accommodate all applicants
worthy of admission, a most happy condition, the Board reporting upon
this subject as foll ows :
"We are pleased to again report that there are no applications on
file. At no time during the year were any of the applicants kept
waiting, and it is gratifying to this Board t o have been so situated that
we could promptly meet every appeal for those deserving adt?ission."
The Home is supported by donations from Lodges and individuals
but principally by appropriations by the Grand Lodge, although an
Endowment Fund is in process of creation, and it is the hope that this
fund shall become ultimately so large that the income therefrom will
be sufficient to maintain the Home. The Endowment Fund is a matter
in which the Grand Lodge assumes an active and intimate contern
and at this Communication the following resolution was adopted:

Brother in each of the Subordinate Lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction
and, by personal letter, urge· upon him to place before the brethren

to use his utmost endeavors in securing donations thereto."
Zeal and co-operation of this kind will certainly in due time place
the Home on a self-supporting basis.

been charged with drunkenness while in attendance upon the last

rights and privileges of Masonry for one year." The Jurisprudence
Committee, presumably to protect the fair reputation of Tennessee
from the aspersion that might be cast upon it for appearing wholly to
condone drunkenness, even though mitigated by shooting, modified the
Grand Master's sentence to the extent of making the suspension indefinite, instead of for one year, and then to further effectually put
the stamp of their disapproval on just plain drunkenness unaccompanied
by shooting, they expelled another brother and printed his name in
large type in the proceedings for having partaken of liquor too freely
at this Communication.

MASONIC WIDOWS' AND ORPHANS' HOM'E.

In Texas there is at Fort Worth a Masonic Home for orphans and

the widows of Masons, one of the best in this country, and of which
the Grand Master in his address uses the following language :
"It gives me much pleasure to report ~hat the Home is in a prosperous condition. Texas Masons have a right to be proud of the (a~t
th1t in less than sixty years after the first Lodge had beep opened m
Texas they had established and were successfully conductt~g a Home
for the destitute widows and dependent orphans of their deceased
brethren.
"While the Grand Lodge of Texas is not a pioneer in this l~udable
work of benevolence, nor the first to undertake such ~n enterpnse1 ~he
stands in the front rank of her sister Grand Lodges m thus prov1dmg
for those dependent up.on the Fraternity.
.
"The Home has been in successful operation now for nine years,
and during that time several hundred boys ~nd izirls ha~e ~een. cared
for and provided not only with a home w.1th all. that 1.s .1mphed ~Y
the term but have had such literary and mdustr1al trammg as will
be most ~seful to them in after life."
The beneficiaries of the Home are now 15 widows, 106 girls, and
77 boys, a total of 198. No Masonic Home in this country manifests
a greater degree of s·uccess in gathering in the children tha~ ?oes ~he ,
Home in Texas, and no Home is doing better work, the admm1stratton
is exceedingly capable and the farm and dairy connected with the
Home is made to show a profit during the year of $2,352.61; something
almost unique among Masonic Homes. The cost of maintenance of
Home per capita is remarkably low-$149.34, and to this is added the
cost of maintaining the Home school for the ·children, $21.21, making
the total per capita cost $170.55, much less than the average of the
Masonic Homes in this Jurisdiction, even where children are sent

151

It is the policy of the Fraternity in Texas, as also in some other
States, J:o accumulate an endowment fund that shall render the Haine
in time self-supporting, and considering the fact that the Home has
only been in operation for nine years, a remarkably good St<;lrt in the
way of an endowment has already been made, the permanent fund now
amounting to $125,000.
The per capita tax for the benefit of the Home is apparently 50
cents. In California this tax is $1.CO and the result in many respects
are certainly less satisfactory.

The Grand Master's report is an able and comprehensive review
of his acl,ministration, and its consideration i11duces a concepti o1~ of the
magnitude of his Jur.isdiction, embracing the area of an empire and
containing more than 800 Subordinate Lodges :ind nearly 50.000 Master

other Grand Lodges and his especial notices of the death of Past
Grand . Master R:. W.'. Norton Moses and William Brawnlette, and
also the distinguished Brothers Cleveland .and Murchison.
The Grand Master very properly denounces as clandestine two socalled Masonic Lodges, one at Corpus Christi and the other at
Brownsville, the first claiming to work under a charter granted by
the Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico, the latter under grant from some
other foreign Grand Lodge. These claims are unquestionably spurious.
A representative of the Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico in the person
of Worshipful Brother Manhead, was present, before the Jurisprudence
Committee, and verified the fixed supposition that the claim of t!te
spurious body as to the posses11ion of a warrant from his Grand Lodge
was false. The twenty-two Lodges, charters for which were authorized,
at the last Communication, were regularly constituted, and dispensations were issued during th.e year to form nine new Lodges, and requests for· dispensations from nine others were refused.

152

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The following from the Grand Master's address on the subject of
profanity will win universal applause:
"The grand and noble men who, after they had won the independence of Texas, established Freemasonry in this State, were so
convinced of the degrading effect and influence of these vices that they
wrote it in the Constitution· of this Grand Lodge that 'The intemperate use of intoxicating driQks, gambling and profane swearing are
contrary to the principles of Masonry, and .it is the duty of each Lodge
to. punish any brother guilty thereof.' Yet it is not unusual to hear
a man wearing the emblems of Masonry utter the vilest oaths, even
in the presence of- young men. It is true that no Lodge in this jurisdiction would long tolerate a member who was known to be an
habitual drunkard or a gambler, but it is greatly to be regretted that
many Lodges are too tolerant of the more prevalent vice of profanity.
It is also true that the teachings and precepts of Masonry have done
mqch to purify society of the baneful effects of drunkenness and
g<tmbling, yet there is much to be done to rid the Lodges of th~se outwardly respectable men who habitually emit vile oaths. A Mason owes
it to himself and to the Fraternity to be clean in his language, as he
should be upright in his conduct and dealings with his fellow men, if
he would keep his white apron free from untempered mortar. For
the slave to the habit of drink we can have some compassion, and for
cne who, from want and poverty, is tempted to steal to satisfy his
hunger there is some excuse; but for the man claiming to be respectable, who is habitually guilty of using profane language, there is
neither paJliation nor excuse. Nothing can be more unbecoming a
Mason. It is a useless habit. It is coarse and vulgar, suited only
to the gambling house and the brothel. It is offensive to any person
of refined sensibilities. What man coufd tolerate or excuse profanity
in his wife or his mother? And yet, his wife or his mother have as
much right to swear' as he has; and, besides, she can sweat without
violating any obligation of Masonry. while he can not. What Lodge
would tolerate a member who would habitually use profane language
in the Lodge room? And yet the offense would be no greater for
him to violate his obligation in the Lodge room than in any other
respectable society, on the streets or in public places. Indeed, he has
the same right to emphasize his statements with profanity while the
Lodge is at labor as he has to interlard his conversation with vulgar
·Caths after the Lodge has been closed. That man who habitually
violates his obligation and ·the writteh Jaw of Masonry by the use
of profane language is out or place in a Masonic Lodge, and if he
will not separate himself from the vices, the Lodge ought, after fraternal warning, to separate him from Masonry by expelling him. Such
a man bririgs the Fraternity into bad repute with the better class of
citizenship. Let us cut loose from the profane swearer if he will not .
leave off his vicious habits. Let us purify our Lodges of all who thus
.daily and habitually violate their obligation."
The decisions of the Grand Master, aside from some local questions of disputed jurisdiction between Lodges were seven in number,
and with two exceptions were promptly approved by the Jurisprudence
Committee. Of the two disapproved, the Jurisprudence Committee has
this to say·:
"In Decision No. 2, the Grand Master holds, in effect, that the
law requiring an application for affiliation to lie over till • the next

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

153

stated meeting requires such application to lie over a full month
notwith.• tanding the Lodge may, under its By-Laws, hold more that~
one st:it~d meeting per month. We believe that applications for affiliation may be balloted upon at the next stated meeting of the Lodge,
though the time intervening be less than one month, this being, in
our opinion, a proper construction of Article 406, Digest of Masonic
Laws. But this applies to affiliations only, not to applications for degrees in Masonry.
"In Decision No. 5, the Grand Master rules that the casting uf two
black balls against a petition for initiation from one who was Jes!>
than twenty-one years old when the petition was received, operates
as a rejection of the candidate for two years. We hold the action of
the Lodge in receiving the petition of a person less than twenty-one
years old was void; that the Lodge acquired no jurisdiction of the
petitioner, and that the ballot thereon was an absolute nullity. The
candidate stands in the same attitude as if he had never petitioned the
Lodge at all."
Concerning the Grand Master and his report, the Jurisprudence
Committee utters the following· glowing encomium:
." We are profoundly impressed with the splendid dignity of this
able paper. We believe the administration of our Grand Master rices
not suffer by comparison with .those of his predecessors, and his benevolence and true Masonic spirit, manifest on every page of his address, ·
command our .most hearty sympathy and approval. He has upheld
and enforced the law in every instance, but with such kindness
of spirit that all must at once bow to the rod so firmly held in his
unerring hand. We extend to him our heartiest felicitations and
congratulations upon his successful work of leadership, and. indulge
the hope that he may be spared for many years of usefulness to the
Craft."

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

The Grand Master's address is a comprehensive stateme.n t of his
activities during the year. He mentions in a fitting manner the fraternal
dead of his own and other jurisdictions, a full report upon this subject
being rendered later during the Communication by the Committee on
Necrology.
~
The Grand Master refers to the temple debt and to the special per
capita assessment of 30 cents upon the membership, intended to provide
for the liquidation of the debt, but calls attention, however, to the very
slow process of payment through this small per capita assessment, so
large a portion of the assessment being needed to provide for the interest
upon the debt, and he recommends that this per capita be increased for
a period of three years to $1. This recommendation was referred to
the Committee on Finance, who recommended in lieu of the $1 p.er
capita assessment, an assessment of . 50 cents per member for three
years, and this recommendation upon being submitted to the Grand
Lodge was not adopted but further consideration in the matter was
postponed for one year, so that, notwithstanding the recommendations
of the Grand Master and the Finance Committee, no change whatever
was made concerning the per capita assessment for the liquidation of
the temple indebtedness.
The Grand Master is of the opinion that the Lodges do not exercise
su.fficient vigilance in purging themselves of members who become undesirable from a moral standpoint, and submitted for the consideration
of the Grand Lodge the following resolution, which met the approval of
the Jurisprudence Committee and was unanimously adopted:
··' Resolved, That whenever a member of a Subordinate Lodge or
a brother residing within this jurisdiction, by his miscond'uct, bri'ngs
himself into disrepute before the world and consequent shame upon
the Craft in general, it shall be the duty of the Junior Warden of the
Lodge to which he may belong or of the Lodge in whose jurisdictict?
he resides, to immediately cause charges to be preferred against him..
Nothing in this resolution shall be construed as r emoving the right
or duty of any Mason to prefer charges against a brother or as changing the existing rules of procedure in regard to charges and trials."

as 1727, and in Benjamin Franklin's diary is recorded the entry of his

MA$0NIC HOME.

There is in Virginia a Masonic Home which has hitherto been
under the management of a corporation, in a sense independent o{ the
Grand Lodge, hut by virtue of action taken at the last two Annual
Communications .of the Grand Lodge, the management of the Home
has been restored to the direct control of the Grand Lodge, and enhanced usefulness of the institution is expected to result therefrom.
The Home appears to be simply an· orphanage, and derives its revenue
from various sources; from appropriations by the Grand Lodge; contributions from Lodges, from individuals, etc. A movement which has
received official sanction has been inaugurated, looking to the creation
of an Endowment Fund for the benefit of the Home, but from such
information as can be gathered from. a perusal of the printed proceed~
ings of the Grand Lodge, it would appear that the Endowment Fund
project is in the nature of a private promotion scheme for the purpose
of yielding commissions to the promoter, rather than the concrete
expression on the part of the me111bership of a P.re-existing high ideal;
and if the mainspring of the proposed Endowment Fund is a mercenary
purpose to earn a profit for some one, it requires no gift of prophecy
to foretell its failure.
Virginia, known as the "Old Dominion," called also the "Mother
of Presidents'" home while they lived-of Washington, of Monroe
and Madison, of Thomas Jefferson and Patrick Henry, of John Marshall and Edmund Randolph-a State rich in romance, replete in heroic

The "official visitations" of the Grand Master were numerous

"There were more than two hundred· present in this old hall,
for many years the meeting place of the Grand Lodge of Virginia.
The old records were on exhibition, beginning in 1787 and including the

among them a sabre left in the anteroom by one of the many United

their way to Appomatox."
While no complaint has been heard of financial stringency in the

The "decisions," numbering fifty-five, were mostly of an elementary
or local character, and were all approved by the Jurisprudence Committee and Grand Lodge. A few that may be of interest' are as follows:
"That a Lodge cannot be 'called off' to meet at some future date.
Our ritual and ancient customs only provide for calling from fabor
to refreshment. To extend such a recess to some future date would
be violating Masonic custom and perverting the meaning of the words
used in our ritual."
·
Elementary it is true, but Lodges in California have been known
to do the same thing.
"That it was not proper that I endorse a plan of Lodges insuring
each a member's life in a so-called Masonic Mutual Insurance Company
for the benefit of the Masonic Home. I think the plan itself outside oµr system, and do not like the name Masonic attached to any
business venture, even when confined to and insuring only Masons.

It has been tried before, and has failed and resulted in scandal, as

Sound advice. Insurance schemes, masquerading under the name
"Masonic," or "fraternal," are always delusive, usually fraudulent, and
whether simply delusive or both fraudulent and delusive, they inevitably

"That a profane who has lost two joints of the fore-finger .of
the right hand is eligible."
This decision was made after submitting the question to the Grand
Lecturer, who held that he can comply, as he has since done, with

assistance." It would seem that no reasonable objection would be
urged against this decision, but opinions will differ as to its soundness,
which illustrates the fact that each jurisdiction in the matter of physical
qualification, or disqualification, is "a law unto itself."
"That a Lodge in Virginia, which was requested to confer degrees

approved and commended by the Grand Master of the Foreign Jurisdiction.''
Unquestionably right, but unusual.
In conclusion the Grand Master refers to the love and affection

esteem of his brethren, and that, when he has taken his place with

MASONIC HOME.

A fund for the establishment of a Masonic Home has been in
process of accumulation in Washington for a number of years past and
the actual realization of the Home is almost at hand. In referring
to this subject, the Grand Master, in his address, uses the following
language:
"I trust material progress will be made at this Session in the
matter ,of the establishment of a Masonic Home. I have found an
interest in the project wherever I have visited the Lodges and believe
the necessity for it is growing more imperative each year."
At this Communication a site for a Masonic H ome was offered,
but, not appearing suitable, was not accepted, and the choice of a site
was deferred for the present. The sum total of the fund now accumulated for the purpose of a Home is about $36,000.

sion of gratitude, the fact that the official ranks of the Grand Lodge
had not been broken during the preceding year by death.

eight in person, and one by deputy. H e mentions dispensations to
form ten new Lodges; eight within the State of Washington, and two
in Alaska, in which territory Washington already has several Subord-

During the Annual Communication, the Grand Lodge was enter~
tained and instructed by Worshipful Brother William H. Acuff, Grand
Orator, who delivered an eloquent and scholarly address, which upon
motion, duly seconded, was ordered printed in the proceedings.
The general theme of his address was the gradual improvement
in the world through the influence of all of those forces that work
together for good, among them the Masonic precepts of benevolence
and love, crystallized in the ideals of the Brotherhood of Man and
the Fatherhood of God.
The following quotation from his address will convey an idea of
its central thought:
"The world today has more of Love than ever before. Truth
stands forth brighter and clearer. Our hearts rejoice and are not
cast down. He who is tempted and falls finds sympathy and help all
about him, when he comes to himself and tries again; yet wrong
and cruelty still exist; the kindly ministration is often denied; the
cheering word remains unspoken. Many there are today in prison
and bearing the burden and shame of a wrong-doing, who would
not be there had the light of Love come to them.
"Love, sympathy-what power for Truth I How they bring sunshine into darkness, and joy and hope where only sorrow and despair
dwelt I The only creed that Masons are taught is Love, and it includes
all that is true and noble. Beneath its canopy all may find safety
from the blight or hatred and malice. Masonry has no controversy with
him of any faith, but she has supremest charity and an open heart
which yearns to embrace the weary wanderer from the ways of Truth
and Love. She has no weapon of war ; her mission is 'peace on earth,
good will toward men.' Love, Relief and Truth-by these subtle influences all her victories are won."

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The Quarterly Communication held April 23, 1908, was devoted
to a general summary of the work during the year, and especially t<>
the consideration and approval of the Articles of Recognition of the
·Grand Lodge of Western Australia by the Grand Lodge of Scotland.
The Grand Lodge of Western Australia had been ten years in forcing
this recognition which was only accorded by Scotland after the recognition of Western Australia as a Sovereign Masonic power, had
been accorded by nearly all of tRe Grand Lodges throughout the
world, and even in this final recognition, Scotland sought in a measure
to limit the sovereignty of the Grand Lodge of Western Australia
by the insertion of the following clause in the Articles of Recogni-.
tion, towit:
"Second : The Grand Lodge of Scotland shall not in future grant
charters for any new Lodge within the colony of Western Australia;
and the Grand Lodge of Western Australia shall not, nor shall its.
Grand Master, grant any warrant for any Lodge without the said
colony.''
The nerve of the Grand Lodge of Scotland in presuming to die-·
tate to any other sovereign Grand Lodge, where it shall, or shall
not, erect Lodges, is astonishing; and except for the fact that the
recognition of sovereignty is inconsistent with any limitation whatever, and therefore, this clause is of no effect, it would entail a con·
dition upon Western Australia that would render the Grand Lodge
less than sovereign, and, therefore, not entitled to a place among the..
independent Grand Jurisdictions of the world; but the effort of canny'
Scotland to cut off any possibility of the Grand Lodge of W estem
Australia chartering Lodges in outside territory, that' might conflict
with the desires of Scotland in that direction, must be considered a
nullity, and while it is altogether unlikely that Western Australia
will ever have any wish or desire to charter Lodges outside of its.
own territory, yet, if it should desire to do so, this attempted limitation
upon such right by Scotland, would properly be treated as of absolutely
no effect whatever.
From the reports of the various Grand Officers, the following
statistical information is obtained. The Grand Lodge was established
in 1900 with 33 Subordinate Lodges and a total membership of 2,000.
There are now 85 Subordinate Lodges with a total membership of
3,878, the Grand Lodge having more than doubled in number of subordinates during the past nine years, and nearly doubled in membership. The income of the Grand Lodge from dues, etc. amounts to·
about £2,000 annually and its total assets in excess of liabilities amounts
to about £13,000.
The jurisdiction is in a prosperous and healthy condition, anc?
now that its differences with Scotland have finally been settled, it~
no doubt, has entered upon a career of increased usefulness and power.

MASONIC CHARITY.

There is no Masonic Home in this jurisdiction, but in lieu thereof
the Grand Lodge has a standing committee known as "Committee on
Grand Lodge Education<!-! Fund," an appropriately high sounding
title for an altogether somnolent committee, whose functions appear
to be wholly defensive ; and inasmuch as no evidence of atmospheric
disturbance had penetrated their cyclone cellar, they were enabled
to emerge therefrom a sufficient length of time to report to the Grand
Lodge that not one farthing of the fund for the education of orphans
and children of Master Masons within this jurisdiction, entrusted to
their vigilance, had been expended; and that the Charity Tank, with
all that it contained, was absolutely intact. This is a slight advance
in the way of economy over the per capita charity tax of 10 cents in
vogue in another jurisdiction, and is respectfully recommended for
the ccnsideration of income savers. A careful scanning of the Grand
Treasurer's repcrt fails to discover the payment of so much as one

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

dollar for charity, but an item of $200 for Grand Lodge banquet is
clearly in evidence, as is also another item of $445.61, as commission
to the Grand Treasurer. On total disbursements during the year of
$6,427.42, the "commissions" to the Grand Treasurer, amount to about
seven per cent., and if the Grand Lodge inay not be viewed in the light
of an eleemosynary institution by the world at large, it may with
marked propriety be considered .from that standpoint by Grand Treasurer Myers.
If there was little or no opportunity for the Grand Lodge to manifest during the year its functions of benevolence, there was no ground
for complaint that it was not able in its department of operative
Masonry to display before the world its skill as a band of true mechanics, for, of the sixteen Special Communications of the Grand
Lodge held during the year, eleven were for the purpose of placing
corner stones (mostly of M. E. churches). It is to be hoped that a
silver trowel went with each ceremony.
The Grand Master fittingly refers to the death of Past Grand
Master Turner, and in accordance with the impressive custom of this
jurisdiction the Grand Lodge arose ~nd stood in silence during the
reading of the roll of the honored dead of other jurisdictions.
Dispensations to form three new Lodges were granted by the
Grand Master during the year, and charters were at this Communica.tion granted to the several Lodges so formed .
The Grand Master reports the failure of the masters of two of
the subordinate Lodges of his jurisdiction b pay attention to certain
repeated written communications from him asking for original papers,
until too late to be of service, to decide a question of disputed jurisdiction between two Lodges; and instead of disciplining the recalcitrant Masters, as he should have done, he reports the matter to the
Grand Lodge, where the Jurisprudence Committee, which had it under
consideration, gracefully sidestepped responsibility, sagely announcing
at the conclusion of its report, which carried no recommendation, "that
subordinate Lodges must be taught to respect the requests of the
Grand Master." This, under the circumstances, must have been very
terrifying.
Concerning perpetual penal jurisdiction over reje~ted candidates,
the Grand Master, whose sentiments on the subject will be very generally approved, has this to say:
"This Grand Jurisdiction adheres to the law of perpetual jurisdiction over rejected candidates. I do not believe the law is a good
one and certainly not in keeping with the progressive march of other
jurisdictions. It is not a landmark, but a custom which bas been
adhered to in a few Grand Jurisdictions only, and I believe it works
injury to the cause of Masonry."
There are only fourteen jurisdictions in the country that still
maintain the doctrine of perpetual penal jurisdiction.

The decisions of the Grand Master, ten in number-three of
them on questions of physical disability-:-are for the most part unimportant, and were all approved by the committee. Of the ten the
following is quoted :
"Concurrent Jurisdiction ~oes not give a b~other. of another Lodge
the right of franchise, but 1t ?oes clot?e h.1m . with the power . of
objection, and even if the ballot 1s clear his obJ ect1on shall be effective,
and has the same force as a cube and stands for one yea:r unless the
objection is removed. His right to object under the c1rc~mstances
should not be questioned, and ought to b~ held. as sacred ~s if he had
voted a ball or a cube. This is in keepmg with our obligation to a
brother.''
That may express the law as it exists in West Virginia. It is
not the law in California, where each Lodge is the sole judge of the
qualifications of its own members: and, while the objection of a member of another. Lodge which held concurrent jurisdiction before the
profane became a petitioner, would be entitled to and w~uld rec~ive
most careful and respectful attention, it would not, even 1f not withdrawn, have the effect of a cube, or black ball.
Fraternal recognition was extended to the Grand Lodge Valle de
Mexico, and denied to the so-called "Grand Logia Cosmos" of Chihuahua and the Grand Orient of Spain.
On~ of the chief attractions of the Annual Communication is a
banquet served on the evening of the first day of the session, at which
all members of the Grand Lodge are supposed to be present. The
customary annual appropriation of $200 heretofore made to ~over the
expenses of the function was found, on account of the growing mem- .
bership of the Grand Lodge, to be inadequate for the purpose, and,
that there might be no abridgment of the menu, the largess of the
Grand. Lodge was increased to $250. At this banquet the principal
orator appears to have been R.'. w:. Brother John D. Barnes, and
his address "My Impressions of Freemasonry," was thought so excel·
lent by th~ Grand Lodge that its introduction into the printed pro·
ceedings was ordered. The most profound impression, · s~ he states,
is the idea conveyed to him that the legend of the Third Degree
is a symbol of the resurrection of the physical body, "these v~ry
bodies " as he explains it. He will find few who have any such 1mpressi~n; the symbol most certainly has a spiritual significance only.

He recounts the wonderful growth of Masonry throughout the
world, and sounds the one note of warning in times of great prosperity
especially to be heeded, "Guard well the Outer Door." Commenting
on the statement of one of the reviewers that, in his judgment, the
Roman Catholic Church will soon remove the ban from Masonry,
Brother Howard sententiously remarks :
"You may rest assured, my brother, that when the Roman Church
abolishes the confessional, then, and not until then, will it remove
the ban on Masonry. And as to its 'misconception of the facts,' why,
bless you, the Romanist is as well posted in regard to the aims and
practices of Freemasonry in America as any of us are."
Under the caption "Canada," he quotes a decision of the Grand
Master concerning restoration of members suspended for. non-payment
of dues:
"If a member suspended for non-payment of dues tenders the
amount of arrears, and all other amounts owing to the Lodge, he mustbe restored. But charges may be preferred against him for any other
offense of which he may have been guilty, either before his suspension
or during his suspension, when he may be tried just as if he had·
never been suspended.
"I approve" of this ruling. It seems to me much more equitable
brotherlv and charitable than our West Virginia law requiring ~
two-thirds vote to reinstate."
He quotes, with apparent approval, the following decision of the
Grand Master of Arizona :
"Each Grand Lodge, as well as its Subordinate Lodges,· are resl?o'?sible for t~e indigent of its ow~ Jurisdiction and that this Jurisd1ct1on holds 1t to be good Masomc law that when a Subordinate
Lodge is unable to care for its needy, that the Grand Lodge should
supply the required relief."
.
And while the Pacific Coast, which is the Mecca of the physically
decrepit from all over the world, and, in consequence thereof, tens
of thousands of dollars are appropriated every year by Pacific Coast
Grand Lodges for the relief of sojourning brothers, will concur in
the decision, yet the weight of Masonic opinion generally will doubtless
disapprove the proposition, as Squinting toward the so-called "contractural relation."

There is no Masonic Home of any kind in Wisconsin, and the
total expense by the Grand Lodge for charity and charged against
the Charity Fund, which is maintained in lieu of a Masonic Home,
was, during the preceding year, $2,225, rather economical, it is true,
and certainly less expensive, as is affirmed by some Wisconsin authorities, than Masonic Homes. The Charity Fund reservoir which now
contains $6,051.38, is replenished by a yearly per capita tax of ten cents
upon the membership, and it is believed, even with no material increase
in the dimensions of the spillway, that the raging torrent of beneficence that surges in from the Grand Lodge will not endanger the
structure.

MASONIC HOME.

The first preliminary step toward the ultimate acquisition of a
Masonic Home in Wyoming was taken at the last Annual Communication, when a per capita assessment of 50 cents was voted for the
purpose of creating a fund which shall ultimately be used for the
purpose of establishing a Home, and in the appointment of a committee
for the purpose of assuming full direction of the movement.
The following is the first report of the Masonic Home Committee:
"To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Wyoming:
"Your Committee on Masonic Home beg leave to report that the
fund accumulated so far amounts to $1,634, which we think is a
splendid showing for the first year's work, and we wish to thank
the Subordinate Lodges for their generous response to this worthy
cause, and heartily recommend that we continue to collect fifty cents
per capita and placed to the credit of the Home fund in the hands
of the Grand Treasurer.
"Fraternally submitted,
"M. R. JOHNSON,

"C. H. 'towNsl!ND,

"Committee."

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

The address of the Grand Master is a comprehensive statement
of his official actions during his occupancy of the Oriental Chair of
the Grand Lodge. His activities consisted in constituting the L6dge
to which a charter was granted at the last Annual Communicatio"n; in
issuing dispensations to form three new Lodges; in presiding at several
Special Communications of the Grand Lodge for the purpose of laying
corner stones of public buildings; in granting special dispensations for
various proper purposes ; and especially in a large number of official
visits by him to subordinate Lodges throughout his jurisdiction. He recounts the fact that in making his visits he traveled thirtyfive hundred miles, four hundred and sixty-eight of which were by
stage; and to convey an idea of the immense area of his jurisdiction,
and of the extremely large territory embraced within the particular
jurisdiction of individual Lodges, he dtes the fact that the territory
belonging to· one Lodge is greater, by three thousand square miles,
than the entire State of New Hampshire; or, by more than four
thousand square miles than the State of Massachusetts; and that
another subordinate Lodge has a territory as large as Delaware,
Rhode Island and Connecticut combined; and that, territorially speak-

The usual rule in most jurisdictions is to permit an appeal to . the

"Statement.-A Brother petitioned a Lodge for affiliation. After
the ballot had been taken the Master asked the J. W. how the ballot
stood in the South, but before receiving an answer he was informed
by the S. W. that it was fair in the West. H aving examined the ballot
himself, he stated that it was light in the East and declared the brot.her
elected to membership in the Lodge. At the next Regular Communication the minutes were approved without protest, but before the close
of the Lodge the J. W. rose and stated that the ballot at the previous
meeting was dark in the South. A brother also arose and stated that
he cast a black ballot.
"Question.- Is the brother duly elected to membership?
"Answer.- 'Phe Master having declared the brother elected to
membership and there having been no objections to the ballot when
the officers of the Lodge declared it white, no question can arise at
any subsequent meeting, nor can the ballot be set aside by the Master,
Grand Master or Grand Lodge. (See Section 84, G. L. By-Laws.)"

FORJiIGN CORRJiSPONDJiNCJi.

The report on Foreign Correspondence is by the Right Worshipful
William I. Kuykendall, Grand Secretary. Brother Kuykendall's reports
are universally conceded to be excellent and his discrimination in the
selection of material for quotation and observation of a high order.
The following quotation from his "Conclusion" will be most heartily
seconded by many :
"With the Country filling up with clandestine individuals and
bodies of that character and suspended and expelled Masons, and
frauds and dead-beats parading around as members in good standing, many Grand Lodges now require that all visitors not personally
vouched for must present documentary evidence or not be allowed to
visit. To this a reviewer here and there says: 'It is an infringement
on the rights of every brother who presents himself and is willing
t o prove himself in the good old way which should not be departed
from.' One answer to this is, that a clandestine or a suspended or
expelled Mason and others who travel about fleecing Masons and
Lodges, care nothing fo r the test oath and the .good old examination
in which they are exceptionally proficient. Another is that our brothers
holding that view seem oblivious of the fact that railroads and close
proximity of Lodges have changed the question of visiting as in many
other things from the time when Lodges were far removed from each
other and Walker's line was often about the only means of travel.
Then it did not pay frauds and dead-beats to carry on their nefarious
work and said oath and examination was all sufficient as it was
nearly certain that a visitor was what he represented himself to be,
but now Lodges and Masons have to be constantly on their guard
against the army of frauds who have determined to beat their way
through the world without work and at the expense of those who
do, and recently many of our Jurisdictions have been invaded by degree
peddlers establishing Lodges for the money there is in such fraudulent
work; all this combined has .m11de the use of documentary evidence an
absolute necessity. Two or three other reviewers have objected to
its use on the ground that 'it is simply an agency for collecting dues
and should not be adopted for that reason.'
"Now the fact is, we do not believe one of its advocates ever
thought of its being used for that purpose. That, however, is one
of the very best reasons why it should be adopted everywhere, for
it would save many from being suspended for non-payment of due~,
probably most of whom have bec0me residents of other Jurisdictions
when so suspended. Others object on the ground that 'other societies
use documentary evidence, therefore, Masonry should have nothing to
do with it.' If they keep their members and Lodges from being the
prey of the multitude of frauds and dead-beats, except in cases where
they fail to insist upon such evidence, then there can be no better
reason fo r its adoption. Other equally weak objections have been urged,
when if every Jurisdiction would adopt, adhere to and get its members

182

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

to understand that without" such evidence they cannot be examined,
much less be admitted within the Tyled Lodge as now required in
many Jurisdictions, there would soon be no trouble about beneficial
results, and many frauds would have to find another occupation."
M. P. Wheeler (Caspar), Grand Master.
W. L. Kuykendall (Saratoga), Grand Secretary.

CONCLUSION.
In the foregoing reports, · some attention has been given to the
matter of Masonic Homes, and a certain amount of information pre·
sented upon -what is probably the most important practical question
with which American Grand Jurisdictions have to deal. The idea of
Masonic Homes is very generally approved, and such jurisdictions as
have them not, are, as a rule, acquiring them. Massachusetts, Mississippi and Montana have, during the past year, opened their Homes,
and Alabama and Arkansas have their Homes under way, and advanced to a degree that indicates completion for the reception of beneficiaries within a year. North Dakota appears to be the only State
that, after having entered upon the idea of acquiring a Home, abandoned the project. The Jurisdictions that have achieved a marked
degree of success in the management of their Homes, and whose
methods may be worthy of consideration by other Jurisdictions, whose
experiences have been less favorable are Kentucky, Tennessee, Texas,
Missouri, and for an example of a Home simply for orphans, North
Carolina is pre-eminent. Kentucky and Illinois have seperate Homes
for the aged and the children; and Pennsylvania, when its plans are
fully consummated, will have the most comprehensive system of Homes
and schools of any Jurisdiction in the world.
The average yearly per capita cost of maintenance for H omes of
a general character is about $200, although the cost in Kentucky is only
$127, and in Tennessee about $96 and the average cost in the North
Carolina Home, where more than 300 orphans are sheltered, is less
than $80 yearly for each beneficiary.
The following lists of Jurisdictions that have Homes (either for
one or all of the several classes 0 1£ beneficiaries) ; of those that have
none; of those that have Homes in process of establishment; and of
those that have approved the idea, but have not as yet adopted definite
plans, may be of general interest.
